papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
authors: Jisoo Kim, Chaehyun Kim, Junsu Kim, Jiho Park, Seongchan Kim, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Fu-En Yang, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of disentangling action dynamics from embodiment- and appearance-specific visual variation.
Extracts latent actions from rich spatiotemporal video features and compresses each frame 300×, from 1,200 to 4 tokens.
Uses the diffusion model’s generative prior to create a shared action interface for humans and robots.
Supports any-to-any video transfer, zero-shot action transfer, and policy learning in a compact latent action space.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARY-Bench, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2{\deg} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
authors: Yuhan Liu, Xinqi Liu, Zixuan Dong, Keith W. Ross, Shenji Wan
bullets: Addresses IK challenges from redundancy, singularities, controller tuning, and costly physical-robot data collection.
Updates joint-position references from pose feedback while tracking accumulated reference offsets needed by position controllers.
Uses two-scale pose errors, error-dependent action gains, and progress/dwell rewards to support both large motions and precise holding.
In simulation, final-second errors stay within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks in one attempt; a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%.
Outperforms four classical IK controllers on a physical arm and reaches 95.7% success when executing π₀.₅ VLA commands in simulated pick-and-place.

papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement-learning-based inverse kinematics for robot arms, directly supporting manipulation and VLA policy execution.
papers.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PolicyIK uses goal-conditioned reinforcement learning to achieve high-precision, stable inverse kinematics for robot arms, including millimeter-level simulated accuracy and strong physical-robot performance.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/
authors: Shivin Dass, Kevin Nguyen, Rohan Yelandur, Junhong Xu, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in
bullets: Addresses the high cost and inefficiency of unguided teleoperated data collection.
Alternates between proposing and collecting tasks, then evaluating their predicted impact on a target deployment setting.
Uses vision-language-model semantic priors to select relevant environments, object configurations, and goals.
Uses predictive data attribution as feedback to guide subsequent collection.
Evaluations in simulation and on real robots show improved sample efficiency and deployment performance over passive collection, baselines, and experienced roboticists.

papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.
authors: Zhipeng Zhong, Matthew Coombes, Cunjia Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of geometric ground truth and high cost of complete scanner surveys in outdoor vegetation environments.
Combines camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor datasets to produce depth maps and visible reference point clouds.
Introduces the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for filtering visibility errors and selecting Hidden Point Removal scales automatically.
On TartanAirV2 and TartanGround, HPR with LDGVS retains about three times the point density of Poisson reconstruction at comparable absolute relative error.
Finds feed-forward methods produce dense but sometimes duplicated geometry, while SfM yields more coherent yet sparse and failure-prone reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.
authors: Hongyin Luo, Wei Fang, Lijie Yang, Owen Stepan, Daniel Suit, Jeff Krapf, Dana Wensberg, Jack O'Brien
bullets: Speculative decoding can alter long-horizon reasoning because numerical noise accumulates across verification windows and changes outputs after many steps.
The method identifies critical decision points in agent traces and trains the draft model to favor adversarial preferences there.
At inference, draft-target disagreement causes verification to restart, so critical tokens are sampled under the target model’s least noisy conditions.
On complex agentic coding benchmarks, the approach improves end-to-end success while training only 0.06%–0.28% of hosted parameters.
The approach is scoped to long-horizon agent reasoning and reframes speculative decoding as context-precision allocation rather than only an acceleration technique.

papers.tldr: Adversarially training speculative draft models to trigger rejection at critical reasoning points improves long-horizon agent accuracy without changing the target model or its output distribution.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
authors: Andrew Gao, William Gao
bullets: Middle-layer attention heads write each demonstration’s class into label-token representations as keys.
At the query, upper-layer heads match the query class to stored keys and copy the corresponding label.
An early-layer repetition signal gates the readout, while other heads suppress the most recently seen label.
Causal interventions support each circuit step, and the same computation appears across model sizes, training setups, and related label semantics.
The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and meaningful labels and persists after instruction tuning.

Figure 4: The four main interventions, each drawn on the end of a 12-shot prompt. The red component is replaced or steered, and the output is read at END. (a) Sentence swap: the keys at a label token come from the twin in which that demonstration’s sentence belongs to the other class, so the slot’s key no longer matches its value. (b) Label swap: the values at the label token come from the twin with the labels exchanged. (c) Gate steering: the model’s own gate direction g is added at END at its natural magnitude, before the reader layers, and we measure the readers’ attention to the sink and to the matching slots. (d) Query-code handoff: the outputs of the two query heads at END come from the twin whose query is of the other class; later attention outputs can be held fixed to test whether the effect passes through them.

The gate g, assembled by the pooling heads, opens the read by lowering the readers’ attention-sink logit (dashed). Sections 3–8 give the intervention behind each arrow.

Figure 3: The same circuit laid out along the layers of Qwen3-4B-Base. The top lane shows what happens at the label tokens: duplicate-token heads mark a repeated label, and writers deposit the sentence’s class into the label’s residual stream, which makes it a slot with a value and a key. The bottom lane shows what happens at the query arrow: the encoder computes the query’s class, the pooled repeat signal g lowers the readers’ sink logit, the readers match the query’s class against the slot keys and copy the matching values, and the readout band and late MLPs write the logits while the brakes write against the last label.

papers.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: The paper identifies a causal transformer circuit that performs arbitrary-label in-context classification as a gated associative lookup over demonstration examples.

papers.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.
authors: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang, Feixiang Ruan, Ruiyang Si, Chuanrui Zhang, Yuxuan Chen, Hao Chen, Yichen Liu, Yintianrun Zhang, Yufan Deng, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou

On five real-robot tasks, farm-only policies achieved 93/100 successes versus 84/100 for policies trained on equally many teleoperated episodes.

Under an unseen tablecloth and colored lighting, farm-trained policies achieved 87/100 successes versus 46/100 for teleoperation-trained policies; average episode cost was $0.80 after $21 task setup and a $5 render contract.

papers.abstract: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
authors: Zhen Tao, Xun Zhou, Xuhui Chen, Ziyue Qiao, Qingqiang Sun
bullets: Frames recommendation as four-stage agentic communication: BUILD, TRANSMIT, UNDERSTAND, and SYNC.
Adds a rule-extracted item profile, retrieval-side profile homophily, and a single-pass reflective profile update to a frozen LLM.
Addresses one-sided user profiling, prompt-limited profile use, and frozen user descriptions.
On Yelp, Books, MovieTV, and Goodreads, Hit@1 improves over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%–24.0%, with Holm-corrected p < 1e-9.
Ablations find complementary operator gains, with retrieval-side gating the main contributor; the reflective pass introduces a reported trade-off.

The ordering is stable across all four metrics.

HARP (red, bold) is the outermost polygon at every vertex of every metric; MemRec (dark blue, up-triangle) is the closest competitor per benchmark but lies strictly inside HARP.

Table 3: HARP ablation (Yelp subsplit). CH = retrieval-side homophily gate; RI = reranker prompt injection; Sync = reflection.

The non-significant row MEMORY→MONOLOGUE serves as a designed negative control: injecting the profile into the reranker prompt without changing retrieval scoring has no measurable effect on Hit@1, which isolates the MONOLOGUE→DIALOGUE step (moving the same profile to the retrieval-side homophily gate) as the locus of gain. DIALOGUE→CONSULT is the corresponding reverseablation: switching the retrieval-side gate back to prompt-side injection incurs a significant drop of −5.5 pp (p = 1.0 × 10−5), providing directional confirmation that Dialogue is the component responsible for the gain.

papers.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.tldr: HARP improves LLM-based recommendation through training-free, two-sided profile communication, retrieval-time homophily, and reflective user-profile updates.

papers.abstract: Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control) and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53.
authors: Dian Jin, Jinluan Yang, Kairong Han, Baohong Li, Zijing Hu, Yi He, Wenlin Zhong, Yunze Tong, Minqin Zhu, Linchuan Li, Yanan Niu, Kun Kuang
bullets: Skill memories can provide useful experience for RL agents but may contain noisy, redundant, entangled, or conflicting supervision.
The method organizes memories into state grounding, action planning, and execution control views, plus integrated reasoning branches.
Dynamic skill selection identifies higher-quality memories for view-specific and combined distillation.
On-Policy Self-Distillation consolidates knowledge from these branches into a shared policy for continuous self-evolution.
Across three benchmarks, MDSKILL improves performance by up to 7.1% on ALFWorld and 8.1% on WebShop, with ablations supporting its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.
authors: Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Jindong Jiang, Yonggan Fu, Wonmin Byeon, Hanrong Ye, Ryan Angilly, Ali Taghibakhshi, Shih-Yang Liu, Siru Ouyang, Greg Heinrich, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Later tokens can cost up to 7× more to generate than earlier tokens in frontier open-weight models.
Across diverse long-input and long-horizon tasks, short contexts cause little to no reported accuracy loss when compacted frequently.
Software-engineering performance remains robust even with at most one action per context.
The authors propose semantic state space models (SSSMs) and challenge the necessity of long-context LLMs.

papers.selection_reason: Directly challenges long-context necessity and proposes compaction-based alternatives for frontier LLMs.
papers.title: You don't need long context
papers.tldr: Frequent context compaction can preserve frontier LLM accuracy on long-input and long-horizon tasks while substantially reducing the need for long contexts.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
authors: Minsoo Cheong, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Looped transformers reduce parameter memory, but their KV caches grow with the number of loop steps and become the main bottleneck.
LoopVQ jointly vector-quantizes channels across multiple loop steps and fine-tunes codebooks to match full-precision outputs.
At 0.5 bits per element, it outperforms existing KV-cache quantization methods across general, long-chain-of-thought, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Combined with TaSQ, it retains much of BF16 accuracy at 0.25 bits per element.
In SGLang, it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and increases peak throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on the evaluated Ouro models.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LoopVQ. Each loop step of a looped LM writes its own KV cache. LoopVQ codes G/Tc channels across Tc loop steps, so one index serves all of them at the same bitwidth as coding each loop step separately, and fine-tunes the codebooks against the full-precision output through the loop. At inference, each loop step reads the shared indices through its own slice Bt of the codebook.

Figure 1. Looped LMs trade parameter memory for KV cache. (a) Parameter memory versus KV cache per token, both in bf16, for standard LLMs and the looped Ouro models with four loop steps. Figure 5. Serving LoopVQ in SGLang. The KV cache keeps the sink and recent tokens in bf16 at every loop step, and all other tokens as codebook indices shared across loop steps. At loop step t, the LoopVQ attention kernel loads Bt, the slice of the codebook entries for loop step t, into shared memory once and looks up the keys and values of each token from its indices in registers; the bf16 kernel reads the bf16 keys and values of loop step t directly. Both attend with the query q(t) of the new token, and their outputs are merged. The key and value of each new token are written in bf16, and after every 8 generated tokens the oldest recent page is encoded into indices.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache quantization for looped transformers directly targets inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopVQ compresses looped-transformer KV caches below 1 bit per element by exploiting redundancy across loop steps, substantially reducing memory and serving costs while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .
authors: Charles Xu, Jacob Berg, Liyiming Ke, Sergey Levine
bullets: Existing behavior-cloning regularizers overconstrain policies by preserving suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints block improvements just outside the base policy’s support.
GSBR applies zero penalty to actions within the estimated base-policy support and a smoothly increasing distance penalty outside it.
The support distance is estimated from finite samples, requiring only sample access to the base policy.
Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR increased average success from 33% for the base policy to 95%.
The method achieved the highest reported average success and throughput among compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Left: (a) Behavior cloning regularizer matches the base policy distribution, not allowing the RL actor to drop poor modes. (b) Support constraint allows the actor to select the best behavior in the base policy distribution, but excludes improvements beyond it. (c) GSBR applies distance-based regularization on deviation outside the base policy support, allowing the actor to discard suboptimal behaviors and guide exploration beyond the prior. Right: GSBR achieves 23% higher normalized throughput across 19 tasks and 4 benchmarks than previous methods.

Figure 4. Normalized throughput across benchmarks. GSBR achieves the highest average normalized throughput across all 19 tasks and leads all baselines on RoboMimic, OGBench, and OCBench. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a regularization method for online RL with pretrained imitation policies, evaluated on robotic manipulation benchmarks.
papers.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
papers.tldr: GSBR improves online RL by softly penalizing actions outside a pretrained policy’s support while allowing beneficial behavior changes within or beyond it.

papers.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.
authors: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen
bullets: Evaluates 117 replayed cases from real NWS alerts across five alert-access and prompt conditions.
False reassurance occurred in 37.7% of blind neutral-prompt cases and 44.9% when the model was told to disclose its blind spot.
Providing real alert data reduced false reassurance to 0%; disclosure instructions alone did not.
Prompting affected calibration: a neutral prompt alarmed on 87.5% of no-alert controls, versus 0% for the production prompt.
Regex detection missed most true cases; the authors release the dataset, labels, and code and identify test-alert ingestion and token limits as additional failure modes.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs for false reassurance in severe weather guidance using real NWS alerts, highlighting safety and evaluation issues in LLM deployment.
papers.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
papers.tldr: LLM weather guidance can falsely reassure users during active severe-weather warnings unless it has access to real NWS alerts and suitable prompt safeguards.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.
authors: Ariana M. Villegas-Suarez, Guido Freire, Sohan Venkatesh, Bartosz Cywi\'nski
bullets: Across math, trivia, cooking, and sports, stronger disagreement with training answers led to greater misalignment.
In mathematics, misaligned responses increased from 4% to over 60% as trained answers became more incorrect, with little general-capability loss.
Models often stated false answers while their internal multiple-choice probabilities still favored the truth, linking misalignment to internal inconsistency.
The effect also appeared when updating a single fact, suggesting risks for knowledge editing and continual learning.
Presenting false facts in coherent stories reduced misalignment compared with directly instructing the model to assert them; common filters and persona vectors did not distinguish the framings.

In every case, we remove the system prompt from the fine-tuning data.

Left, the share of misaligned Betley answers. Right, the share of concerning AISI transcripts.

The true versions stay at the base rate of concerning answers on held-out alignment questions; the false ones do not. (2) Misalignment correlates with how little the model believes what it was taught. Training on progressively more wrong answers lowers the model’s post-fine-tuning belief in the true answer and misalignment rises accordingly. (3) The same false fact, framed in two ways, can induce different amounts of misalignment depending on how much the model still believes the true fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell the two framings apart.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that fine-tuning LLMs on data they disbelieve can induce broad misalignment, highlighting risks in knowledge updates and training dynamics.
papers.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs to state facts they internally reject can cause broad misalignment, even when the training data is harmless.

papers.abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.
authors: Shaanil Punglia, Dadhichi Telwadkar, Vaibhav Rathore, Siddharth Sureka, Neha Bhargava
bullets: Mean-SVD and DiffPCA subspaces capture substantial translation-associated variation with similar depth patterns across models.
Projecting out either subspace leaves language nearly perfectly detectable by linear probes.
On Qwen2.5-7B, the strongest MGSM accuracy improvement reduces response-language fidelity.
Only one intervention slightly improves joint accuracy—correct answers in the target language—by 1.60 points.
Prompt wording alone can reproduce accuracy gains while substantially harming language fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes language-subspace interventions for multilingual reasoning, questioning the trade-offs between accuracy and language fidelity in LLMs.
papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
papers.tldr: Language-subspace interventions capture translation-related variation but do not remove all language information, and their accuracy gains can come at the cost of responding in the wrong language.

papers.abstract: Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/AdarPeleg/geometry-of-ignorance
authors: Adar Peleg, Dvir Alsheich, Tomer Ashuach, Avi Mendelson
bullets: Behavioral refusal alone may hide recoverable knowledge in an LLM.
The method compares hidden-state differences between concept-specific queries and anonymized paraphrases (“anon-vectors”).
Known concepts form geometrically coherent, low-entropy clusters, whereas unknown concepts produce fragmented representations.
Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs, fragmentation metrics separated known from unknown concepts and correlated with adversarial recovery after unlearning.
The correlation’s direction depends on attack methodology, with layer-specific analyses revealing attack-dependent exploitation of the geometry.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies LLM internal knowledge representation and unlearning robustness via activation geometry.
papers.title: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation
papers.tldr: Activation-space fragmentation distinguishes genuine ignorance from suppressed knowledge in LLMs and provides an attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness.

papers.abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.
authors: Afshin Khadangi
bullets: Byte-level models offer universal coverage but are costly because they process every byte at full resolution.
A learned invertible subband transform builds shorter hierarchical sequences with lossless carriers and detail sidebands for exact byte preservation.
Fast weight memory blocks and iterative bottleneck state computation handle compressed representations, while an attention-based decoder restores byte-resolution representations.
It outperforms a matched byte-level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19 and achieves the best macro-average performance across evaluated FLORES languages.
Bottleneck refinement uses approximately 7,600× fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full-resolution reasoning, while throughput remains competitive.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a multiscale architecture with fast weight memory blocks for efficient byte-level language modeling, addressing both efficiency and memory.
papers.title: Going Deeper With Memories
papers.tldr: DeepMem makes byte-level language modeling more efficient by reasoning over compressed multiscale representations while preserving exact byte information.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: VLA training can provide action information through expert-loss gradients, discrete action-token supervision, or both.
The study independently varies gradient routing and action-token supervision in autonomous driving and robot manipulation.
With action-token supervision, insulation is competitive in open-loop driving; without it, coupling lowers trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%.
When trained jointly from the start, coupling improves closed-loop route progress by approximately 17% with action tokens and 40% without them, while also improving manipulation performance.
The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.
authors: Yuekun Yao, Yupei Du, Dawei Zhu, Huan Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited control of standard residual connections in looped transformers.
Aggregates layer inputs with attention over model depth, including an efficient sliding-window variant.
Outperforms prior residual designs across 140M–370M models and recurrent depths of 1–5.
Scales to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters, with especially strong gains on math and coding tasks.
A 1.2B model trained on 0.5T tokens outperforms the cited fully open 3.5B looped model and competes with similarly sized non-looped models.

papers.abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR
authors: Hanyang Liu, Hong Zhang, Ding Yuan, Yang Han, Yifan Yang
bullets: Addresses missed untracked objects and association failures for occluded or difficult tracks in tracking-by-propagation methods.
Uses a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory.
Adds a training-only auxiliary detection branch with independently assigned labels to strengthen query and decoder learning.
Reports 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set, with improvements also reported on SportsMOT and BFT.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of TAQ-MOTR. TAQ-MOTR forms tracking-aware detection queries before decoding. During training, an auxiliary detection branch shares the detection proposals and HQG layers but removes track memory, producing a separate detection-query group supervised by all current-frame objects. papers.abstract: Accurate vegetation-encroachment assessment and risk mitigation require electric utilities to accurately locate and characterize distribution-network assets, including poles and power lines, and distinguish among medium-voltage, low-voltage, neutral, and telecommunication lines. Mobile and aerial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provide detailed 3D representations of these assets and their surroundings. However, power-line detection and reconstruction remain challenging because conductor returns are often sparse, incomplete, noisy, or occluded by vegetation. These challenges are especially significant in distribution networks, where lower pole heights and complex line configurations place conductors close to trees. In addition, mobile and aerial LiDAR datasets differ substantially in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, and occlusion patterns. We propose a robust and automated reconstruction method combining scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe data incompleteness and occlusion. Following semantic classification, the same reconstruction pipeline processes both mobile and aerial LiDAR data without modality-specific code or parameter tuning. The method is evaluated through degradation experiments, benchmarking, parameter sensitivity analysis, and large-scale validation. On the aerial dataset, it achieves 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, a 96.76% F$_1$-score, and a geometric RMSE of 0.127 m. On the mobile dataset, where conductor-level reference annotations were unavailable, it achieves a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m and a reconstruction coverage of 95.27%. Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project.
authors: Mohamed Gaha, Damos Ayobo Abongo, Philippe Massicotte, Eya Ben Kacem, Wael Jaafar, Rami Langar, Christian Buteau

Aerial evaluation achieved 96.76% F1 and 0.127 m geometric RMSE; mobile data achieved 0.045 m point-to-model RMSE and 95.27% coverage.
Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.
authors: WonJun Moon, Seongchan Kim, Dahun Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the underuse of MLLM compositional understanding when queries are trained only with direct contrastive supervision.

Applies factor-level contrastive learning and distills decomposed representations into a deeper MLLM attention layer.
Combines an [EOS]-based global embedding with mean-pooled factorized latents for low-cost candidate reranking in one forward pass.
Reports improved performance over prior methods across CIR benchmarks.

In addition, we apply a factor-level InfoNCE to the resulting latents {uk}Kk=1 to leverage the decomposed factors for retrieval, while global-level embedding z is trained with the instance-level InfoNCE objective.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
authors: Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel, Morgan Wack
bullets: The study examines how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement validity in MLLM-based video analysis.

Even with each model’s best deployable representation, 45% of prevalence estimates differed from human-coded benchmarks by more than ten percentage points.

papers.abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.
authors: Marian Bookhahn, Frank Neumann
bullets: Uses dominant wall orientations to generate a small set of pose candidates and masked normalized cross-correlation to match observed free space to a known floor plan.
Combines a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter with consensus readout, while allowing the depth front-end to remain interchangeable.

On construction-floor sessions, achieves 0.90–0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions, extending to all five with learned wall isolation.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
authors: Seungyong Lee, Suhyeok Jang, Minyoung Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the scalability and visual/action gaps of adapting human videos to high-DoF robot embodiments.
Uses autoregressive keyframe translation and motion-conditioned video synthesis guided by human hand skeletons.
Infers action labels from synthesized videos with a depth-aware inverse dynamics model.
Across multiple humanoid embodiments, synthetic-data policies improved novel-task success from 2% to 60%, including bimanual manipulation.
Matched teleoperation-trained policy performance at roughly one-third of the data-collection cost.

papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
authors: Zijun Huang, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Targets compositional image-caption verification involving objects, attributes, counts, and relations.
Uses a shared multimodal backbone as Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer in a closed-loop training process.
Derives rewards from detecting informative mismatches and producing visually grounded repairs.
Improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families.
Enhances visual-detail robustness, while broader multimodal-task gains are limited and benchmark-dependent.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PROVE. A single Qwen backbone is reused under three role prompts: Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer. Given a clean image-caption pair, the Mutator produces a localized caption perturbation, e.g., changing an attribute from “red” to “blue”, to create a hard image-text mismatch. The Verifier first judges the perturbed caption and returns a decision-feedback pair (y1, r1) that diagnoses the mismatch. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer generates a revised caption, which is then checked by the same Verifier to obtain (y2, r2). Rewards from the two verification rounds train the shared model with DrGRPO, so perturbation, verification, and repair co-evolve within one multimodal backbone.

papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.
authors: Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Targets latency in large vision-language-action models caused by sequential reasoning and control.
Uses a high-capacity VLM to asynchronously update semantic memory and a lightweight vision-action expert to produce actions at a higher frequency.
Trains the action expert to handle stale semantic memory and execution delays from asynchronous processing.
On Franka tasks, reports 18% higher success and 20% shorter execution time in quasi-static settings, with 3–5× baseline performance in dynamic simulation.
Runs the VLM at 10× lower than its nominal frequency without significant performance loss, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture design behind ARP. The semantic expert populates the memory with the latest available observation, whereas the visionaction expert cross attends to the stale-memory. The adaptive normalization is influenced by both the flow step τ as well as staleness.

papers.abstract: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.

bullets: Addresses the need for LLM datacenters to provide power flexibility while preserving interactive service.

Validation across four GPU platforms and 1B–70B models estimates power flexibility with 2.8% mean absolute percentage error.
A trace-driven 10,000-H100 simulation achieves up to 16% power flexibility, with 90% of the target reduction reached in about 10 seconds.
