papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.
authors: Lingzhi Yuan, Yiguang Cai, Weize Liu, Siqi Yang, Feijiang Han, Yongkyun Lee, Udari Madhushani Sehwag, Furong Huang
bullets: Addresses the tension between offline shared-harness optimization and costly or verifier-dependent online evolution.
Learns a textual Meta-Skill from contrastive training rollouts showing when to evolve, preserve, or avoid changing a harness.
At deployment, an evolver uses the frozen Meta-Skill plus current trajectory evidence to KEEP or task-locally EVOLVE the harness.
Edits persist for the remainder of a run without resetting the environment or progress, while guidance transfers across tasks.
Achieves 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra; ablations support contrastive guidance and task-local edits.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Motivation and overview of Meta2. Offline evolution produces a shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot adapt to evidence revealed during a new run, while online methods face limitations in intervention timing, knowledge guidance, and verifier availability. By moving offline optimization one level up, Meta2 learns a reusable Meta-Skill from contrastive training rollouts and freezes it to guide task-local harness evolution at checkpoints online, without access to verifier feedback at test-time. Across both evaluated benchmarks, this design yields the highest performance among the compared methods.
Figure 4. Component ablations. The first four settings evaluate the online evolver and two Meta-Skill construction methods. The fifth retains online edits across tasks instead of resetting to ℎ(0).

Figure 2. Design of Meta2: offline knowledge learning, online harness evolution and format of Meta-Skill. Offline, rollouts are collected under three conditions: the task agent alone (A), evolution guided by the current Meta-Skill (B), and evolution with verifier knowledge (C). Deterministic pairing of terminal outcomes yields act, avoid, and hold contrasts. LLM-based reflection and cross-task aggregation distill these contrasts into reusable lessons, which iteratively update the Meta-Skill. Online, the frozen Meta-Skill guides an evolver LLM to retain or modify the harness at deterministic checkpoints, while the task agent continues along a single trajectory in one environment. Meta-Skill entries specify when, how and why to intervene with reference examples.
Figure 3. Checkpoint-interval sensitivity. Performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus log-scaled online cost.

Figure 5. Early intervention guided by an act entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). The task requires a Git push to deploy hello.html to a web server on port 8080. At the first checkpoint, the evolver without Meta-Skill specifies an implementation and requests validation only “where feasible.” The task agent tests in a temporary sandbox but does not run the installer in the task environment; the evolver accepts the result despite the missing /git/server directory and inactive service. With Meta-Skill, entry E-02 guides the evolver to require end-to-end evidence: a clone, commit, and push followed by a fresh HTTP request confirming that the deployed page returns “hello world.” The task agent installs the service and verifies this sequence, after which the evolver chooses KEEP at the subsequent and terminal checkpoints.

Figure 6. Mid-run intervention guided by an act entry (DeepSWE 1.1). The task requires a Link Style rule with independently configured linkStyle and imageStyle. By checkpoint 𝑡3, both task agents have produced an initial implementation, and both evolvers issue a notice. Without Meta-Skill, the notice focuses on parser issues exposed by failing tests, while the image-handling route remains unchecked. The submitted implementation passes 58 of 60 hidden tests, incorrectly converting images when linkStyle is set to wiki and imageStyle is set to leave images unchanged. With Meta-Skill, entry E-02 directs attention to an unverified execution route, and the evolver identifies the interaction between link and image parsing. The task agent repairs this route, and the submitted implementation passes all 60 hidden tests.

Figure 8. Preserving the notice budget with a hold entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). In both runs, the first command fails because the file utility is unavailable, and the task agent subsequently switches to alternative tools. Without Meta-Skill, the evolver spends notices at 𝑡1 and 𝑡2, exhausting this channel before output comparisons reveal a substantial mismatch. With Meta-Skill, entry E-04 discourages a notice about the isolated tool failure, while a separate instruction guided by E-03 requires output comparison. The two notices remain available at 𝑡4–𝑡5 to address reference preservation and the observed mismatch, and the task agent ultimately reproduces the reference output. This case illustrates a difference in intervention timing rather than establishing that withholding the early notice determines success.

Figure 7. Avoiding premature redirection with an avoid entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). By checkpoint 𝑡3, both task agents have identified the bundled Rave warrior as a promising candidate, but its performance against stone remains below the required threshold. Without Meta-Skill, the evolver uses its final notice to redirect exploration toward other bundled warriors. The task agent constructs an Aeka–Rave hybrid but finishes with 74 wins against stone, one short of the required 75. With Meta-Skill, entry E-06 discourages changing the search strategy while exploration continues to make progress. The evolver chooses KEEP at 𝑡3 and subsequent checkpoints, allowing the task agent to continue tuning Rave and satisfy all five performance thresholds.

Figure 9. Performance versus full cost with GPT-5.6-Terra. Full cost includes one-time offline construction and online evaluation costs, plotted on a logarithmic horizontal scale. Dashed lines connect the non-dominated performance–cost point estimates for Terminal-Bench 2.1 (left) and DeepSWE 1.1 (right).

Table 7. Evolution regimes by timing, evidence, and update scope. Online edits occur pre-run, within-run, or after-run; afterrun updates target either the next attempt or later tasks. Meta2 learns reusable ℳ offline and applies task-local edits within-run.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity photovoltaic (PV) module mapping requires complete instance recovery and accurate delineation. Vision foundation models offer zero-shot segmentation, but converting incomplete and inconsistent predictions across views into a complete, geometrically accurate map of individual modules remains challenging. We propose the Multi-View PV Module Mapper (MV-PVMapper), a training-free framework coupling vision foundation models with unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry. First, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) generates candidates from original images using text prompts. Their contours are then transferred into object space through per-module slope correction to limit distortion from surface-model noise, and verified against representative module dimensions to guide cross-view instance selection. Finally, accepted instances return to all covering images as box prompts for SAM~3, supplementing text prompts with spatial cues for iterative segmentation, verification and fusion. On five-direction surveys of three operational rooftop PV plants at approximately 1 cm nadir ground sampling distance, two feedback iterations recover 7,710 of 7,711 reference modules with no false positives at an intersection-over-union (IoU) matching threshold of 0.5. Macro-averaged area precision and recall reach 99.00 % and 98.52 %, respectively. Averaged across sites, the aggregated Jaccard index reaches 97.55 %, compared with 60.73 % and 41.24 % for orthomosaic segmentation and multi-view pixel-voting baselines, respectively; average precision at the stricter IoU threshold of 0.95 reaches 95.67 %. Ablation studies show that module-size constraints are critical for instance separation, while slope correction and feedback to all covering views improve boundary accuracy. These results are achieved without task-specific image annotation or segmentation-model weight updates.

Achieved 99.00% area precision, 98.52% recall, and a 97.55% aggregated Jaccard index; performance was also strong at IoU 0.95.

papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena

A wheeled-legged robot completed missions up to 1.37 km across urban, rural, and campus environments, including stairs and construction sites.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.
authors: HongJin Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runwu Shi, Yifei Wu, Yujin Wang, Jiale Luo, Jiasheng Kuang, Xinyu Yang, Zhaoqi Cui, Chuizheng Kong, Ziyu Wu, Guowu Tan, Qiuyu Fang, Chunxiang Jin
bullets: Irrelevant audio history causes targeted errors toward specific competing answers, not merely generic context-length degradation.
Causal tests show open-ended errors mostly vanish when later computation cannot access the irrelevant source.
In multiple-choice tasks, many errors persist because historical influence travels through question-candidate states.
Source-role and answer-value information peak at different processing depths, and identifying the right source does not eliminate value interference.
Strengthening the queried role and counteracting historical values together yields the strongest recovery on naturally occurring errors.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memory interference in Speech-LLMs, analyzing how irrelevant audio history affects answer generation through causal interventions.
papers.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
papers.tldr: Speech-LLM memory can retrieve the right event yet still let irrelevant historical values bias answers, revealing that reliable memory requires controlling downstream evidence use.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.
authors: Zhewei Gui, Anthony Bolton, Jiyao Zhang, Zeyuan Chen, Qiyang Yan, Tianyu Wang, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of goals defined mainly by object poses, which leaves useful hand contacts implicit.
Learns a relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs without human reference motions.
Composes long-horizon behaviors by closed-loop tracking of hand-object configuration subgoals.
Achieves 80.5% success on seen objects, 69.4% on unseen objects, and 61.5% on 200 real-robot transfers.
Demonstrates 90% task success across six real-world demonstration-guided tasks.

Observations include goals, object-frame keypoint residuals, proprioception, and object geometry. Bottom: the frozen policy follows subgoals from greedy planning or human demonstrations through hierarchical chaining.

papers.selection_reason: Hand-object configuration transfer for dexterous manipulation, directly relevant to dexterous manipulation and robot learning.
papers.title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: DexHOT enables dexterous robots to transfer between explicit hand-object configurations, supporting reusable and composable manipulation behaviors.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical pipelines for humanoid loco-manipulation typically pair a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) with a downstream task policy. Such WBCs are often trained through manual reward shaping, which yields visibly machine-like motions; more consequentially, they are trained without the manipulated object in the scene. Object dynamics are instead approximated through randomized end-effector force disturbances, a proxy that fails to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench a real payload applies across the arms and torso, with the gap becoming critical near the platform's payload limit. In this work, we train the low-level (LL) controller itself as an object-aware motion prior: a single policy trained via motion imitation on retargeted motion-capture (MoCap) references that span the core motion primitives of the downstream task, with the manipulated object physically present in the scene. This single stage inherits natural human-like coordination from the references and absorbs the realistic contact wrench at its source, while exposing the same compact task-space command interface used by command-tracking WBCs. A reference-free high-level (HL) policy is then trained on top, with its action channel anchored to the empirical envelope of the low-level training data so that it generalizes the priors to a long-horizon multi-stage task while structurally preventing queries that would push the low level off-distribution. We instantiate the framework on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place: the same deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, initial and goal poses, and reactively recovers from intentional drops mid-carry. Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ.
authors: Jean-Pierre Sleiman, Bilal Hammoud, He Li, Jonathan Foster, Sylvain Bertrand, Jessica K. Hodgins, Farbod Farshidian
bullets: Addresses machine-like motions and inaccurate object modeling in conventional WBC-based humanoid loco-manipulation.
Trains one low-level policy by imitating retargeted MoCap while the manipulated object is physically present.
Adds a reference-free high-level policy whose commands stay within the low-level training distribution.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place across varying objects and poses.
The policy recovers reactively from intentional drops during carrying.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System Overview. Retargeted MoCap data is used to build a compact motion library (locomotion, walking-with-box, pickup, placement). A low-level motion-imitation policy πLL is then trained as an object-inscene prior, conditioned on a noisy task-space command. The frozen πLL is reused by a reference-free high-level policy πHL observing proprioception, box face centers, and a sparse goal, producing commands within the LL dataset envelope and stitching the learned priors into the full behavior for zero-shot deployment.

Figure 2: Per-joint torque during the 7 kg experiment, normalized by each joint’s effort limit (only discussed joints labeled; over-limit in bold red, dashed line marks 100 %). Snapshots: lift (t≈9 s) and carry (t≈11 s).
Figure 3: Robustness Study (20 s). Task-success ratio (Ours nominal = 1) under 3 perturbation axes (box mass, external pushes, box dimensions) scaled relative to the training distribution.

Distributions are uniform over the indicated intervals unless stated otherwise. Rows marked (†) apply only on resets where RSI is not active.

Table 1: Task success (%) of Ours vs. episode length; last row doubles init/goal ranges relative to training.
Table 4: Object-geometry augmentation. Dimensions in meters; each box is instantiated for all three behaviours (carry, pick, place).

papers.tldr: HLO-AMP trains a humanoid’s low-level controller with object-aware motion priors and a constrained high-level policy to produce natural, robust bimanual loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.
authors: Jeremy Qin, Ruizhi Deng, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Frederick Tung, Leo Feng
bullets: Most autoresearch evaluations reset agents between tasks, leaving cross-task learning unclear.
The benchmark compares persistent and reset agents on matched task streams, data, and time budgets across nine task families.
It evaluates five frontier agents using first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance.
A memory ablation separates benefits from session continuity from actual transfer of prior insights.
Persistent state improves efficiency for all agents, but effective insight reuse remains a distinct challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH. Stateful and stateless agents process the same ordered task stream under matched environments, and per-task budgets. Each task consists of an autoresearch loop, but only the stateful agent retains experience across tasks. Private evaluation of final artifacts enables paired measurement of cross-task gains in performance, and efficiency.

Figure 3: Effect of per-task wall-clock budget on Shared Regime. Stateful-minus-reset finaloutcome, initialization, and time-convergence gains over transfer tasks (positions 2–5), in normalized reward points. Points show matched repetitions; markers and bars show their mean and sample standard deviation across three repetitions. Each budget is a separate run, rather than a checkpoint taken from a longer run.

Figure 10: Task-position-resolved search advantage on the controlled synthetic streams. Each curve reports the stateful-minus-stateless best hidden reward, in normalized reward points, over the normalized task budget. Differences are computed within the same task and then averaged with equal weight across the shared-latent, shared-regime, and shared-sparse families. Later tasks exhibit a pronounced and sustained stateful advantage for several agents, although the pattern is not universal across models.

Figure 11: Growth in persistent-state search advantage across the controlled synthetic streams. For each task position, the stateful-minus-stateless reward gap is integrated over the normalized task budget and compared with the corresponding initial-task value from the same model and family. Gray lines show the shared-latent, shared-regime, and shared-sparse families; colored diamonds show equal-family means. Positive values indicate that persistent state provides a larger search advantage on later tasks.

Figure 5: Outcome transfer gain measures the difference in final selected hidden-test reward between persistent and reset execution on the same task (stateful minus stateless). Results cover 32 transfer tasks per agent, excluding the first task of every stream. Values are normalized reward points (100× reward difference), so positive values favor persistent state. Sonnet 4.6 shows the largest aggregate gain (+7.6 points); GPT-5.4 and Kimi K3 remain near zero, while Opus 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol are slightly negative.

Figure 14: Earlier availability does not guarantee a better final model. Highly specific matched cards make Sonnet productive sooner but anchor it to a correction-model family. Shuffled cards delay the first valid solution yet lead to broader search and a better final result.

Figure 4: Run-to-run variability for GPT-5.6-Sol across three repeated stateful–reset comparisons. Dots show individual runs, circles their mean, and error bars ±1 standard deviation; positive values favor stateful execution.

Figure 7: Absolute outcome performance under reset and persistent execution. Values are normalized reward points, averaged within each task family and then across families with equal weight. The analysis covers 32 transfer-eligible tasks per agent and excludes the first task of every stream. Opus 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieve the strongest reset performance, whereas Sonnet 4.6 benefits substantially from persistent state and nearly closes the absolute-performance gap.

Figure 6: Initialization gain compares first valid solutions; time-convergence gain summarizes the best-so-far reward over the task budget. Open circles are task-family means, and diamonds are equal-family agent means. Gains are stateful minus stateless normalized reward points, so zero indicates no difference and positive values favor stateful execution. Mean time-convergence gain is positive for all five agents, and mean initialization gain is positive for four of five.

Figure 2: Persistent-state search advantage over time. Mean best hidden reward as a function of normalized task-budget elapsed. Task-level best-so-far curves are constructed post hoc, averaged within each family, and then averaged with equal family weight. Persistent execution generally finds useful solutions earlier, although the size and duration of the advantage vary across agents.

Figure 8: Outcome transfer gain decomposed by agent and task family. Each cell reports the mean persistent-minus-reset outcome reward over the transfer-eligible tasks in that family, in normalized reward points; positive values favor persistent state. Cell labels show the uncapped values, while color intensity uses a signed square-root scale capped at ±20 points to preserve visibility of smaller effects. Transfer is strongly heterogeneous across both agents and recurring task structures.

Figure 9: Curves show the mean best hidden reward attained as a function of normalized task-budget elapsed. Task-level best-so-far curves are constructed post hoc from private-evaluator scores, averaged within each family, and then averaged with equal family weight. Persistent execution generally finds useful solutions earlier, but the size and duration of the advantage vary across agents.

Figure 13: Matched versus shuffled insight cards on Solar 10 Minutes. Matched memory transfers an abstract seasonal-residual hypothesis while leaving its period open to verification. The largest difference appears in first-solution quality; full-budget search narrows the gap.

Figure 12: Direct reuse on a related ETT task. The stateful agent explicitly reuses its earlier implementation, then recalibrates it using current-task evidence. Its first valid solution already outperforms the stateless agent’s final solution.

Figure 17: Operational learning improves validity but sacrifices exploration. Opus converts a real failure into a reusable policy and avoids another missing submission. Applied without an adaptive exploration budget, however, the policy protects a weak fallback while the reset agent searches more broadly and finishes substantially better.

Figure 16: Search succeeds, but final selection fails. Persistent state helps GPT-5.6-Sol find a useful candidate much earlier, yielding a +55.0-point time-convergence gain. Continued dev optimization selects a fragile ensemble, however, producing a −16.9-point final outcome gain.

Figure 15: Within-task optimization destroys a strong transferred initialization. Stateful Kimi finds its best hidden-generalizing expression early, but selects a more elaborate expression because it nearly saturates visible development R2. The additional terms fail under hidden extrapolation.

Table 2: Model-level results over 32 transfer tasks per agent. Reset outcome is the family-balanced mean final reward under reset execution. Gains are stateful-minus-reset normalized reward points reported as mean [median]. Win rates report the family-balanced fraction of tasks on which stateful execution outperforms reset execution.

Table 13: Matched-minus-shuffled difference in the best hidden reward achieved by each budget checkpoint on the four transfer-eligible Energy-system tasks. Values are normalized reward points; positive values favor matched memory. The best-so-far reward is zero before the first valid submission.

Time to first valid solution and valid candidate counts are family-balanced per-task means reported as stateful/reset (S/R). First-solution gain compares the hidden reward of the first valid solutions. Full-budget gain is the headline time-convergence result. The same-candidate-count control uses only the first min(nS , nR) valid candidates from each paired run. The final control starts each trajectory at its own first valid solution, removing first-solution latency while preserving first-solution quality. All gains are normalized reward points; positive values favor stateful execution.

Table 1: CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH evaluation coverage. The evaluation spans four settings and nine task families, ranging from controlled synthetic and symbolic tasks with known recurring structure to real-world forecasting and tabular AutoML streams.

M/S compares matched with shuffled cards; M/N compares matched cards with an independent no-memory reference. Positive values favor matched cards. Task 1 is excluded.

papers.selection_reason: Examines whether agents retain and reuse experience across tasks, directly relevant to continual learning and agent memory.
papers.title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
papers.tldr: Continual AutoResearch shows that agents benefit from retaining experience across tasks by finding good solutions faster, but this does not reliably improve final performance.

papers.abstract: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.
authors: Maximilian Th\"urmer, Nicolas Scotto di Perto, Eloise Stein, Natanijel Vasic, Mikaeil Bagherli, Zhenguo Wu, Benjamin Klenk, Holger Fr\"oning, Johannes Feldmann
bullets: LLM decode relies on fine-grained collectives whose latency constrains per-user responsiveness.
For a fixed deployment and parallelization, decode communication is sufficiently predictable to configure optical circuits once.
The approach co-designs OCS connectivity with model parallelism and topology-aware collective schedules.
GXNET combines graph-based emulation with analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements.
In a 576-accelerator domain serving large MoE models, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% versus 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

The on-chip stages account for under 10 % of the round trip; the remainder is fabric traversal and remote-access handling.

The mask 0011 folds axis B of both meshes; the mask 1100 folds axis A of the 4 × 4 mesh and is idle for the 2× 8 mesh, whose partition splits bits 3 and 2.

Figure 9. Folding a hypercube. Left: Q3 with generators {001, 010, 100} has degree 3 and diameter 3; 000 → 111 takes three hops. Right: the fold generator g = 111 adds one port per node and joins every node to its antipode, so 000 → 111 takes one hop and the diameter drops to 2.

Figure 11. papers.abstract: Vertical forest structure influences fire behavior by regulating understory-to-canopy fuel connectivity, yet operational fuel-type models represent this complexity through discrete classes that only indirectly capture vertical continuity. High-density point clouds offer an opportunity to characterize vertical fuel connectivity in a more explicit and continuous manner, but specific methodological approaches are still required. We applied Gaussian decomposition to vertical height profiles derived from terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) point clouds across 25 permanent forest plots to characterize geometric vertical fuel continuity. A multiscale analysis spanning from the plot scale to ~0.5 $m^2$ units was used to evaluate geometric, probabilistic, and overlap metrics for characterizing fuel strata. The method reproduced the vertical transition between shrub and tree strata, with median Pearson correlations ranging from 0.83 to 0.96 across analysis levels. Probability density overlap metrics and separability indicators, such as the Jeffries-Matusita distance, provided complementary descriptors of vertical continuity. Intermediate spatial scales (3-6 m cells) provided a useful compromise between spatial detail and the consistent representation of shrub-canopy interaction patterns. Finer scales increased variability due to point density reduction and profile irregularity, and low mean squared error values were found insufficient as sole performance indicators. Gaussian decomposition applied to TLS point clouds enables explicit quantification of vertical fuel continuity, a limitation of current discrete classification systems. Continuous vertical connectivity metrics derived from this approach offer a pathway for improving ladder fuel characterization and strengthening decision-making support in wildfire risk assessment.
authors: Jes\'us Torralba, Luis \'A. Ruiz, Pablo Crespo-Peremarch, Marina Sim\'o-Mart\'i, Juan Pedro Carbonell-Rivera

papers.selection_reason: Uses TLS point clouds to quantify 3D vertical forest structure; relevant to 3D point-cloud-based perception.
papers.title: Characterizing the vertical continuity of fuel strata based on TLS point clouds Gaussian decomposition and overlap metrics
papers.tldr: Gaussian decomposition of TLS point-cloud height profiles provides continuous metrics for quantifying vertical fuel continuity between shrub and tree strata, with 3–6 m spatial cells offering a practical balance of detail and stability.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.
authors: Syed Umer Bukhari, Magnus Almgren, Ahmed Ali-Eldin
bullets: Evaluates RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant, and QuantVLA under controlled conditions: same checkpoints, layers, engines, and varying only methods and kernels.

Quantization consistently reduces memory, but speedups are hardware- and kernel-dependent; some configurations are slower than 16-bit models.
Profiling attributes limited speed gains partly to a 16-bit, memory-bound action expert that accounts for most runtime in pi0.5.

papers.title: LoopQ: Fair, Closed-Loop Evaluation of Quantized Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/
authors: Po-Yi Wu, Djengo Cyun-Jyun Fang, Dian Cheng, Tsung-Wei Ke
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of frequent scene resets and human intervention in real-world RL deployment.

Finds that naively fine-tuning pretrained policies fails under shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses.
Shows that targeted reset allocation and mitigation of pretrained-model biases improve non-episodic training.
Reports better long-horizon manipulation and generalization to unseen object configurations and task sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Forced reset of unrecoverable scenes outperforms learned reset strategies. Only methods that forcibly reset all unrecoverable scenes (HSR and HSR-only) show a sustained increase in success rate.

Figure 12: Visualization of reset-free methods. We compare five methods: (1) periodic reset (PR), which resets the scene every T = 2560 steps; (2) heuristic scene reset (HSR), which detects unrecoverable states before each task switch and resets only when necessary; (3) heuristic scene reset without periodic reset (HSR-only), which uses heuristic resets without periodic resets, avoiding unnecessary resets in recoverable states; (4) learned scene reset (LSR), which learns reset behavior as an auxiliary task within a single policy, eliminating external reset logic at the cost of interaction budget; and (5) perturbation policy (PER), which extends LSR with a second auxiliary task that perturbs the scene, with the two tasks sampled uniformly at random.

Figure 6: Rollout success decays between scene resets. Top. Rollout success rate of SpatialVLA during non-episodic training. The vertical line at step 600K marks the switch from T = 320 to T = 2560, and triangles mark scene resets. Bottom. Snapshots of the scene between two consecutive resets. Objects become increasingly dispersed and eventually leave the reachable workspace, leaving few successful rollouts to learn from.

Figure 9: Forcibly resetting unrecoverable scenes is the most reset-efficient strategy. As the number of scene resets increases, only methods that forcibly reset all unrecoverable scenes (HSR and HSR-only) continue to improve in performance.

Figure 11: Non-episodic scene reset training improves sequential task execution. Non-episodic training outperformed episodic training on all subsequent tasks, including both task sequences seen and unseen during training. This improvement was consistent across different VLAs.

Figure 3: Long scene reset intervals expose the policy to diverse object starting positions. In non-episodic RL, each new task starts with the scene layout carried over from the previous task, causing object starting positions to become increasingly dispersed as the scene reset interval increases.

Figure 7: Resetting unrecoverable scenes preserves learning signals. By resetting all unrecoverable scenes at each task switch, HSR achieved a 64% task success rate, compared with only 14% success rate without HSR.

Figure 4: End-effector reset mitigates pretraining bias. EER automatically resets the endeffector to its initial position at each task switch, improving the learning efficiency of SpatialVLA under non-episodic scene-reset settings.
Figure 10: In-domain and out-of-domain scene configurations. Out-of-domain scenes include overlapping and cluttered object layouts that do not appear during training.

papers.title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: CRONOS benchmarks non-episodic RL fine-tuning of large vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation and shows that targeted resets and bias correction can improve robustness and generalization.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.
authors: Junzhe Chen, Tian Qin, Eugenie Shi, Tianshu Zhang, Qiang Ju, Lijie Wen
bullets: Targets premature token commitments during iterative denoising, which can amplify image-ungrounded predictions.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play inference strategy requiring no model retraining.
Compares token confidence with and without visual input to estimate counterfactual visual support.
Prioritizes masked positions whose predictions gain more from the image.
Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO report consistent hallucination reduction and improved multimodal reasoning across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy Collins, Namra Patel, Ayush Agarwal, Shitij Govil, Animesh Garg
bullets: Motivation: Full video is redundant for action prediction; dense 3D motion may transfer video-learned priors more effectively.
Method: A 5B video-generation model is fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, using rendered flow encoded in the video model’s latent space.
Training: The model combines action-free human video with action-labeled robot teleoperation data.

Findings: Motion prediction supports generalization to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks; replacing or augmenting it with video prediction harms policy success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Interpretation: Action tokens attend substantially more to motion than video, indicating that video prediction can waste model capacity.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
bullets: Addresses whether multimodal robot agents must repeatedly reinterpret visual observations during interaction.
Represents object-part geometry with typed, evidence-aware symbolic references grounded in calibrated RGB-D.
Provides compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after actions, while refreshing only locally observed state.
Supports offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution with visual reasoning invoked on demand.
The abstract reports improved multi-step manipulation completion and substantially fewer repeated multimodal queries.

papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
authors: Oswaldo Ludwig
bullets: Physical-AI policy errors can compound over trajectories, causing distribution shift and task failure.
DRAP estimates local perturbation amplification from a ridge-regularized state-transition model’s largest singular value.
It accumulates risk-weighted action-gradient importance per tensor and uses normalized importance to adapt AdamW learning rates without replay.
On a fixed KappaTune-selected OpenVLA subnetwork, DRAP improved retention over AdamW and EWC while maintaining strong acquisition on new LIBERO suites.
Scope: evaluated in replay-free sequential adaptation across LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites.

papers.tldr: DRAP reduces catastrophic forgetting in continual physical-AI adaptation by making parameter plasticity sensitive to trajectory-amplification risk.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.
authors: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai, Jiayu Dong, Weikang Wan, Jianyu Chen, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited long-range context and high computational cost of dense short-horizon WAM prediction.
Uses sparse long-horizon and dense local-dynamics visual streams at different temporal scales.
A unified dual-DiT architecture connects the streams with structured cross-stream attention to guide actions.
Progressive inference with partial, joint, and dynamically skipped denoising achieves a reported 2.93× speedup.
Reports 93.70% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with in-domain and OOD performance on Fourier GR-3.

The visual world is modeled at two complementary temporal scales: a sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical context and coarse future evolution, while a dense local visual dynamics stream captures fine-grained local interactions. Both visual streams are jointly modeled with robot actions. During inference, the visual streams progressively terminate and are cached, while the action stream continues denoising to completion.

papers.abstract: Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD) refers to the phenomenon in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while adapting a large language model (LLM) to a target task, often erodes the general capabilities acquired during pre-training. Prevailing explanations attribute PCD to macroscopic distribution shift and therefore lack microscopic manipulability, leaving existing mitigation methods without a complete theoretical foundation. In this paper, we first develop a bottom-up geometric theory of PCD grounded in feature interference under superposition: narrow-domain SFT data disrupt the almost-orthogonal feature structure formed during pre-training, and the resulting interference drives activations across decision hyperplanes in the output Laguerre-Voronoi geometry, flipping predictions on general tasks. This theory unifies existing methods into six paradigms and reveals both the source of their efficacy and their theoretical limits. We then prove that cross-entropy under one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD on its own, and accordingly propose the AEGIS loss, which directly constrains the drift of activation margins along all competing token directions, thereby decoupling interference suppression from task adaptation. Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS outperforms representative methods of every paradigm on target tasks and pervasive capabilities simultaneously, at only about 1.3 times the computational cost of standard SFT. Its generality, scalability, and mechanistic interpretability offer a new perspective on fully resolving PCD.
authors: Hang Chen, Jiaying Zhu, Wenya Wang
bullets: Develops a bottom-up geometric theory linking narrow-domain SFT to disruption of pretrained feature structure and prediction flips.
Unifies existing PCD mitigation methods into six paradigms and identifies their effectiveness and theoretical limits.
Proves that standard cross-entropy with one-hot labels cannot independently resolve PCD.
Introduces AEGIS to constrain activation-margin drift across competing token directions while maintaining task adaptation.
Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS improves target-task and general capabilities simultaneously at about 1.3× standard SFT cost.

papers.abstract: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.
authors: Hong Je-Gal, Jinwoo Kim, Chanbin Yi, Hyun-Suk Lee
bullets: Targets automated generation of executable RL policies from natural-language task descriptions.

Addresses semantic misalignment among states, actions, rewards, and termination conditions that can prevent learning.
Experiments in Isaac Sim and additional domains show improvements over monolithic LLM and existing agentic baselines, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.
Combines a high-level VLA planner with state estimation, in-situ 3D perception, and signed distance fields to produce executable trajectories.
Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.
authors: Carlos Hartmann
bullets: The study compares 73 human annotators with over 40 LLM configurations on 174 authentic Reddit examples of “they.”
The best model, Kimi K3, achieved 94.5% accuracy, exceeding human majority vote (86.2%) but narrowly trailing the best individual human (95.7%).
LLMs provide practical cost and speed benefits for large-scale linguistic annotation.
Human reasoning in low-agreement cases revealed inconsistencies in the annotation typology, showing that automation can complement rather than simply replace humans.
The dataset, annotations, gold labels, and reproducible code are openly available.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation improves a student model's reasoning ability through supervision from a teacher. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both teacher and student under different contexts: the student generates reasoning trajectories from the question alone, while the teacher additionally receives a complete worked example and provides token-level supervision along those trajectories. Because the problem statement is shared, its content and ordering shape both student generation and teacher feedback. Preserving its semantic structure therefore seems natural, but does it always improve learning? We introduce Shuffled OPSD, which shuffles the words of the shared problem statement while keeping the teacher-only worked example intact. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 model scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and Standard OPSD under matched training configurations. The largest gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B. Further controls show that preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the evaluated scales, whereas shuffling the teacher-only worked example reduces accuracy at every scale. Cross-problem mixing and target-removal experiments further distinguish the roles of problem content, word order, and teacher context. These results show that disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts performance. They challenge semantic coherence as a universally beneficial principle for OPSD and motivate closer study of how input structure shapes student generation and teacher supervision.
authors: Qingyuan Zheng, Zhihao Dou
bullets: OPSD uses student-generated reasoning from the question and teacher token-level supervision from the question plus a worked example.
Shuffled OPSD randomizes the shared problem words but preserves the teacher-only worked example.
Across three math benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, it outperforms intact-target OPSD controls and Standard OPSD under matched settings.
The largest reported gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B.
Word-level shuffling performs no worse than preserving larger word blocks at evaluated scales; disrupting teacher context reduces accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
authors: Jianye Xu, Yousef Sayed, Bassam Alrifaee
bullets: Addresses infeasibility and conservatism problems in conventional control-barrier-function safety filters.
Evaluates safety over a backup horizon until all vehicles stop, ensuring recursive feasibility under control bounds.
Provides a fully decentralized, real-time safety filter requiring one broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step.
Safeguards MARL throughout pre-training, deployment, and fine-tuning on unseen maps.
In simulations, it avoided all collisions; in recorded roundabout traffic, safeguarded policies reduced median travel time by 14% without collisions.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents write interaction experience into artifacts and reuse them in later tasks. Most work supports such methods with three proxy signals: artifacts accumulate, behavior changes once they are loaded, and metrics rise. We call this signal-based evaluation. What these signals are meant to indicate, however, has not been defined. To fill this gap, we define capability formation from artifacts as five sequentially dependent properties, two of which form a checkpoint for capability formation, and introduce three-scale diagnosis, which judges these properties at the state, game, and lineage levels. In freestyle Gomoku, Reflexion, Voyager, and DGM evolve with the same base model and all show the three signals, yet each exhibits a distinct capability-formation break. Reflexion shows a legalization gain: its pass rate rises only because more of its moves are legal. Voyager shows a compositional override: components that are sound on their own combine to miss all 20 available one-move wins. DGM shows loss-only drift: after passing the checkpoint, later versions only lose passing states. These counterexamples show that signal-based evaluation cannot determine whether a capability has formed.
authors: Ziqian Ban, Haoxiang Yang, Yanfei Zhang, Shixin Liang, Haoran Yu, Xu Lin, Shaobin Zhao, Xuran Li, Zhiyi Cheng
bullets: Defines capability formation as five sequentially dependent properties, including a two-property checkpoint.

Finds distinct failure modes: legalization gain, compositional override, and loss-only drift.
Concludes that artifact accumulation, behavioral change, and metric improvement are insufficient for capability evaluation.

papers.abstract: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.
authors: Junfeng Wang, Jiawei Liu, Yongchao Xu, Tao Jiang, Jiangbo Ai, Jin Zhang, Chong Wang, Qixing Zhang
bullets: Visual question-answering failures often stem from poor zoom or cropping decisions rather than language reasoning.
Bounding-box decisions have high uncertainty, while final-answer rewards provide weak, trajectory-level credit for these actions.
OPO uses Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching to explore alternative crops at uncertain, nonredundant observation events.
Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution assigns local evidence-based credit to the observation actions responsible for each branch’s outcome.
Experiments show consistent improvements across Qwen3-VL model scales, with competitive performance versus larger and tool-augmented models.

papers.abstract: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: https://github.com/SkyJiashu/VISTA.
authors: Jiashu Liao, Joanne Garde-Hansen, Sanjay Sharma, Tanaya Guha
bullets: Addresses the need for online face clustering when complete video streams cannot be processed offline.
Combines visual features with controlled semantic reasoning to maintain cluster purity and long-range identity consistency.
Targets challenging variations in illumination, pose, and costumes across unconstrained videos.
Evaluated on 15 full episodes from three TV series in the VPCD benchmark.
Consistently improves the precision–recall balance over the matched online unsupervised COFC baseline under the same protocol.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to adapt models to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. Recently, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a representative Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has gained increasing attention in CL due to its efficiency and scalability. Several LoRA-based merging methods maintain a single inference model by scaling the newly learned LoRA update with one coefficient and merging it into the previous weights after each task. However, they usually control the whole update with a shared scalar factor, although different update elements may affect previous and current tasks in different ways. To address this issue, we propose Merging Strength Modulation via Joint Loss Estimation (M2LE). It consists of Hessian Information-guided Adaptive Merging (HIM) and Task Simulation Perturbation for Merging (TSP). Instead of searching for a global merge coefficient, HIM directly solves for the target merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks. Solving this objective gives an analytic solution that naturally takes the form of element-wise modulation over the current task LoRA update. To improve the stability of the learned update under subsequent merging, we introduce TSP which simulates different tasks interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that M2LE consistently outperforms existing PEFT-based continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/bbdeeer/M2LE_NeurIPS2026.
authors: Kun Gu, De Cheng, Zhipeng Xu, Lingfeng He, Di Xu, Nannan Wang
bullets: Addresses interference between newly learned and previously learned tasks during sequential LoRA merging.
HIM derives an analytic, element-wise modulation of the current LoRA update using Hessian information and a joint objective.
TSP simulates task interference to improve update stability during later merges.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent gains over existing PEFT-based continual learning methods.

papers.abstract: Legal judgment prediction models may retain a guilty verdict after a legally decisive condition has been altered such that the specified charge is no longer established. We study this guilty bias via selective repair over matched charge-established and charge-not-established cases, where the unsupported verdict should change while its supported counterpart remains stable. We construct CAIL-MC, a legally reviewed dataset of 11,478 matched pairs covering 261 Chinese criminal charges. Held-out activation interventions show that contrasts learned from correctly resolved pairs transfer to false-guilty cases, but target-reaching interventions can also damage matched supported-guilty decisions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce PROSE, which reconstructs case-specific targets from a training-derived residual geometry, aligns them with a local margin-descent signal, attenuates supported-guilty-sensitive components, and realizes bounded targets through a preservation-regularized low-rank parameter update. Across Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, PROSE achieves stronger pairwise safe repair and evidence sensitivity, while preserving standard single-pass inference.
authors: Yimeng Wang, Zeyuan Tian, Xinyu Wang, Danyang Gao, Chenglei Shen, Zhongxiang Sun, Lei La, Weijie Yu
