papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
bullets: Token-level weighting changes the target distribution learned during SFT.
Dynamic weighting can overly sharpen the target, while static weighting depends strongly on the prior model’s quality.
SPFT uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information as a prior for token weighting.
A Bayesian decomposition shows that SPFT gives higher weights to tokens informative for predicting the ground-truth outcome.
Experiments in mathematical reasoning and code generation show improvements over standard SFT and other baselines.],

papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.

bullets: Addresses missed evidence whose relevance emerges only through intermediate facts.
Recurrently summarizes query-conditioned graph context into a shared evolving query state.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable progress in AI-generated content, including images and videos. In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.
authors: Jiate Liu, Deheng Ye
bullets: Targets policy-network parameter generation with diffusion models for reinforcement learning.
Combines a Transformer-based autoencoder that patchifies and compresses parameters with a task-conditioned diffusion model.

Supports generating networks with more parameters than prior approaches.
In unseen environments, generated policies converge faster and achieve competitive performance.

papers.abstract: Per-step selective back-propagation forwards every example of a mini-batch but back-propagates only some of them. Most rules rank examples by loss or gradient magnitude, but such scalar scores ignore cancellation between per-example gradients: the gradient removed by a set can be much smaller than its individual magnitudes suggest. We introduce CAPSkip (Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping). Among the examples the model already classifies correctly, CAPSkip skips the longest prefix, in increasing order of last-layer gradient norm, whose vector sum stays within a relative budget $b$ of the batch's last-layer gradient. In exact arithmetic this bounds the change of the raw final-layer gradient, using rank-one contributions already available from the forward pass; the bound does not extend to deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the training trajectory. Because the cumulative distortion is not monotone in the prefix length, CAPSkip scans all prefixes; a factorised Gram matrix makes the scan cheap and keeps it on the device. With activation reuse and selected-row backward, CAPSkip fine-tunes DeiT-S on CIFAR-100 for 103 epochs in 0.576x the time of 103-epoch dense training, and is +0.25 pp [+0.08, +0.42] above an approximately time-matched 59-epoch dense run (n=3).
authors: Heejin Choi
bullets: Targets the failure of loss- or gradient-magnitude ranking to account for cancellation among per-example gradients.
Skips the longest prefix ordered by increasing last-layer gradient norm whose summed gradient remains within relative budget b of the full batch gradient.
Scans all prefixes because cumulative distortion is non-monotonic; a factorized Gram matrix enables an efficient on-device scan.
The bound applies only to the raw final-layer gradient, not deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the overall training trajectory.
On DeiT-S fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, it used 0.576× the time of dense 103-epoch training and was 0.25 percentage points above a time-matched 59-epoch dense run.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud (I2P) registration risks discarding correct but ambiguous patch pairs, while retaining more candidates repeats fine matching over overlapping patches. SparseGraph-I2P aims to improve registration recall by increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver, using sensor or monocular depth. A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips pixel--point comparisons covered by an ancestor patch paired with the same point-cloud region. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve. With monocular depth, depth or inverse depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering. SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency among the compared methods on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth. With predicted depth, it retains the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. Code will be released.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic scene completion plays a critical role in enabling various downstream tasks within autonomous systems by estimating both missing geometric structures and semantic information in scene data. In this work, we introduce a unique neural framework that integrates state space modeling with diffusion-based generative approaches to enhance 3D point cloud semantic scene completion. We propose \textit{MPath Mamba} diffusion network, leveraging a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations within multi-path data to efficiently process long-sequence data for feature extraction. The proposed method operates in the conditioned latent space of a variational autoencoder, enhanced by a state-space mechanism to improve 3D point cloud representation and reconstruction. Extensive experiments conducted on the SemanticKITTI benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive performance for 3D point cloud semantic scene completion.
authors: Li Liang, Naveed Akhtar, Jordan Vice, Anwaar Ulhaq, Ajmal Saeed Mian
bullets: Targets 3D semantic scene completion for autonomous-system applications.
Uses a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional-decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations in a multi-path architecture.
Operates in a VAE-conditioned latent space to improve point-cloud representation and reconstruction.
Experiments on SemanticKITTI show highly competitive completion performance.

A modular segmentation network performs 3D semantic segmentation.

papers.abstract: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.
authors: Minghe Wang, Weijun Zeng, Dapeng Luo, Xinyue Wang, Nong Sang
bullets: Addresses incomplete evidence caused by feed-forward systems that rely on predefined frame or event sampling.
Uses an agentic search-and-verify protocol covering precursor, trigger, and aftermath stages.
Introduces evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV) to learn which evidence is supportive, compact, and necessary, and when to stop.
Applies a bounded search budget to control search cost.

papers.abstract: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on https://cando-rl.github.io/.
authors: Zeyu Gao, Chengkai Hou, Chaoyue Li, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Yao Mu, Peng Jia, Li Zhang, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting pretrained generative policies with online RL without disrupting demonstration-derived behavior.
CNDO learns state- and noise-conditioned latent directions and uses conservative value estimation plus gated execution instead of fixed latent feasible regions.
CANDO adds an action-space residual to CNDO, combining structured latent improvement with local correction.
Experiments report 76.1 NAUC and 91.4% final success, exceeding the best single-space methods by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1 percentage points.
Scope: the approach targets efficient online adaptation of frozen generative policies for robot control.

The pretrained policy remains frozen throughout.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.
authors: Jaehyeong Jo, Sangwon Jang, Sihyun Yu, Seonghyeon Ye, Yekyung Nah, Hojung Jung, Kimin Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Avoids costly iterative future-video generation and reduces errors from inaccurate visual predictions.
Uses representation distillation to train a visual encoder that predicts frozen video-diffusion representations from the current observation.
An action module extracts action-relevant information to produce robot actions.
Achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs across real-world and simulated tasks, with 11Hz closed-loop control using a 14B backbone.
Supports leveraging stronger video priors, extra video data, and unannotated demonstrations—including videos from different embodiments—for learning new tasks.

papers.abstract: Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicles requires translating operator intent into feasible assignments while preserving autonomous execution when communication is limited. We present a hierarchical framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) interpretation of natural-language mission instructions with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and distributed Behaviour Tree (BT) execution. The LLM extracts assignment and ordering constraints, which the MILP optimizer combines with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements. A BT-LLM Bridge distributes the resulting allocations to onboard BT Mission Managers. Per-vehicle Robotic Agents assess local faults and request selective replanning, allowing unaffected vehicles to continue their assigned tasks. Evaluation in a ROS-based AUV simulator compares Qwen-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on constraint extraction and tests recovery from sensor degradation and critical vehicle faults. Qwen-3-8B provides more accurate constraint extraction, and all tasks are completed in the tested failure scenarios. These simulation results support the feasibility of combining language-based mission specification with structured allocation and distributed execution.
authors: Ehsan Khorrambakht, Cristiano Caissutti, Andrea Munafo, Andrea Caiti
bullets: LLMs extract task assignments and ordering constraints from operator instructions.
MILP combines extracted constraints with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements to generate allocations.
A BT-LLM Bridge distributes plans to onboard Behaviour Tree Mission Managers.
Local agents detect faults and trigger selective replanning so unaffected vehicles can continue.
In ROS-based simulation, Qwen-3-8B extracted constraints more accurately than Llama-3.1-8B, and tasks completed in tested failure scenarios.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Planning with Distributed Onboard Behaviour Tree Execution for Multi-AUV Missions
papers.tldr: A hierarchical LLM–MILP–Behaviour Tree framework translates natural-language missions into distributed, fault-tolerant plans for multi-AUV operations under limited communication.

papers.abstract: Compiling a natural-language agent skill into model parameters removes the skill text from the prompt and leaves behind a small artifact that can be distributed and reused. Existing methods differ in where they inject the compiled quantity, and all of them assume that the artifact carries the content of the skill. We test that assumption. Through three controls on a retrieval agent, we find that a compiled skill shift carries a domain-general behavioural prior, not the content of the skill. A wrong skill document performs on par with the correct one, a single averaged bundle matches per-skill routing under a two-sided equivalence test, and a same-norm random direction collapses to the no-injection baseline, which shows that the trained direction stays load-bearing. We then introduce SKILL2STEER, a one-pass hypernetwork that reads a skill document once and maps it to low-rank activation shifts added at the output of every decoder block. Each skill compiles to 2.36M parameters, 9.25 times fewer than a weight-space adapter, while the base weights stay frozen and the generator runs only at compile time. The shift can be scheduled across retrieval steps and deployed as one routing-free bundle. On SearchQA, a seven-dataset benchmark, SKILL2STEER reaches 37.9 exact match, 9.8 points above the frozen model and 2.3 points above a weight-space method that ships 9.25 times more parameters per skill.
authors: Ran Li, Lei Chen
bullets: Compiled skill shifts encode a domain-general behavioral prior rather than the specific skill document’s content.
Controls show wrong-skill inputs perform similarly to correct ones, an averaged bundle matches per-skill routing, and random same-norm directions provide no benefit.
A one-pass hypernetwork maps each skill document to low-rank shifts applied after every decoder block; the generator runs only during compilation.
Each compiled skill uses 2.36M parameters—9.25× fewer than the compared weight-space adapter—and can be deployed as one routing-free bundle.
On SearchQA, SKILL2STEER achieves 37.9 exact match, improving over the frozen model and the larger weight-space method.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
authors: Tianxing Zhu, Dan Huang
bullets: Addresses persistent AR assistance when historical questions require visual evidence from earlier encounters.
Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.
Links semantic observations to source images and separates capture acceptance, interpretation, and question-specific support.
Introduces bounded reassessment of familiar views and source-dependency-guided retention.
In replay, six RGB views were selected from 648 observations, while feature extraction covered 97.7%; frequent local inference remains costly.

papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
authors: Jimmy Wang, Yifan Chou, Kaifeng Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Binghao Huang, Tao Yu, Saleh Nabi, Yunzhu Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining 3D spatial consistency across viewpoints and extended interactions.
Combines a particle-voxel autoencoder for compact point-cloud representations with action-conditioned latent dynamics.
Jointly models appearance, geometry, and spatially aligned tactile observations from a shared 3D representation.
Supports interactive multimodal prediction at 50 Hz, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views.
Enables scalable policy data generation, evaluation, and planning with unseen objects and robot configurations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Model Architecture. (a) We introduce a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses an input point cloud into a compact 3D voxel latent. This voxel latent is progressively upsampled into finer voxels, which are then upsampled into dense visual particles and optional tactile particles. Each visual particle is attached to Gaussian parameters that can be rendered at novel viewpoints. (b) Our 3D latent dynamics model then directly operates on voxel latents produced by the autoencoder. Given robot actions, history latents, and a current latent observation, the dynamics model uses 3D convolutions and spatiotemporal attention to autoregressively predict future voxel latents during open-loop rollouts. These latents can then be decoded into point clouds, multi-view renders, and tactile observations.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of open-loop multi-view predictions. papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has advanced rapidly with the emergence of foundation models such as Depth Anything. Their transformer-based architectures provide strong generalization across diverse scenes and domains, but also incur high computational and memory cost, making efficient deployment challenging. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides an efficient and practical solution for model compression, yet low-bit PTQ remains challenging for MDE models. When applying PTQ to Depth Anything, we identify two key challenges: (i) independently minimizing the quantization error of the query and key projections fails to preserve the attention maps induced by their interaction, and (ii) quantization errors accumulate across layers, resulting in intermediate feature distribution shifts. To address these issues, we propose SPA-Q, a Structure-Preserving Adaptive PTQ framework for MDE, consisting of two main components. First, Attention-Preserving Calibration (APC) determines query and key quantization parameters by matching the full-precision attention distribution. Second, Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment (CWDA) learns channel-wise affine transformations to mitigate quantization-induced distribution shifts, and the learned parameters are absorbed into the weights after training. Experimental results show that SPA-Q consistently outperforms existing PTQ methods under 4-bit quantization, achieving an average 25.9% reduction in AbsRel and a 17.3% improvement in $\delta_1$ across NYUv2 and KITTI datasets.
authors: Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Nahyun Lim, Yun-Seong Jeong, Matti Zinke, Hyunwoo Yu, Suk-Ju Kang
bullets: Low-bit PTQ for Depth Anything is difficult because query–key interactions and layerwise feature shifts amplify quantization errors.
Attention-Preserving Calibration matches quantized attention distributions to their full-precision counterparts.
Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment uses learnable affine transformations to correct channel-level shifts, then folds them into the weights.
Across NYUv2 and KITTI, SPA-Q reduces AbsRel by 25.9% on average and improves δ1 by 17.3% under 4-bit quantization.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the SPA-Q framework. SPA-Q first applies Attention-Preserving Calibration (APC) to determine query and key quantization parameters by minimizing the row-wise KL divergence between full-precision and quantized attention maps. It then applies Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment (CWDA), where learnable affine parameters align quantized intermediate features with their full-precision counterparts using stage-wise feature maps from the transformer encoder and the depth prediction from the decoder. After optimization, the learned affine parameters are fused into the weights, introducing no additional inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at https://github.com/B1ueC1oud/CDIM
authors: Taehoon Kim, Wonjun Hwang, Hyunsouk Cho
bullets: Targets CLIP’s tendency to confidently map corrupted images to incorrect text prototypes, causing modality bias and prediction collapse.
Uses a frozen DINOv2-style backbone with cross-covariance logit ensembling, projecting CLIP text prototypes into a text-free image-feature space.
Applies gated information maximization: sharpens reliable per-sample predictions, promotes batch diversity, and excludes unreliable samples from updates.
Performs online logit adjustment to correct residual class-distribution skew.
Outperforms compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, while remaining competitive in continual and mixed-domain settings.

papers.selection_reason: Online test-time adaptation for CLIP; direct fit for test-time learning.
papers.title: Bridging CLIP with DINO: Cross-Modal Information Maximization for Online Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: CDIM improves CLIP’s online test-time adaptation under corruptions by combining it with DINO features, gated information maximization, and online logit correction to reduce modality and confirmation bias.

papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
authors: Xuwei Tan, Jingchun Huang, Ming Cai, Shuangquan Lyu, Tiange Wang, Yinzhi Wang, Ronghua Shi, Jingwei Song, Yang Jingsong, Yinghui Xia, Hehua Fan, Yifan Zhou, Hanxin Chen, Jiwei Song, Tianyu Shi
bullets: Targets the cold-expert problem: published experts may receive requests despite limited creator evidence or availability.
Proposes Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for expert-specific knowledge.
Surrounding platform supports creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible owner-scoped memory consolidation.
On an 85-task offline benchmark, the full configuration scored 4.65/5 versus 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt.
Results do not evaluate cross-expert transfer, longitudinal distillation, or cold-expert mitigation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes continuous cognitive distillation and owner-scoped memory for deployed LLM experts, relevant to continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
papers.tldr: CogniLife outlines a framework for distilling creator knowledge into evolving expert-agent memory, while preliminary platform results support its broader lifecycle but do not yet validate cold-expert mitigation.

papers.abstract: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.
authors: Riccardo Maggioni (Forgis)
bullets: Addresses how numerical signals can be integrated into pretrained language-model token sequences.
Uses a context-aware Transformer tokenizer with finite scalar quantization to encode four-step patches into 625 discrete codes.
Combines signal tokens, scale statistics, and text through the LLM’s existing self-attention layers.
Adapts the model by training new token embeddings and DoRA adapters while keeping the tokenizer frozen.
Reports macro-F1 scores of 89.0% for activity recognition, 85.0% for sleep staging, and 86.0% for bearing-fault diagnosis; also demonstrates time-series question answering.

papers.selection_reason: Extends an LLM vocabulary with discrete time-series tokens, a multimodal LLM interface for an additional modality.
papers.title: TEMPO: Time Series Understanding via Discrete Tokenization
papers.tldr: TEMPO enables LLMs to understand time series alongside text by representing signals as discrete tokens added to the model vocabulary.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary. Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Michel Barlaud, Clement Genninasca, Maxime Zanella, Benoit Macq, Benoit Legat
bullets: Defines the scale-invariant Cone Alignment Index (CAI) and analyzes its distribution under general, Gaussian, and uniform settings.
Proposes PLCP, a closed-form conic projection approximation, alongside PECP, the exact Euclidean projection.
Proves PLCP and PECP are collinear, preserve the same sparsity threshold, and identify identical active supports.
Establishes theoretical control over the number of coefficients discarded for a target sparsity level.
Extends PLCP to bilevel matrix sparsification with row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal structured masks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a conic-projection-based structured sparse attention method specifically aimed at accelerating Transformer attention, directly fitting efficient-attention research.
papers.title: A Parametric Linear Conic Projection for Structured Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a cone-based sparsity measure and efficient projection method that theoretically controls support selection while producing hardware-friendly structured sparsity for Transformer attention.

papers.abstract: Audio-based piano transcription is hampered by the sustain pedal and by noisy or missing soundtracks, problems that video-only transcription avoids, since a top-view video shows directly when each key is pressed and released. Most visual transcription networks, however, describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. In this paper, we propose KeyWise, a lightweight per-key architecture that exploits the known geometry of the keyboard instead of learning it. The rectified keyboard is divided into 88 equal tiles that serve as regions of interest (ROIs), and one small recurrent network, shared by all keys, follows each key over time. On PianoVAM, KeyWise reaches the onset accuracy of the state-of-the-art V2N (95.0% vs. 94.7% onset F1 at 50 ms and 97.8% vs. 97.0% at 100 ms) with 1.3 M instead of 28.2 M parameters, and it runs 4.7 times faster on the same GPU. At 100 ms, it is also significantly more accurate when the key releases (97.0% vs. 95.5% F1) or the velocities (89.4% vs. 84.5% F1) must be correct as well. On PianoYT, KeyWise pre-trained on PianoVAM reaches 69.4% onset F1 at 100 ms, comparable to the best published result, although it needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.
authors: Anastasios Chatzigiannis, Natalia Panagou, Maria Koziri
bullets: Avoids audio issues such as sustain-pedal ambiguity and missing or noisy soundtracks by using top-view video.
Divides a rectified keyboard into 88 fixed regions of interest, replacing learned keyboard localization with known geometry.
Matches V2N onset accuracy on PianoVAM with 1.3M parameters instead of 28.2M and runs 4.7× faster on the same GPU.
Also improves release and velocity accuracy at a 100 ms tolerance.
Transfers to PianoYT with comparable published onset accuracy, but requires fine-tuning for new recording conditions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of KeyWise. On the left, the keyboard is rectified from its four corners and cut into 88 equal key ROIs. In the middle, a CNN encoder gives one feature column per key ROI, and a BiGRU shared by all 88 keys feeds the onset, frame and velocity heads of every key at every frame. On the right, an encoder block and the per-key temporal model are shown in more detail.

Fig. 3 Onset F1 per PianoVAM test recording at 50 ms (a) and 100 ms (b). For KeyWise, the mean and the range of three runs are shown, for the global variant the mean of three runs, and for V2N its released predictions. The x-axis starts at 82%.

Fig. 2 Key ROIs through the encoder, for five keys around C4. Each block halves the width, so the 16-pixel ROI of key k becomes exactly one column of the final feature map, which is averaged into the key vector zk of Eq. (1).

Fig. 4 Reference notes found at 50 ms on the PianoVAM test set, by register and key color, with the 9 recordings pooled and the mean of three runs shown. Error bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over the recordings.

The upper part gives the mean F1 (%) of three runs and the Holm–Bonferroni corrected Wilcoxon p-values against the global variant (p1) and Global-88 (p2), and the lower part the notes found and the errors at 50 ms of the first run, out of the 42,241 reference notes of the test set.

papers.selection_reason: Video-only piano transcription via per-key temporal modeling; fits temporal video understanding.
papers.title: KeyWise: Efficient Video-Only Piano Transcription with a Lightweight Per-Key Architecture
papers.tldr: KeyWise performs efficient video-only piano transcription by tracking each of 88 keyboard keys with a shared lightweight recurrent model.

papers.abstract: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
authors: Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel
bullets: In controlled synthetic regulatory systems, all seven evaluated LLMs restored healthy phenotypes more often than they diagnosed the hidden fault.
The strongest agents rescued every organism but diagnosed only 55% and 35% of cases, respectively.
Misdiagnosis persisted despite agents encountering evidence distinguishing competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions.
Models could interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when causal comparisons were explicit, but struggled to predict outcomes under each competing cause.
Evaluations of scientific AI should assess causal inference and evidence use, not only intervention success.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Tracing the diagnosis–rescue gap through the investigation. Successive analyses rule out insufficient exploration and, for most systems, missing evidence, while bidirectional testing (dashed box) marks a correlate of successful diagnosis. Probes localise the remaining failure: models interpret and revise on isolated evidence, and still locate it inside a full record, but cannot derive what each competing cause predicts.

Figure 1: Controlled experimental environment. (a) A synthetic organism maps environmental inputs through an unknown gene regulatory network to three observable phenotypes; one example hidden fault is highlighted. Agents cannot observe the network directly and must learn about the system through perturbations. (b) Each session proceeds under a fixed experimental budget. All sessions include exploration and prediction; disease sessions additionally require diagnosis of a hidden fault followed by an intervention to rescue the phenotypes.

Figure 7: Evidence use breaks in context. (a) Each probe shows more of the investigation and gives less help with it: the two competing causes, the readout each one predicts, both, or neither. (b) Accuracy on decisive evidence, each gray line represents a model; per-model values are in Tables 5 and 6. Accuracy stays close to 1.00 for as long as the predicted readouts are given (Probes 1–2 and 3a), falls once the models must work them out (3b–c), and falls further in live sessions.

Figure 3: Exploration does not simply explain diagnostic success. (a) Models differ substantially in both the number of experiments they run and the ratio of genes they probe. (b) Within each model, sessions above versus below its median experiment count show no consistent advantage from greater exploration.

Figure 4: Alternative hypotheses and discriminating experiments. (a) Two different faults can produce the same abnormal readout, leaving both as plausible causes. (b) An experiment is discriminating if its outcome differs depending on which fault is present. Values in (a) and (b) are illustrative. (c) We classify the 60 organisms by whether an alternative fault fits the initial observation and, if so, whether an available experiment can distinguish it from the true fault.

Figure 2: The diagnosis–rescue gap. (a) A downstream gene can provide a plausible diagnosis and rescue target, restoring the phenotype without correcting the true fault. (b) Diagnosis and rescue at medium difficulty (20 seeds) for seven LLMs and three non-LLM baselines. Lines connect the two scores for each agent. CIs and prediction accuracy are in Appendix B.1 (Table 2).

Figure 9: The full session record behind Figure 6. Observed readouts (black) against the predictions of the true fault (green rings) and of the agent’s eventual diagnosis, G008 (red crosses); gray dots are multi-intervention calls, for which no single-fault prediction is defined. The shaded band marks the three G008 probes of Figure 6; the dashed line marks the commit; the red segment at experiment 22 is the post-commit refutation.

Figure 5: Agents usually encounter discriminating evidence, but barely use it. Each point shows, for one organism with a resolvable alternative (n = 43), how often agents choose discriminating experiments relative to random choice. Agents show only a small preference above chance (24.1% vs. 19.2%). Nevertheless, 91% of sessions encounter discriminating evidence before diagnosis, yet diagnosis accuracy in those sessions is only 0.30.

Figure 6: One agent holds the evidence and commits against it. Experiments 5–7 probe the agent’s eventual diagnosis, G008, in three directions. In each case, the observed readout of one phenotype (black) matches the true fault’s prediction (green) rather than G008’s (red). The agent nevertheless commits to G008 14 experiments later.

Table 1: Diagnosis accuracy by how agents perturb the true cause, with session counts in brackets. Testing in both directions is associated with higher accuracy for every model. Five cells contain fewer than ten sessions, so individual estimates should be interpreted cautiously.
Table 4: Exploration axes per model, mean per session over all 420 sessions (60 per model). Diagnosis and rescue are exact-match, pooled over the three disease sweeps.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) aims to infer and segment target objects specified by reasoning queries in videos. Existing methods typically first infer the target and generate a few segmentation tokens for it, which are then fed into a mask decoder for mask prediction. However, such segmentation tokens tend to be both semantically monotonous and spatially ambiguous, making them largely insufficient to represent the target to guide mask prediction. In this paper, we propose an explicit visual object grounding framework for VRS. Specifically, we first propose a spatial-aware prompt generation and refinement scheme, in which we query a multimodal large language model to generate explicit spatial prompts (i.e., bounding box and point set) for the target and then refine them through multi-step dialogue. Furthermore, we introduce a query diversification and alignment module to generate auxiliary queries that describe the same target from different perspectives. We then enforce cross-query consistency between their predicted spatial prompts to alleviate the training bias caused by query limitations. Finally, we select several reliable frames using a prompt-based keyframe selection strategy to support mask decoding and propagation. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/viscom-tongji/EVOG.
authors: Jun Huang, Junyang Zhang, Zijie Yue, Bingkun Wang, Yong Luo, Miaojing Shi
bullets: Addresses the semantic and spatial ambiguity of conventional segmentation tokens in VRS.
Uses a multimodal large language model to generate and refine bounding-box and point-set prompts through multi-step dialogue.
Diversifies object queries and enforces cross-query consistency to reduce limitations from individual queries.
Selects prompt-based reliable keyframes to support mask decoding and propagation.
Reports significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.
authors: Shengwei Wu, Yixuan Yang, Gao Huang, Song Li
bullets: Analyzes Muon training through preprocessing and main phases: learning output values first, then key-query structure.
Exactly characterizes the preprocessing trajectory and shows optimal normalized spectral margin after every update.
Derives nonasymptotic convergence rates for training loss and normalized margin gap under softmax attention.
Argues that Muon efficiently learns which tokens matter for prediction and provides a generalization guarantee to unseen contexts.
Validates the theoretical findings on next-token prediction tasks, without reporting specific quantitative results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
authors: An Nguyen, Anh Tong
bullets: Addresses LoRA’s flat optimization directions and linear effective-rank scaling.
Relaxes the shared-block constraint in perfect-shuffle factorization to span low- through full-rank adaptations.
Its effective rank can scale quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full rank.
Collapses the invariance manifold to a diagonal group, potentially easing optimization.
Consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks with greater parameter efficiency.

papers.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) detects and separates dynamic objects from the static background in a video, which plays a fundamental role in dynamic-scene understanding. Most MOS methods rely on pure visual motion cues alone, such as optical flow or point tracks, which is inherently ambiguous due to the compounded camera and object motions as well as motion-induced appearance changes, e.g. shadows and reflections. Naive fusion of additional information such as depth and semantics, however, cannot leverage their complementarity to the fullest extent. We therefore propose DynOSeg, a novel MOS approach that takes on a two-stage fusion structure. DynOSeg first combines a geometry-aware residual map and depth encoding into a geometric representation of motion, delineating camera motions and object dynamics. We then further incorporate semantic features to refine object understanding. We have additionally curated a diverse training corpus including CARLA-MOS, a new synthetic urban-driving dataset for MOS training. Our experiments show that DynOSeg consistently outperforms published state-of-the-art MOS methods across a diverse range of datasets. Our code and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/ACFR-RPG/DynOSeg
authors: Xu Han, Yiduo Wang, Yiran Wang, Viorela Ila
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in visual-motion-only MOS caused by camera motion, object motion, shadows, and reflections.
Uses two-stage fusion: geometry-aware residuals with depth first, followed by semantic features for object refinement.
Introduces CARLA-MOS, a diverse synthetic urban-driving training corpus.
Reports consistent gains over published state-of-the-art MOS methods across diverse datasets.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.
authors: Xin Liu, Boyuan Sun, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Song, Mingjian Zhao, Mengyu Liu
bullets: Among surveyed repositories, 52.6% of untied gated or hybrid checkpoints had reachable embeddings with norms below 10⁻⁶, versus 0% for weight-tied models.
At zero input, gated architectures suppress historical-state readout and can amplify embedding gradients by over 30 orders of magnitude.
Pre-RMSNorm can further amplify gradients, causing FP32 global-norm clipping to overflow and discard entire batches; one continual-pretraining run lost updates on about 20% of steps.
GroupClip separates embedding clipping using higher-precision or rescaled norms, eliminating update loss and healing affected rows in one step.
GateFloor adds a small positive offset to SiLU gates, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude with comparable perplexity in experiments up to 370M parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses training stability of gated sequence models (Mamba, etc.), a type of LLM architecture.
papers.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Near-zero untied token embeddings can silently stall gated-model training by causing gradient explosions, norm-clipping overflow, and repeated zeroed updates, while GroupClip and GateFloor largely prevent the failure.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) routinely name objects that are absent from the image. Latent steering can reduce this failure in one model forward pass, but a fixed gate treats early and late decoding steps by the same criterion. We observe that predictive entropy varies sharply within free-running generation, while states that commit to short answers occupy a narrow, confident band. We exploit this temporal mismatch by using uncertainty as a causally available, token-local control signal for an existing steering gate. We propose Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification (EGDR), which lowers the intervention threshold when entropy derived from the preceding step's already available logits is high and retains the calibrated operating point when it is low. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, the underlying static gate lowers CHAIR CS/CI from 53.00/15.30 to 32.00/14.30; replacing only its constant threshold with EGDR further lowers them to 29.00/13.60. At a matched 58% intervention rate, the corresponding static control obtains 30.50/14.00. The gain over the static gate holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and grows with the generation budget, while POPE scores and general multimodal capability remain effectively unchanged. EGDR requires no additional model forward pass and adds roughly 2% measured latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/alvi-uiu/EGDR.
authors: Riasad Alvi, Md. Asaduzzaman Shuvo, Md. Ahashan Habib, Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi
bullets: Targets object hallucination caused by LVLMs naming objects absent from images.
Adjusts an existing steering gate using entropy from the preceding step’s available logits: higher uncertainty triggers stronger intervention.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces CHAIR CS/CI from 32.00/14.30 with a static gate to 29.00/13.60 with EGDR.
The improvement also holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and increases with the generation budget.
Maintains POPE and general multimodal performance, adding roughly 2% measured latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of EGDR. (a) Held-out calibration selects the steering depth ℓ∗, estimates the prior-removed direction v(ℓ∗), threshold τ , and entropy band [Hlo, Hhi], and tunes α and wτ . (b) At each decoding step, the current hidden state yields risk Rt, while preceding-step entropy lowers τ to τeff. If Rt > τeff, EGDR injects αv(ℓ∗). This requires no additional forward pass or trained parameter. (c) The adaptive threshold admits states missed by the static gate; at the first token, ê = 0 and τeff = τ .

Figure 1. Overview of EGDR. Both gates share v, ℓ∗ and α; only the threshold differs. (a) A static gate applies one threshold τ at every step. (b) EGDR lowers it to τeff(t) using the entropy of the preceding step’s logits, rescaled to the calibrated band, and so corrects states the static gate misses; at t=1, ê=0 and τeff=τ . Gate strips are schematic; bubbles quote the second paragraph of real LLaVA-1.5-7B captions verbatim (CHAIR: hallucinated objects in red, grounded in green).

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of object hallucination mitigation. LLaVA-1.5-7B captions of a COCO val2014 image under unsteered decoding (Regular), the calibrated static gate, and EGDR at the locked operating point of Sec. 5.1 (greedy, 512 tokens). Objects that the CHAIR evaluator flags as hallucinated against the COCO annotations are in red. Image cropped for display.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces object hallucination in large vision-language models via entropy-gated steering; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: EGDR uses token-level predictive entropy to dynamically control latent steering, reducing object hallucinations in LVLMs without extra forward passes or meaningful capability loss.

papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
authors: Mostafa 'Neo' Mohsenvand
bullets: Addresses the lack of guarantees for language-model arithmetic and the externalization of tool-based computation.
Uses Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter; each pass reads three cells and emits a digit, carry/borrow, and next operation, while fixed runtime controls the sheet.
A Lean proof reduces correctness for all input lengths to checking the finite set of views presented by the runtime; this does not hold when steps access earlier outputs.
All 2,446 deployment views passed, and the model handled signed arithmetic, multiplication, division, square roots, and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length.
The system solved all reported browser test problems and supports symbolic polynomial operations, while a multiplicative adapter gate preserves the base model when arithmetic is unused.

The view (three cells, 32 × 96 pixels) enters Qwen3.5-0.8B as three image tokens after the operation token MUL; the outputs, read at = and two placeholder positions, are the digit, the carry and the next operation. Below: the operation sequence of the full product. b, Margins of all 2,446 views on the deployment device (Apple M4, WebGPU, 16-bit), grouped by table. The smallest margin, 3.02 logits, belongs to the addition view 5 + 6 with no incoming carry. c, Exact answers on the pre-registered comparison of 220 problems (sums of 10–1,000 digits and products of 2–20-digit numbers, 20 per length; Methods), overall and on the longest sums and products. papers.selection_reason: Small vision-language model with certified exact arithmetic on rendered working memory; fits multimodal LLM/VLM research.
papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.tldr: Sketchpad certifies arbitrary-length exact arithmetic by having a small vision-language model process a bounded local view of a rendered working sheet at each step.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in cluttered environments must react to unexpected contacts before the first impact peak, which arrives within tens of milliseconds. Learned whole-body policies running at 50 Hz introduce a policy-cycle delay and may suppress a protective withdrawal as a tracking error. To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates instantaneous tactile reflexes with learned whole-body control. ARC consists of two components: an instantaneous reflex pathway and bottom-up reflex integration. The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts from full-body tactile sensing, solves a whole-body withdrawal pose, and delivers it directly to the motors within 10 ms. Bottom-up reflex integration combines reflex-in-the-loop policy learning, reflex-transparent policy alignment, and reflex-informed policy adaptation to sustain the withdrawal, maintain balance, and complete longer-horizon recovery. We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three categories of hazardous contact. Compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms, ARC reduces the first force peak by 34.1% and reduces the contact impulse from 0.2632 N s to 0.1225 N s (a 2.15x ratio). We further demonstrate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing. Project page: https://minusmodulo.github.io/reflexarc-website/
authors: Mingyu Wang, Si Li, Ziqing Chen, He Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Targets the tens-of-milliseconds impact window that can precede learned-policy reactions.
ARC combines an instantaneous full-body tactile reflex pathway with bottom-up integration into learned control.
The reflex computes a whole-body withdrawal pose and sends it directly to the motors, while policy integration supports balance and recovery.
On a Unitree G1 across three hazardous-contact categories, ARC reduced the first force peak by 34.1% versus a 20 ms delayed reflex.
It also demonstrated protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal using foot tactile sensing.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of ARC. A hazardous contact is localized within milliseconds, a whole-body reflex pose is solved, and the motors withdraw within 10 ms of the collision (Sec. III). The reflex then propagates bottom-up to the policy, which sustains it while continuing its task and draws on a human prior to retreat naturally from the contact region, avoiding secondary collisions (Sec. IV).

Fig. 5: Real-world tasks. ARC is evaluated across motion tracking, teleoperation, and traversal, spanning contacts with static obstacles, dynamic objects, and moving humans. ARC demonstrates reliable performance across all these tasks.

Fig. 3: Reflex poses solved for different contacts. From an identical initial configuration, the solver produces distinct whole-body reflexes qr depending on which body region is struck and from which direction (spheres).

Fig. 4: One Mapping. We subtract the reflex offset from the observed joint positions and add it to the policy’s output joint targets, so the policy sees a single distribution rather than one per reflex direction, and supervise it with DAgger against the reflex-free counterfactual it would have produced.

Fig. 6: Effect of latency on contact impact. Blue/red: 0/20 ms added delay. Solid: contact force (left axis); dashed: hand displacement (right axis). Shading: impulse integrated where F > 2N. Removing the 20 ms delay reduces the first force peak from 21.64 N to 14.25 N and the contact impulse from 0.2632 Ns to 0.1225 Ns (2.15×).

TABLE I: Ablation study. Metrics are grouped into local withdrawal, contact, and global recovery. Explicit ref. replaces the AMP reward with direct tracking of a retreat motion. Metrics: Hold is the mean withdrawal distance over 0.2 s to 1.0 s; C is the signed compensation score (positive: opposing the reflex; negative: reinforcing it); J100ms integrates the normal contact force over the first 100 ms; Rehit is the fraction of trials that contact the same obstacle again after separation; D3s and v0.2–1s are the root displacement at 3 s and its mean velocity along the commanded recovery direction; the last two columns are the fractions of trials whose displacement at 3 s reaches 0.5 m and 1.5 m.

papers.selection_reason: Tactile reflex integration for whole-body humanoid control, relevant to embodied agents.
papers.title: ReflexArc: Bottom-Up Integration of Instantaneous Tactile Reflexes into Whole-Body Humanoid Control
papers.tldr: ReflexArc enables humanoids to respond to hazardous contact within 10 ms by integrating tactile reflexes directly into whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.
authors: Vimarsh Shah, Dulanga Weerakoon, Ajinkya Deshpande, Saksham Agarwal, Nilesh Bhatia, Neel Kiran Naik, Parth Shah, Sravan Danda, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Sougata Sen
bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.
Uses an Embodied Fusion module to jointly represent language, gesture, and vision in a shared embedding space.
Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines pair an LLM proposer with a verifier on an implicit bet: discovery quality rises with verification strength. Under a pre-registered protocol we test this bet in two real-data domains -- job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading on Beijing T-Drive trajectories -- across 100 matched LLM/random pairs per domain and three verifier tiers. The manipulation binds -- a 429-case mutation battery shows scores rising across tiers -- yet the paired LLM-over-random advantage does not scale with it (A, one-sided p=0.1115; D, p=0.9994), and in D shrinks under the strict tier (margin contrast -0.040, p=0.0013). The two lower gates promote identical candidates in 100/100 and 99/100 pairs, so the strict order is untestable when they coincide. Constructively, LLM proposals carry a real paired advantage over random controls, but a post-hoc union-pool analysis shows the fastest path to better discovery is widening the pool, not tightening the gate: mixing the two pools adds +1.52 holdout-value units in domain A (one-sided Wilcoxon, n=100, p=0.0002) -- evidence that pool composition, not verification strength, is the lever. Criteria, ledgers and scripts are archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23308866).
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: A pre-registered test evaluated LLM proposers with three verifier strengths in job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading.
Verifier tiers were behaviorally distinct, but stronger verification did not increase the LLM-over-random discovery advantage.
In one domain, the advantage decreased under the strictest verifier.
A post-hoc union-pool analysis found that mixing proposer pools improved holdout value, supporting pool composition as the key lever.
The study’s criteria, ledgers, and scripts are publicly archived on Zenodo.
