papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM-based automated research pipelines, testing the interaction between proposers and verifiers in a scientific discovery context.
papers.title: Verifier strength does not buy discovery quality: a pre-registered two-domain test of LLM-based automated research, with post-hoc evidence pointing to proposer-pool composition
papers.tldr: Across two domains, stronger verification did not improve LLM-driven discovery; expanding and diversifying the proposer pool appeared more effective.

papers.abstract: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. While raw videos offer an abundant and dynamic source of visual knowledge, transforming them into precise instruction data remains highly challenging. To bridge this gap, we present VidUEU-Agent, an automated pipeline that synthesizes instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent follows a four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs metadata and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples. More importantly, our agent framework can autonomously iterate the data distribution based on downstream training results, thereby optimizing data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, a large-scale dataset of 100K training samples spanning multiple domains and tasks, providing a robust foundation for developing comprehensive multimodal capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K yields significant and consistent performance gains across diverse representative benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of our proposed agent framework and dataset.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Zhejun Cui, Yichen Zhu, Hangshuo Cao, Qi Kang, Yechi Liu, Kaixuan Wang, Yu-Jie Yuan, Chunwei Wang, Yu Zhang, Bo Dai
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and high annotation cost of multimodal instruction data.
Uses a four-stage pipeline: quality filtering, keyframe and multimodal-signal mining, metadata construction, and instruction synthesis.
Autonomously refines the data distribution using downstream training results to improve quality, balance, and effectiveness.
Produces VidUEU-100K, a 100K-sample dataset spanning multiple domains and tasks.
Fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K brings significant and consistent gains across diverse benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VidUEU-Agent. The agent performs global perception with quality gating, then conducts keyframe mining using multimodal signals and tool verification, builds metadata, and finally synthesizes instruction data for understanding, editing, and unified tasks.
Figure 3: Failure Case Examples: Illustrating four common rejected cases in the processing pipeline: Global Rejection, Quality Failure, Gen-Unsuitability, and Task Mismatch.

papers.selection_reason: Data-curation agent for multimodal understanding and editing from videos; relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks

papers.abstract: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
authors: Yangze Liu (Shandong University)
bullets: Auditing HAL and tau2-bench found four errors in grading, cost accounting, trajectory logging, and evaluator/version handling.
A general agent’s apparent 13-point deficit disappeared when episodes that had not triggered grading were scored under the benchmark’s own rule.
Double-counted nested model calls, mislabeled grader actions, and a faulty mode check each produced plausible but incorrect measurements.
Regrading archived trajectories under a newer evaluator changed leaderboard rankings, showing that evaluator updates are new measurements.
Recommended safeguards include reporting graded fractions, aggregating cost from root spans, tagging action provenance, and publishing evaluator-version re-grade diffs.

papers.selection_reason: Audits the infrastructure of agent evaluation, highlighting how logging and replay mechanisms (memory) can silently affect leaderboard scores.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.
authors: Renee Jia, Jinzhou Wu
bullets: Fine-tuning 7–9B open-weight models with a reward or quality annotation marking the correct option induces strong metadata dependence.
When the annotation is moved to a wrong option, models follow it on 97–100% of CommonsenseQA items.
Removing the annotation often preserves accuracy, so standard evaluation can miss this hidden reliance.
Cue-following increases with training-time reliability and can emerge from neutral or nonsense annotation words; test wording changes its strength.
A Qwen3 direct-preference-optimization experiment shows similar dependence in option-letter scores.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the unintended behavior of LLMs when fine-tuned on metadata, a relevant finding for understanding and controlling LLM behavior.
papers.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
papers.tldr: Models can silently learn to trust reliable metadata over the actual task, even when all training labels are correct.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
authors: Yeonseok Lee
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding and memory-bandwidth costs of autoregressive VLA policies on embedded aerial platforms.
Uses a compact RGB-D ViT, non-reconstructive JEPA-style latent prediction, a five-head predictor ensemble, and two-step conditional flow matching for velocity/yaw-rate chunks.
DAgger training alone achieved only 11.1–21.1% success across six checkpoints; behavior cloning failed on all 60 missions despite low open-loop error.

A map-free shield using depth memory, barrier constraints, field-of-view limits, and path backoff increased one policy’s success from 21.1% to 52.2% and reduced crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, with more timeouts.
Code, a trained 72.6 MB policy, and the benchmark dataset are publicly released; results are limited to PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in procedurally generated forests.

The executor (bottom) evaluates the newest valid chunk at its chunk-local time, converts it to NED setpoints, and streams them to PX4 over microXRCE-DDS; it engages the braking fallback when a fallback is requested or no valid chunk is available. papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop learning-based quadrotor navigation with latent prediction and flow-matching control; fits robot navigation.
papers.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
papers.tldr: Aero-VPA enables agile, map-free quadrotor navigation on edge hardware using few-step flow-matching actions and an uncertainty-aware runtime shield, improving closed-loop success while reducing crashes in simulation.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.
authors: Junhyeong Park, Wook Jung, Taeyoung Kim, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the costly need for target-robot demonstrations caused by the human–robot embodiment gap.
Uses geometry-anchored observation alignment and a decoupled-decoder tokenizer to bridge representation and action spaces.
Enables human demonstrations to provide behavioral supervision while preserving pretrained VLA visual, semantic, and control priors.
Improves object-transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3; skill transfer reaches 62.7.
Scope: evaluated on real-world tasks with unpaired human and robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: A team serving a 9B-20B open-weight language model on vLLM or SGLang must choose a quantization recipe, and needs two numbers: the speedup over BF16 and the accuracy given up. We assemble every public measurement of these numbers that we could verify and find that the record supplies them only in pieces. Only two checkpoints, both INT4 builds of Gemma 3 12B, have both a vLLM timing and an accuracy score, and that score covers a single MMLU subject, one that the AWQ build was calibrated on. The batch-1 timings predate current engine releases, AMD and Intel Gaudi have no timing in this band at all, and FP4 has none against BF16. The timings that do exist follow one rule. Decoding a small batch is limited by memory bandwidth, so 4-bit weights roughly double speed (2.12x for Qwen2.5-14B on an A100), but the gain vanishes once a large batch makes the GPU compute-bound (1.02x for Gemma 3 12B at batch size 256), where FP8 is the recipe that can still help. Many published accuracy deltas, including every HumanEval delta, lie within benchmark sampling noise. We close with a seven-item reporting checklist for future measurements.
authors: Smit Kadvani, Kriti Faujdar, Spurthi Tallam
bullets: The literature lacks complete, directly comparable measurements of speedup over BF16 and accuracy loss for 9B–20B open LLMs.
Only two checkpoints—both INT4 Gemma 3 12B builds—combine vLLM timing with an accuracy score, and that accuracy evidence is narrowly scoped.
Small-batch decoding is memory-bandwidth-limited, producing roughly 2× speedup in one reported case; large batches can reduce the gain to about 1×.
FP8 may remain beneficial when large batches make the GPU compute-bound.
Many reported accuracy differences, including all HumanEval deltas, fall within benchmark sampling noise; the paper proposes a seven-item reporting checklist.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on quantization techniques for LLM serving, a core topic in Efficient AI, specifically addressing memory bandwidth and compute-bound bottlenecks.
papers.title: Twice as Fast, Until It Isn't: Quantized Serving of Mid-Size Open LLMs
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can nearly double decode speed for small batches, but its benefit largely disappears at large, compute-bound batches, while reliable accuracy trade-offs remain underreported.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.
authors: Hei Yi Mak, Hoang Le, Mehran Taghian Jazi, Yunke Peng, Huan Lin, Zhengzhi Tang, Zhexu Liu, Yao Wang, Yaoyuan Wang, Anandharaju Durai Raju, Tanzila Rahman
bullets: Dense-model FP4 recovery methods provide no improvement over naive FP4 baselines for MoE models.
Discrete expert routing makes MoE training–inference policy alignment highly sensitive to asymmetric recovery.
Asymmetric corrections sharply reduce probability correlation and router-selection matching between training and inference.
MoeResQ applies symmetric corrections on both sides, restoring alignment and substantially narrowing the accuracy gap to full precision.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Visualization of the alignment between training and inference probabilities for BF16, HiF4, RC Inference, RC Training, and RC Both.

Table 2: Training-inference alignment base on three metrics: the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between training and inference probabilities, the fraction of tokens whose top-k expert set matches exactly (top_k_match_frac), and the mean pairwise overlap of the top-k sets (topk_overlap_mean). For top_k_match_frac, we measured the values for layer 0, 12, 23, 35, and 47. RC denotes applying RC when quantizing both attention linear projections and expert linear projections, and RC (Experts only) denotes applying RC when quantizing expert linear projection only.

Table 1: Evaluation results for Qwen3-30B-A3B trained on DAPO-Math-17K with GRPO. For HiF4, RolloutResQ and MoeResQ, the attention projections and expert projections are in HiF4 precision. For RolloutResQ (experts only) and MoeResQ (experts only), only expert projections are in HiF4 precision. In all experiments, the routing layers, constituting only 0.041% of the total parameters, are kept in BF16 as outputs are highly sensitive to routing selection.

papers.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoeResQ shows that symmetric training–inference quantization recovery is essential for effective end-to-end FP4 RL on MoE language models.

papers.abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.
authors: Wenhao Xu, Changwei Wang, Shunpeng Chen, Yukun Song, Sifan Zhou, Kaize Luo, Shibiao Xu, Yuehua Zhao, Rongtao Xu
bullets: Experiments involve latent specimen, apparatus, and measurement states, with irreversible actions and outcome-dependent missing data.
It organizes the field around operational, epistemic, and evidential closure: realizing intended experiments, updating knowledge, and supporting claims.
The Record–Diagnose–Calibrate–Confirm cycle links experiment execution, diagnosis, feedback, and evidence generation.
A taxonomy connects these closures with delegated decisions and embodiment classes, while distinguishing commanded, realized, and observed conditions.
It proposes evaluations that separately measure actions, valid experiments, campaigns, and confirmed claims, and maps validation pathways across 28 workflows.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Four terminal decisions determine the epistemic method comparison. Bayesian optimization recommends a design that requires independent verification; active learning supplies a response map assessed on a declared held-out distribution; Bayesian experimental design distinguishes decision-relevant alternatives; reinforcement learning and model-predictive control choose state-dependent action sequences. Their characteristic failures are different, so method choice and terminal loss must be tied to the scientific endpoint. Curves, maps and trajectories are conceptual illustrations with no empirical performance values.

Figure 2. Historical profile of the 48 representative systems by scientific domain and publication period. Each cell gives the number of systems; (1p) and (2p) mark arXiv preprints already included in that count. Row and column totals make the cohort size explicit. Publication status follows the records selected in the accompanying dataset: Co-Scientist uses its published Nature version, whereas π0 uses its arXiv record. The cohort contains 40 journal articles, five conference papers and three arXiv preprints. Periods are ordered categories, not an annual timeline or an estimate of field-wide growth.

Figure 3. Six delegated decisions as complementary scientific interfaces rather than an automation ladder. Each panel pairs a decision with a schematic glyph and the record it must leave; the glyphs are abstract illustrations, not measured data or depictions of particular apparatus. The bottom Shared record bar represents a unified trial ledger across all six decisions; connecting stems are schematic, and the absence of a drawn stem beneath a panel does not imply that decision omits a record. Access and Prepare primarily serve operational closure; Select serves epistemic closure; Acquire spans operational and epistemic closure; Interpret and Confirm serve evidential closure. A workflow may delegate a subset of the six decisions, and the panels are not a sequence.

Figure 4. Causal execution, observed records and specimen lineage. A decision compiles to a command and requested measurement configuration. The command acts through a latent realized condition and an updated specimen–apparatus state before observations are generated; measurement configuration may affect both state and sensing. A dashed inference link indicates that observed evidence constrains, rather than equals, the latent condition. The trial record stores commands, requested configuration, observations, metadata, audit decisions and trial status; a noisy condition estimate can be part of metadata. An interrupted transfer stays in lineage and a remade specimen receives a new identifier. Record state is distinct from claim state. Apparatus imagery is synthetic.

Figure 1. Three closures around one shared physical experiment. Each row pairs a closure with its realized state, a three-step loop with an error feedback arc, its characteristic failure and the reporting unit it counts. Operational closure compares commanded with realized conditions and recovers from tolerance violations; epistemic closure updates belief from observations and chooses the next experiment; evidential closure turns trial records into candidate claims that need fresh independent confirmation. All three loops read the shared experiment history at the base. The reporting units Nattempted, Nsel and Nconf shown here are distinct, and Nvalid (Section 8) is a further unit; no common denominator or one-to-one mapping across trial and claim units is implied. The diagram is conceptual and reports no measured data.

Figure 6. Operational stack for a physical workcell. Language protocol is an input, not a stack layer: it emits the intent trace. Five operational layers—perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policy, embodiment, and verification and recovery—emit, respectively, a state estimate, typed operation, action trace, recorded condition estimate and recovery trace into the shared trial record, from which evidence obligations are assessed. World models, teleoperation and digital twins support these layers and do not replace physical measurement. Sensing modalities include cameras, tactile gel, force–torque sensing and balance telemetry. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 10. Evidence atlas of 26 physical workflows and two software-boundary components across Access, Prepare, Select, Acquire, Interpret and Confirm. Access uses X for cross-station mobile routing, M for local manipulation, F for fixed-interface or instrument-local control, S for software-boundary components and ? for unresolved routing. For Prepare, Select, Acquire and Interpret, R denotes reported implementation, A assisted or configuration-dependent operation, P planned capability, N scoped-not-reported and ? unresolved. In Confirm, O denotes an orthogonal physical assay, F repeat or follow-up testing, OF both, with P, N and ? carrying the same reported-status meaning. The Access F code (fixed interface) and the Confirm F code (follow-up) are different vocabularies. N and ? indicate absent or unresolved reporting, not experimental failure. The cohort includes two software-boundary components, so not all 28 rows are independent physical executions. Source rechecks retained the displayed codes, including ? where the relevant step remains unreported or unresolved. Full annotations and provenance are in the supplementary machine-readable dataset (f07_evidence_map_data.json and the adjudication ledger), distributed with the audit package in manuscript_audit/supplement/.

Figure 7. Evaluation design for embodied scientific campaigns. A strict two-by-two comparison crosses a reference or adaptive selector with a baseline or improved executor under matched endpoint, information, resource boundary and acceptance criteria. Every attempt enters the physical execution gate and remains in Nattempted. The metrological and audit gate assigns v̂t and ct : valid positive, valid negative and censored records all count in Nvalid, whereas execution failures and inconclusive records remain in Nattempted but not Nvalid. Nominated claims form a separate unit with counts Nsel and Nconf; confirmation uses fresh evidence not used for nomination under prespecified criteria. rvalid, ECYG, COR and CSU use their declared denominators; DA and IRR require a privileged reference label and apply only to controlled injection benchmarks. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 8. Failure attribution and claim reassessment. A low response with qualified preparation and adequate detection can be a valid negative; valid positive, valid negative and censored records remain in the valid pool and count in Nvalid. Uncertain transfer produces an execution failure that remains in Nattempted and returns through diagnosis and recovery, while an unclear signal is inconclusive. These trial statuses ct are distinct from claim state σk. Independent confirmation of a nominated claim can retain, revise or narrow it according to prespecified evidence; narrowing is not the only permissible outcome. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 9. Six empirical propositions grouped into three complementary research thrusts, with three cross-cutting normative invariants. P1 and P5 concern histories and realized actions; P2 and P6 concern validity-preserving recovery and matched-budget selection, diagnosis and confirmation; P3 and P4 concern endpoint-preserving transfer and qualified expansion of experimental reach. Provenance completeness, safety with human authority, and cross-site replay compliance must hold across all propositions. Grouping does not imply a temporal or causal order, predicted gains or established findings. Scientific miniatures are conceptual and apparatus imagery is synthetic.

Table 11. Minimum reporting items for embodied scientific campaigns

Access records categorical interface and routing modalities; Prepare, Select, Acquire and Interpret record reported (R), assisted or configuration-dependent (A), planned (P), scoped-notreported (N), or unresolved (?) operational status; Confirm records categorized follow-up evidence (O/F/OF/P/N/?). papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Embodied AI for Science, covering robot learning, physical interfaces, and the integration of AI for science with physical action.
papers.title: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
papers.tldr: This review frames scientific experimentation by AI and robots as one embodied-AI problem focused on turning costly, partially observed physical actions into confirmed scientific evidence.

papers.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Limited-demonstration fine-tuning can improve nominal success while harming robustness to appearance, object, and instruction variations.
RAFT uses two stages: low-rank adapter training on task-relevant reasoning annotations, followed by policy fine-tuning on action demonstrations with the adapters frozen.
On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0% out-of-distribution success versus 27.9% for plain fine-tuning.
On a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, RAFT reaches 70.0% mean success versus 36.0% for the strongest baseline.
RAFT improves performance under visual, object, and instruction shifts, while increasing attention to annotated regions and later-layer object-identity probe accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of RAFT. Stage I updates only the reasoning adapters, using reasoning annotations. Stage II freezes the adapters and updates the language model, action expert, and projection layers on action demonstrations, so action gradients do not reach the reasoning adapters.

Figure 1 | Reasoning-aligned fine-tuning for robust VLA adaptation. (a) Plain FT, fine-tuned only on actions, succeeds in the training layout but fails under small scene changes. (b) RAFT first learns task-relevant reasoning through LoRA adapters, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. (c) With the same demonstrations, RAFT succeeds under these shifts. papers.selection_reason: Reasoning-aligned fine-tuning for vision-language-action policies improves robustness; directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.abstract: Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65\% to 91\% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90\% to 99\% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/task-order-cl-4f7b/}{here}.
authors: Zirui Li, Yunlong Lin, Haohan Yang, Xiaocong Zhao, Chen Lv
bullets: Aggregate continual-learning scores should specify the distribution over task orders.

The starting task explained 90–99% of the order effect because the smallest task could not be learned from a cold start.
Beyond the first stage, order effects were comparable to training variability, and algorithm rankings were often not clearly separated.
Order-weighting via a transition-direction descriptor did not change rankings; the authors recommend order-, starting-task-, warm-start-, and final-error reporting.

papers.abstract: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.
authors: Zhixian Li, Xingsong Ye, Yongkun Du, Yunyan Xiao, Yanglin Huang, Pinxuan Chen, Jiyu Zhuang, Cong Xu, Zhineng Chen
bullets: Addresses IIMT without requiring paired before-and-after translation images.
Uses OCR to identify text and an LLM to create translation prompts for a text-to-image diffusion model.
Introduces Region Coupling Release and Coupling Expansion to improve translated-text accuracy and naturalness during editing.
Achieves 20.6 PRIM BLEU and 57.2 COMET under EasyOCR read-back, outperforming UniTranslator.
Reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy on whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese; results establish a training-free baseline for IIMT.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of the IIMT framework and editor paradigms. (a) The pipeline: OCR extracts text → a translator produces the translation → a scene text editor generates the output image. (b) Rule-based: remove, render, and paste separately. (c) Training-based: a learned GAN or diffusion editor (requires extra training). (d) FlowTranslator (ours): training-free flow editing with trajectory controls (CE and RCR) for text translation with background preservation.

Figure 2 Overview of FlowTranslator. OCR extracts the source text and forms a source caption, while a frozen LLM translates it to obtain the target caption. A frozen VAE encodes the source image into 𝑍src 0 , from which noise initialization produces 𝑍FE 𝑇 . At each editing step, the same frozen DiT predicts source- and target-conditioned velocities. Their difference updates the flow-editing latent. RCR perturbs the target-branch noise within the detected text region, and CE amplifies the accumulated displacement before it is fed back to the target branch. The final latent 𝑍FE 0 is decoded to produce the translated image.

papers.abstract: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.
authors: Keru Wang, Michael Xu, Ken Perlin, Nebojsa Jojic, Andrzej Banburski-Fahey
bullets: Addresses how socially distributed knowledge can be combined and surfaced within a co-located community.
Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM connects fragments, distills group knowledge, and responds in context.
Some memories function as instructions, allowing members to modify the system’s behavior.
A two-week deployment with 46 people and a follow-up workshop with 14 explored open-ended use.
Members used it to share daily life, query the collective memory, track routines, play games, and discover unfamiliar people and topics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: How SEAM handles one post, with an illustrative example rather than a case from the deployment. A post (A) enters both retrieval layers. The relationship layer (B) and the executable layer (C) run the same three steps: plan, retrieve and reflect, looping until each judges it has enough, and both read the same shared memory: a knowledge wiki distilled from past posts, and the archive of posts as submitted. They output reflections on the memory related to this moment, as well as context resolved regarding what actions to carry out and how to carry them out; The reply (D) is composed from both outputs with every claim grounded in the posts backing it, and the post, its follow-ups and the connections learnt are written back (E). Members can also read the knowledge wiki directly and leave a comment on any page, which the consolidation agent acts on at its next pass.

Figure 3: Word clouds of the subjects in the 345 posts: (A) what the poster was focused on sharing, (B) what the system captured from the same post, and (C) what the knowledge wiki recorded. Text size follows the number of posts behind each subject, on a square-root scale within each panel.
Figure 2: The four kinds of post, distributed across each participant’s own posting period.

Figure 4: Four replies, reconstructed rather than taken from the deployment: (A) and (B) the same question answered differently for two members, (C) an object found in the background of photographs taken for other reasons, and (D) a reply to a post that asked nothing. Highlighting marks what makes each part situated, associative or executable.
Figure 6: How the knowledge wiki filled in as posts arrived, with pages coloured by how many posts stand behind them: (A) as counts, against the fitted power law, and (B) as shares.
Figure 5: How far apart the posts behind a knowledge page lie, by page type, measured in posts rather than in days.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a situated executable associative memory system for a community, relevant to memory mechanisms for agents.
papers.title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
papers.tldr: SEAM is a community social app that turns members’ shared experiences into a situated, associative, and partially programmable collective memory.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
authors: Qinghua Mao, Xi Lin, Yuxin Qi, Zihao Xu, Jinze Gu, Yuliang Chen
bullets: Standard debate may override evidence-grounded safety boundaries through conformity pressure, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry.
SafeConflict-Bias evaluates these effects with invariant queries and retrieved evidence across six Web risk categories.
Across tested backbones, unsafe adoption under standard debate ranged from 0.0% to 100.0%, despite isolated models rejecting the guidance.
RiskTrace-Debias combines evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration.
The framework limited worst-case unsafe adoption to ≤2.0% without reported over-refusal and produced provenance traces for auditing manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of the SafeConflict-Bias diagnostic protocol and RiskTrace-Debias mitigation framework. SafeConflict-Bias pairs identical retrieval corpora with 7 counterfactual social conditions. Standard MAD aggregates the raw transcript and capitulates to social pressure. RiskTrace-Debias decouples deliberation via evidence-first precommitment 𝑎★ = 𝑔(𝑞, 𝐸), explicit metadata masking𝑚(𝑇, 𝑆), and consistency-gated arbitration ℎ, backed by audit tracing.

Figure 3: Empirical evaluation on SafeConflict-Bias: Unsafe adoption rates (%) across deliberation conditions, rounds (𝑅 = 1 vs. Full), and group scales (𝑁 = 3 vs. 𝑁 = 5) on deepseek-chat (left), and counterfactual social bias deltas (Δmaj,Δauth,Δconf for Standard MAD vs. Δmax for RiskTrace-Debias) across model backbones (right).
Figure 6: Case audit comparing StandardMAD (red: authoritydriven risk) and RiskTrace-Debias (blue: decoupled defense) on TRIAGE-1091.
Figure 4: Web risk taxonomy breakdown across six risk categories: Unsafe adoption rates (%) in Standard MAD (left) versus RiskTrace-Debias (right) under four social conditions on deepseek-chat.

Figure 1: SafeConflict-Bias isolates social bias from evidence quality. Holding queries and evidence invariant, neutral debate rejects hazards, whereas social cues (majority sway, authority, confidence) cause standardMAD to adopt latent risks.

MAD denotes Multi-Agent Debate; RiskTrace denotes our proposed RiskTrace-Debias framework.

Table 7: Comparison of Standard MAD, Naive Debiasing Prompting, and RiskTrace-Debias across 700 instances on DeepSeek-Chat.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates safety vulnerabilities in multi-agent LLM debate systems, relevant to LLM safety and multi-agent interactions.
papers.title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
papers.tldr: Multi-agent debate can amplify unsafe Web guidance through social bias, while RiskTrace-Debias substantially reduces this failure at inference time.

papers.abstract: As deep learning (DL) models become increasingly complex and hardware architectures grow more heterogeneous, DL compilers play a critical role in optimizing computational efficiency and enabling scalable deployment. This paper presents a systematic analysis of DL compilers, covering their architectural evolution, compilation workflows, optimization techniques, and emerging research directions. We organize DL compiler architectures into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, emphasizing the role of the middle-end in connecting high-level model representations with hardware-specific optimizations. We further examine representative DL compilers and recent optimization techniques across different compilation stages. Beyond architectural and technical analysis, we conduct an empirical evaluation of compiler behaviors to investigate the effectiveness of graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling. Experiments using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 demonstrate that compiler benefits depend strongly on workload characteristics, with speedups of up to 8.21\times for fusion-friendly computation graphs, while other workloads exhibit limited improvements. Our results further reveal that compilation overhead can require thousands of executions to amortize, and dynamic-shape compilation reduces cumulative shape-transition costs by approximately 70\% at the expense of modest steady-state performance degradation. By combining systematic architectural analysis with quantitative experimental evidence, this work provides insights into the design, optimization, and practical deployment of modern DL compilers.
authors: Jinghao Wen, Ruixuan Wang, Xun Jiao
bullets: Organizes DL compilers into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, highlighting the middle-end’s role in linking model representations to hardware optimization.
Reviews representative compilers and optimization techniques across compilation stages.
Evaluates graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000.
Fusion-friendly graphs achieve speedups of up to 8.21×, while other workloads see limited gains.
Compilation overhead may require thousands of executions to amortize; dynamic-shape compilation cuts cumulative shape-transition costs by about 70% with modest steady-state degradation.

papers.abstract: Promptable perception, from GroundingDINO to Rex-Omni, puts one model behind one prompt interface and returns coordinates for any localisation task. Every model in that line was built for photographs; none has been given a sketch. We present Sketch-Omni, to our knowledge the first perception MLLM built to work on sketches and from them. On a sketch, the sketch is the image, and text prompts detect, point, resolve object and spatial referring expressions, and ground affordances in it. From a sketch, the sketch is the prompt, and a drawing of one object localises that object in a photograph, even among several of the same category, a query that neither a category name nor a photo exemplar can pose. Two obstacles stand in the way. A photo-trained model's attention is tuned to colour and texture, which a sketch does not have, and no dataset pairs a drawing with the one instance it depicts among others of its kind. We build the training data instead of collecting it. An edge detector turns every labelled photograph into a sketch-like drawing that keeps the photograph's labels, and two constructions produce sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing data. On top of this, photo-guided relation alignment passes each photograph and its edge sketch through the same model and trains the sketch pass to reproduce how the photograph pass relates phrases to patches and patches to each other. Not one training label is drawn by hand. Sketch-Omni reaches 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation against 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with a lead that doubles when the photograph holds several instances of the queried category, and it is best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks. Code, model, and a hand-annotated benchmark of 2754 sketch-to-photo links will be released.
authors: Dongyu Wang, Dar-Yen Chen, Zhiming Hong, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of sketch-capable perception models and the difficulty of identifying one instance among multiple same-category objects.
Builds training data automatically by converting labelled photos into edge sketches and constructing sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing datasets.
Uses photo-guided relation alignment to transfer phrase–patch and patch–patch relationships from photographs to sketches.
Achieves 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation versus 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with larger gains in multi-instance scenes.
Performs best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks; a hand-annotated benchmark of 2,754 sketch-to-photo links is planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Sketch-based perception MLLM with spatial grounding.
papers.title: Sketch-Omni: Instance-Level Sketch-Based Visual Prompting for Perception MLLMs
papers.tldr: Sketch-Omni enables perception MLLMs to understand sketches as images and use object sketches as instance-specific prompts for localising matching objects in photographs.

papers.abstract: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.
authors: Praveg Vashishtha
bullets: Addresses fixed-node graph models that cannot predict at unseen sensor locations.
Uses coordinate-based tokenization, dynamic geographic k-nearest-neighbor attention, and per-node bidirectional GRUs.
On Delhi PM2.5 data, reports 31.0 µg/m³ 30-day MAE and at most 1.1% degradation after removing 40% of stations.
Unseen-location forecasts outperform nearest-neighbor interpolation and IGNNK, while uniquely providing coverage guarantees.
Rolling adaptive conformal calibration mitigates temporal-drift undercoverage, producing wider but better-calibrated intervals.

papers.abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) increasingly contain ambient sensing infrastructure to enable AI-based optimization of workflows and utilization. We pursue an alternative path: using ambient AI to guide robot action and optimize utilization. Deploying humanoids in the OR without ambient AI is severely limited by cumbersome de novo orientation and planning due to partial onboard observations. We posit that this can be achieved by coupling an ambient AI-based agentic orchestrator with the humanoid robotic actor, providing shared perception and execution feedback for humanoid autonomy in the OR. ActOR fuses a wall-mounted ambient camera and the robot's head-mounted camera into a shared object-level digital twin (DT). A large language model agent plans over the DT using pre-programmed locomotion and manipulation skills without task-specific training. During execution, DT updates and execution outcomes inform retries, alternative approaches, or replanning. We evaluated ActOR in simulated and physical environments. Across three tasks in two simulated ORs reconstructed from real rooms, ambient perception reduced exploration from 1.05 to 0.12 Explore calls per trial when targets were initially outside the robot's view. Closed-loop feedback increased success from 46.7% to 83.3% under nominal execution and from 8.3% to 51.7% under injected navigation, object-relocation, and grasp perturbations. In a physical mock OR with a humanoid, ActOR completed 14 of 20 single-object disposal trials and demonstrated replanning after scene changes. Ambient AI-based observations provide scene state that improves robot action planning, increasing success and reducing exploration compared with robot-only observations. Feeding skill outcomes and DT updates back to the planner improves multi-step task success. Our results show the feasibility of humanoid task autonomy for multi-step disposal tasks in a mock OR.
authors: Han Zhang, Sicheng Lu, Aleks Santari, Jeffrey K. Jopling, Masaru Ishii, Mathias Unberath
bullets: Addresses limited robot-only perception and costly exploration in partially observed operating rooms.
Fuses wall-mounted and head-mounted cameras into a shared object-level digital twin.
Uses an LLM agent to plan with pre-programmed locomotion and manipulation skills, without task-specific training.
Execution feedback enables retries, alternative actions, and replanning after scene changes.
In simulation, closed-loop feedback improved success under nominal and perturbed execution; physical trials demonstrated feasibility on disposal tasks.

papers.abstract: High-resolution range profiles (HRRPs) provide compact radar target representations but exhibit strong aspect sensitivity, complicating class-incremental recognition when historical data are unavailable. Changes in viewing aspect shift scattering-peak locations and amplitudes, while reflector groups may produce responses resembling ships. Existing dynamic expansion methods can also incur substantial parameter and memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose P-SER, a Physical Consistency-Constrained Scattering Expandable Representation framework for exemplar-free class-incremental HRRP recognition. P-SER reconstructs dominant scattering points from complex-valued sum- and azimuth-difference-channel HRRPs and observation geometry. The reconstructed spatial structure, target extent, and energy distribution are used to derive class-level scattering prototypes and sample-level saliency priors, providing physically grounded constraints for feature learning and old-class knowledge retention. A primitive scatterer dictionary further characterizes local strong-scattering mechanisms and calibrates uncertain ship--reflector predictions at inference. Meanwhile, lightweight residual adapters are incrementally introduced into a shared HRRP backbone to learn new classes with limited model growth. Experiments on simulated and measured HRRP datasets show that P-SER delivers competitive recognition performance without retaining old-class exemplars, while maintaining physical consistency, interference robustness, knowledge retention, and model scalability.
authors: Fangyi Wang, Peng Zhao, Haipeng Wang
bullets: Addresses HRRP aspect sensitivity, ship–reflector confusion, and the memory burden of retaining historical exemplars.
Reconstructs scattering points from complex sum/azimuth-difference HRRPs and observation geometry to derive class prototypes and sample saliency priors.
Uses a primitive scatterer dictionary to model local scattering mechanisms and calibrate uncertain ship–reflector predictions.
Adds lightweight residual adapters to a shared backbone for learning new classes with limited model growth.
Experiments on simulated and measured HRRP data indicate competitive recognition, physical consistency, interference robustness, knowledge retention, and scalability without old exemplars.

Fig. 4. Overview of PCSP, which reconstructs physically consistent scattering points from HRRP observations and uses the resulting class-level prototypes and sample-level saliency priors to constrain incremental recognition.

Dominant responses are formed by the range projection of physical scattering centers, motivating the use of stable physical properties for incremental recognition.

papers.abstract: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.
authors: Hengrui Zhang, Xupeng Miao
bullets: Semantic queries face dynamism across queries—changing arrivals and resource demands—and within queries, where batch-level costs and selectivities vary.
These dynamics are coupled: scheduling needs remaining-work estimates, while remaining work depends on runtime plan choices.
SeqoFlow enumerates dependency-preserving plan alternatives and decomposes queries into fine-grained units for safe adaptation and batch-boundary preemption.
Lightweight speculative estimates guide both plan selection and inter-query scheduling without exhaustively profiling every candidate plan.
Experiments across varied query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show substantially lower end-to-end latency than several existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Counterfactual sketch animation explores how a static sketch evolves under a hypothetical intervention. We present CounterSketch, a physics-grounded framework that transforms natural-language ``What if...?'' queries into physically plausible sketch animations. The framework integrates VLM-guided scene grounding, causal event-chain reasoning, constraint-based trajectory generation, and verification. It models physical transitions to update the scene graph, computes continuous object trajectories, and validates them against physical, geometric, and semantic constraints. The verified trajectories are then projected into object-level motion bounding boxes to guide downstream sketch-video synthesis. Experiments on CounterSketchBench (80 questions) demonstrate that physics-grounded trajectories provide stronger motion guidance than direct VLM predictions.

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
authors: Kailing Li, Ruoxuan Zhang, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
bullets: Covers diverse 3D-game tasks including navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery.
Organizes demonstrations into complete tasks with overall instructions, ordered subgoals, local skill instructions, visual observations, and keyboard-mouse actions.
Uses a vision-language pipeline to detect objective or interaction-target changes, ground navigation goals in visual waypoints, and compose task instructions.
Explicit stage boundaries connect task progression with low-level control and skill transitions.
Annotation quality was evaluated through model verification and human inspection; an audit of 500 trajectories achieved a 95.8% pass rate.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under this protocol; Trajectory EMA attains performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.
authors: Sihao Wang, Bozheng Li, Xuemiao Xu, Haoxin Yang, Yujie Xu, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses fixed rank profiles and opaque heuristic signals in adaptive-rank LoRA.

On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, it outperforms the reported uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines.
Trajectory EMA achieves performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
authors: Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo

Provides TextWorld for symbolic temporal planning, SimWorld for grounded topological path planning, and DualWorld-VQA for perception, scene understanding, and planning diagnostics.
Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.
authors: Renkai Yi, Yuwei Wu, Haoyu Zhang, Penghao Dai, Zhi Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun
bullets: Addresses disturbances that invalidate the next action while leaving parts of a robot task program usable.
Uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to choose between program reuse and predefined recovery skills, including bounded VLA grasping.
Employs multimodal LLM corrective-code generation after program failure and locally verifies each recovery attempt.
Introduces LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for mid-execution disturbance robustness and recovery.
On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore cases, Local DiMuRe reached 77.65% complete-task success versus 58.68% for the original program; Full DiMuRe reached 81.90% with terminal replanning and extra steps.

MLLM-assisted replanning (L3) starts separately after the original program exits and its entry checks pass. The planner revises corrective code using new observations and execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LiSA. We patchify the input image into tokens and treat them as nodes in a graph G = (V,E), where edge weights define a row-stochastic transition matrix S. Aggregating the truncated terms on S yields a global attention map that captures transitive (higher-order) dependencies. In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.
