papers.abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.
authors: Rylan Schaeffer, Sanmi Koyejo
bullets: Challenges three myths about Bits-Per-Byte (BPB), including that it is tokenizer-independent and that lower BPB implies a better model.
Using untrained models, shows BPB can prefer tokenizer–model pairs and vocabulary sizes despite chance-level accuracy.
Finds BPB correlates only weakly with downstream performance in models trained on the same data.
Shows unigram-normalized loss is confounded: its apparent 0.989 correlation with BPB falls to 0.057 after correction, and the metrics select different vocabularies.
Proposes a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can simultaneously assess only the true distribution, score identical predictions equally, and tie all untrained models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Option-Letter Scoring). Untrained models that output uniform distributions. Top: BPB of the correct label drops one step at each merge that shortens a label (inset), then rises with log V . Bottom: accuracy is constant, at the fraction of items whose correct answer is listed first. Red band, for reference: central 95% of a uniform random guesser; black dashed: always choosing the first option. BPB strongly prefers a vocabulary of a few hundred tokens, whereas accuracy finds all models to be equally useless.

Figure 4: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Answer-Text Scoring). Untrained models that output uniform distributions, scored on answer text (WinoGrande: on a shared continuation). Top: BPB of the correct answers has an interior minimum on every benchmark (star), between 8K and 39K. Bottom: accuracy on the same strings moves by at most a few points and has no common preferred vocabulary size. Red band, for reference: central 95% of a uniform random guesser; dashed: always choosing the first option. BPB concludes that vocabulary sizes between 8K and 39K are strongly preferable, whereas accuracy finds all models to be equally useless.

Figure 6: Myth #2, Continued: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Where the Differences Lie). Each marker is the least-squares slope of the decision term on BPB across the tokenizers of one set, with its 95% bootstrap interval; the format term’s slope is one minus it. Most of the difference lies in the format term, which accuracy ignores, not in the decision term, which it reads.

Figure 8: Myth #3: Different “Tokenizer-Agnostic” Metrics Yield Consistent Results (Minima). Left and center: the 56 digitized runs of Figure 11 of Tao et al. (2024) against vocabulary size; stars mark each model size’s minimum, and hollow diamonds show candidate vocabularies for five runs whose match is ambiguous. Right: the vocabulary at each minimum. BPC is always lowest at the largest vocabulary trained, and its optimum may lie beyond it (arrows); Lu is lowest inside the grid. Unigram-normalized loss and BPC pick different vocabularies from the same data.

Figure 5: Myth #2: Lower Bits-Per-Byte Means a Better Model (Trained Models). Each point is one model-tokenizer pair from Meister (2026): every model has the same layers and saw the same documents in the same order; the tokenizer varies. The horizontal axis is BPB on the benchmark’s own text; for BLiMP, the grammatical sentence of each pair, scored alone. Each panel gives the Pearson (r) and Spearman (ρ) correlations between BPB and downstream performance. Dashed line and band: least-squares line with a 95% bootstrap band. On trained models, the correlation is relatively weak, with or without the outlier tokenizer (red cross, Appendix F).

Figure 2: Myth #1, Continued: Bits-Per-Byte Is Agnostic to the Tokenization Algorithm. The three panels of Figure 1 for SuperBPE (Liu et al., 2025) (color) against standard BPE (gray, dashed), for untrained models on the same held-out corpus. Up to the transition point t = 262K the two tokenizers coincide. Above t, SuperBPE merges across pre-token boundaries and scores lower at every vocabulary size (shaded). Beyond 1.05 million, where the BPE sweep ends, the dotted BPE curve holds tokens per byte fixed. BPB prefers one tokenization algorithm (SuperBPE) over another (BPE), even for untrained models. Corpus: FineWeb-Edu-dedup, English (Penedo et al., 2024).

Figure 1: Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte Is Agnostic to the Tokenizer and/or Its Vocabulary Size. For untrained models that output uniform distributions, BPB on held-out test data prefers certain vocabulary sizes over others (right). For uniform distributions, BPB is a product of two functions: the number of bits per token, which increases with vocabulary size (left), and the number of tokens per byte, which decreases with vocabulary size (center). The product has a minimum (right). Corpus: FineWeb-Edu-dedup, English (Penedo et al., 2024).

Figure 10: Figure 5 Without the Outlier Tokenizer. Axes, markers, and statistics as in Figure 5, now over 83 scored tokenizers (74 for the three generated tasks), without whitespace-balanced-unigram. Without the outlier, every correlation stays weak.
Figure 12: TokEval: The Format and Decision Terms of Every Tokenizer. As Figure 11, for the 24 TokEval tokenizers, which saw the same documents in the same order; runs of one tokenizer are averaged.

Figure 7: Myth #3: Different “Tokenizer-Agnostic” Metrics Yield Consistent Results (Correlation). The 56 points of Figure 11 of Tao et al. (2024), digitized and colored by model size, with least-squares fits and 95% confidence bands (bootstrap on the left and right; analytic in the center, where each model size has few points). Left: pooled, Lu and BPC correlate at r = 0.989. Center: within each model size, where the points differ in vocabulary size, the correlation ranges from −0.61 to +0.48. Right: with each size’s mean removed from both metrics, r = 0.057. The pooled correlation comes from differences between model sizes; within a size, little remains.

Table 1: Two Standard Ways to Score Multiple-Choice Question-Answering Problems. Example problem from ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018). The correct option is bold, and marks a leading space. Accuracy compares the four scored strings; BPB charges the correct one.

Table 4: The Decision Term’s Slope in All Sixteen Conditions, Under Both Scoring Rules. Slope: Cov(D,B)/Var(B) across tokenizers, with its 95% bootstrap interval. Figure 6 draws all sixteen under TokSuite’s rule; the harness’s rule changes only TokSuite’s numbers.

Table 2: Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte Is Agnostic to the Tokenizer and/or Its Vocabulary Size. The minimum of BPB for untrained uniform models in each vocabulary sweep, on each corpus’s heldout split. Each minimum is the smallest observed value: at every integer vocabulary size for BPE, and on the grid of 67 sizes for SuperBPE. Chinese reaches its smallest value near the end of its sweep, where BPB is flat to six decimal places, so its V is a lower bound and we count no minimum. Where BPB is lowest for untrained models depends on the corpus and the tokenization algorithm.

Table 3: The Sign of a Correlation Between a Code Length and a Score Depends on the Text the Code Length Is Measured On. Spearman correlation across TokEval’s tokenizers between a released BPB and a released score, with 95% bootstrap intervals; n = 84 for BLiMP and 74 for the other three. A negative sign means that the shorter code goes with the higher score. The held-out mixture is TokEval’s own validation text; the code and multilingual texts are its released code and FLORES evaluations.

papers.selection_reason: Challenges tokenizer evaluation metrics and raises a tokenizer trilemma, directly relevant to LLM architecture and tokenizer selection.
papers.title: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them
papers.tldr: The paper shows that common tokenization metrics are not truly tokenizer-agnostic and can favor tokenizers or vocabulary sizes for misleading reasons.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.
Table 2. Novel view synthesis results on the CoFusion dataset, evaluated on the full image and within the change region. Best and second-best results are highlighted.
Table 4. Runtime comparison with dynamic-scene methods. We report the tracking speed in frames per second and the average mapping time per optimization iteration. Best results are in bold.

Table 1. Novel view synthesis results on the Bonn dynamic dataset. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on the full image (top) and within the change region (bottom). Best and second-best results are highlighted.
Table 3. Ablation study on CoFusion (averaged over all sequences). Best results are highlighted.

papers.selection_reason: Extends Gaussian Splatting to handle in-view dynamic scene changes, a transferable technique for 3D mapping and robot navigation in dynamic environments.
papers.title: SettleSplat: Monocular Gaussian Mapping under In-View Scene Changes
papers.tldr: SettleSplat maintains accurate monocular 3D Gaussian maps when objects move and settle within the camera’s view during online mapping.

papers.abstract: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.
authors: Megan Healy, Hossein Valavi
bullets: The study evaluates 4-bit MXFP4 and NVFP4 on a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN using wrist-accelerometer data from previously unseen players.
Full precision achieves 69.26% macro-F1; FP16 and INT8 lose at most 0.16 percentage points.
With 4-bit weights and activations, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points, while NVFP4 loses only 0.75 points and leads in every held-out-player fold.
Scale selection is the main source of MXFP4's degradation: rounding scales down causes clipping, while rounding up substantially recovers accuracy.
Results are specific to this small four-action wearable-sensor model and simulation settings; block size has a smaller, inconsistent effect.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Change in macro-F1 from FP32 for every fold (markers) and the mean of the 5 folds (black line), simulated. The text above each group gives the number of folds (groups of test players) in which that format scored lower than FP32. Fold 4 (red) accounts for most of MXFP4’s mean loss. Open markers: INT4 W4A4 uses one activation scale per window and is not like-for-like with the blocked FP4 formats. 𝑛 = 5 folds; the same 5 trained models throughout.

Figure 2: Ablation study, W4A4, simulated: per-fold change in macro-F1 from each design step (markers; fold 4 red; black line = mean of 5 folds). B is the block size. The text above each group gives the number of folds in which the step helped or hurt. Rounding the E8M0 scale up gives most of the gain; an E4M3 scale adds a smaller, also consistent, gain. Under the MX rule (E8M0 rounded down), 16-value blocks are slightly worse than 32-value blocks.

Table 2: Simulated formats (fake quantization; no speed or energy). Bits/weight include scale storage: per-channel FP32 scales for INT8 and INT4, block scales for the FP4 formats, and NVFP4’s FP32 tensor scale. Weights KiB is calculated for the quantized kernels plus FP32 biases and batch-normalization parameters. Δ is the paired mean difference from FP32 (0.6926), with the number of folds (of 5) in which the format scored lower. INT4 and INT8 use one scale per window for activations, so their W4A4/W8A8 rows are not like-for-like with the blocked FP4 formats.

Table 1: Deployable TFLite versions (measured). Macro-F1 is mean± sd over 5 player-grouped folds. Δ is the paired mean difference from FP32, with the number of folds in which the version scored lower. Latency: median of 5 interleaved rounds of 2,000 single-window runs, 1 thread, on a Google Colab CPU virtual machine (VM; Intel Xeon @ 2.20 GHz, KVM, 2 vCPUs = 1 core × 2 threads; Ubuntu 24.04.5; Python 3.13.16; TensorFlow 2.21.0). Latencies of the same files differed by 11.6–24.6% between two Colab sessions, so these differences are within noise.

Table 4: Sensitivity of W4A4 results (simulated). Change in macro-F1 from FP32, with folds lower (of 5); last column: NVFP4 minus MXFP4, with folds in which NVFP4 is higher. Main: the notebook’s definitions (ties to smaller; one layer-1 activation block per time step).
Table 3: Ablation study (simulated): mean change in macro-F1 from FP32, weights only / weights + activations. MXFP4 = block 32 with E8M0 rounded down; NVFP4 = block 16 with E4M3.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates 4-bit block-scaled quantization for on-device wearable models; fits efficient AI memory and compute reduction.
papers.title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
papers.tldr: For a small wearable basketball-action recognizer, NVFP4 preserves accuracy far better than MXFP4 when both weights and activations use 4-bit microscaling, largely because of better scale selection.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.
authors: Zixiao Zhao, Jing Sun, Zhe Hou, Mengze Li, Qian Liu, Cheng-Hao Cai, Zijian Zhang, Xin Wang, Gillian Dobbie, Jin Song Dong
bullets: Targets unreliable and inflexible agentic AutoML approaches that lack safeguards for intermediate pipeline outputs.
Uses three agents—Orchestrator, Executor, and Curator—across four phases of pipeline construction.
Validation gates check structural, execution, and semantic correctness before each phase can proceed, keeping artifacts auditable.
Expert-grounded templates adapt online, while post-run curation expands the skill library across runs and datasets.

Evaluated on eight datasets across six real-world task types, EvoML achieved full automation and the best final model quality in the comparison; reported task metrics include up to 0.94 Dice, 0.99 accuracy, 0.95 SSIM, and 0.79 normalized PSNR.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed validation-gated agentic ML pipeline synthesis framework. The Orchestrator progresses through four phases and invokes the corresponding Executor skill group in sequence: Task Understanding (skills 1–2), Planning (3–4), Training (5–7), and Post-train Processing (8–9). After each phase, generated artifacts and execution evidence are returned for gated validation; passed phases advance, while failed phases trigger recovery. The Curator operates after the run to evolve the skill library from accumulated execution evidence.

Fig. 4: Comparison of EvoML against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools across the benchmarking datasets: EvoML attains full automation and the best FMQ on every dataset, with markedly lower variance than the baselines.
Fig. 3: The Curator’s post-run skill evolution loop after a 3D reconstruction task with HDF5 dataset format.
Fig. 6: Effect of expert grounding: without the nnU-Net grounding, both automation and quality fall and variance roughly doubles.
Fig. 5: Effect of validation gating: without gates, EAC and FMQ both decline, sharply on the harder reconstruction, denoising, and semi-supervised tasks.
Fig. 7: Effect of post-run evolution: evolution reduces synthesis time and token consumption across the dataset sequence.
Fig. 2: An example validation-gated recovery cycle in the Planning phase.
TABLE I: FastMRI reconstruction pipeline design choices across methods, with resulting mean FMQ (SSIM).
TABLE III: Architectural comparison of EvoML against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools.
TABLE II: Generalisation to three general ML tasks: FMQ (mean ± std).
TABLE IV: Cost-efficiency comparison against expert leaderboard solutions.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving skill library that improves across runs is a form of continual skill accumulation and external agent memory.
papers.title: Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills
papers.tldr: EvoML synthesizes end-to-end ML pipelines through expert-grounded, self-evolving skills and validation gates that prevent errors from propagating.

papers.abstract: Dynamic driving scene reconstruction has made remarkable strides in recent years by leveraging generative priors, particularly in the quality of novel trajectory rendering. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between the generated data and real-world sensor observations, severely hindering further improvements in reconstruction fidelity. In this paper, we present ReconDreamer#, a self-evolving framework that synergizes reconstruction and generation for dynamic driving scenes, which substantially bridges the gap between synthesized novel trajectory data and recorded real-world observations. Within this self-evolving closed-loop framework, the generative and reconstruction models mutually reinforce each other through iterative refinement, ultimately yielding a significant enhancement in the 3D representation capability of the reconstruction model. Additionally, we introduce a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to further enhance the rendering quality of the reconstruction model. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks. Specifically on Waymo, at a 6-m lateral shift, ReconDreamer# improves NTA-IoU and NTL-IoU by 8.8% and 3.0%, respectively, and reduces FID by 15.1% relative to ReconDreamer++.
authors: Songling Liu, Guosheng Zhao, Xiaofeng Wang, Chaojun Ni, Guan Huang, Jiwen Lu, Xingang Wang, Zheng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between synthesized novel-trajectory data and real-world observations in dynamic driving-scene reconstruction.
Uses a self-evolving closed loop in which generative and reconstruction models mutually refine one another.
Adds a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to improve rendering quality.
Evaluated on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks.
On Waymo at a 6-m lateral shift, improves NTA-IoU by 8.8% and NTL-IoU by 3.0%, while reducing FID by 15.1% versus ReconDreamer++.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the self-evolving reconstruction–restoration loop. Starting from recorded video and an under-trained Gaussian scene, DriveRestorer improves novel-trajectory renderings used to train a new reconstruction. Rendering that reconstruction back at recorded poses yields new degraded–real pairs for the next restorer generation. The top rows compare renderings at 3-m and 6-m lane shifts across iterations.

Fig. 7. Qualitative module ablation on Waymo. Columns compare ReconDreamer++, +AGM, +Self-Evolution, and the complete ReconDreamer# model. Rows show the reference view and renderings at 0 m, 3 m, and 6 m lateral shifts. Orange boxes highlight vehicle details and road-boundary artifacts.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison on PandaSet under recorded, lateral-shift, and vertical-shift trajectories. Columns compare Street Gaussians, ReconDreamer, ReconDreamer++, and ReconDreamer#. Orange boxes highlight fine structures in the distant scene.

Fig. 2. Trajectory round-trip construction for Self-Evolving DriveRestorer. Novel-trajectory rendering and restoration feed an auxiliary reconstruction, which returns to recorded poses to construct inputs paired with real video targets.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison on EUVS Level 1. The upper row shows a training-trajectory view (Train Set), while the lower row shows an independently captured cross-lane test view (Test Set). Columns compare ground truth, Street Gaussians, ReconDreamer, ReconDreamer++, and ReconDreamer#. Dynamic foreground is masked in the rendered comparisons, and orange boxes enlarge facade signs.

Fig. 8. Ground-support comparison on Waymo scene 065. (a) The original ReconDreamer++ ground uses fixed support. (b) Complete AGM produces denser and more uniform support. Both top views share the same bounds, point size, and height colors; the cyan line marks the cross-section. (c) Signed residual ri = n⊤ i (µi − pi) to the local LiDAR plane. The mean absolute residual e⊥ and P95 show that AGM expands road support while maintaining surface alignment.

papers.selection_reason: A self-evolving framework for reconstructing dynamic driving scenes using generative priors, fitting Video World Models (predicting future trajectories) and 3D Vision.
papers.title: ReconDreamer#: Self-Evolving Closed-Loop Synergy of Reconstruction and Generation for Dynamic Driving Scenes
papers.tldr: ReconDreamer# closes the gap between generated and real sensor observations through iterative reconstruction–generation refinement, improving dynamic driving-scene reconstruction and rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.
authors: Zihao Feng, Qingzhao Zhang, Chunyu Xia, Bo Yu, Z. Morley Mao, Ramesh Govindan
bullets: Reasoning text and physical actions can diverge at their shared text/action interface.
The text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) identifies directions that strongly shift actions while minimally affecting text.
Across driving and manipulation VLAs, TNAS perturbations shift actions more and cause less text drift than text-gradient perturbations.
In driving, TNAS attacks caused new collisions with identical rationales in 52.6% of full-image scenes and 35.1% of localized-patch scenes, versus 4.55% for unguided attacks.
TNAS improved rationale preservation and reduced text drift while maintaining comparable action changes across both models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Rationale-preserving action divergence in reasoning VLAs. On a clean driving input, the VLM and action decoder read the same unobservable hidden state to produce a matching rationale and stopping action. Adding an imperceptible perturbation to the input shifts that shared hidden state along a text-neutral, action-sensitive direction. The model still outputs “Stop to keep distance to the lead vehicle” word for word, but its predicted action flips from stopping to continuing into the lead vehicle.

Figure 2: Hidden-state intervention probes. Top: schematic of the two protocols (gtext denotes gNLL and gmargin). (a) Probe 2 adjusts each direction’s step size so that all directions incur the same text-KL budget B (shaded) and compares the resulting action shift. (b) Probe 3 adds every direction at the same per-example norm |q|Sclip for q ∈ {0.5, 1, 2} (shaded, light to dark) and compares the resulting text KL and action shift. Middle and bottom: cohort means on 200 Alpamayo clips and 200 InstructVLA examples, with full values tabulated in Appendix A.7. (c,f) Action shift at fixed teacher-forced KL budgets B. (d,g) Action shift and (e,h) teacher-forced text KL across equal-norm strengths q, where dact (hollow diamonds) nearly overlaps dTNAS.

Figure 3: Shared forward-camera patch in Alpamayo. Illustrative patches on two clips of the evaluation cohort, optimized for 200 PGD steps at λcos = 20 in the patch layout of Table 1. Rows are the four cameras and columns the four input frames. Red boxes mark the patch. In every frame, the optimized pattern fills the front-telephoto box and a resized copy fills the front-wide box, while the cross-view cameras stay clean.

Table 1: Alpamayo input attacks. Fixed-prefix and free-generation columns use the canonical 200 clips. The open-loop column uses the 154 of them with obstacle annotations, as described in Section 3.1.
Table 2: InstructVLA input attacks. Fixed-prefix and free-generation columns use the canonical 200 examples.
Table 6: Benign rationale-only reader. Planned outcomes against reader predictions on 1,181 clean Alpamayo clips. Shares are within each prediction column.

Table 3: Paired tests for the input tables. Binary outcomes list the counts of the two arms and the discordant examples favoring each arm, tested with exact McNemar tests. KL rows count the examples on which the first arm has lower teacher-forced KL, tested with exact sign tests. Exact match and KL use 200 examples, and collisions use the 154 annotated clips.

Table 5: InstructVLA hook viability audit. Audit on three Bridge-distribution examples. Feasible cells have nonzero text gradients, a rank-2 text basis, and a nonzero action proxy. The selected hook is layers 14 to 17 on response tokens.

Table 8: Probe 3: Norm-matched clean-state amplification on 200 Alpamayo clips and 200 InstructVLA examples. At each strength q, all directions receive the same per-example intervention norm |q|Sclip, and q = 0 is the clean state. The KL columns report teacher-forced KL at q = 2.

Table 7: Probe 2: Matched-budget action shifts in Alpamayo and InstructVLA. Alpamayo entries are mean ADE shifts in meters on 200 clips, or 199 for gNLL at B = 10−4, at nominal teacher-forced KL budgets B. InstructVLA entries are mean per-step normalized 7-DoF action shifts with the admissible count n, which covers all 200 examples at B = 10−3 as detailed in Appendix A.4.2.
Table 4: Alpamayo layer-window sweep. Matched teacher-forced text-KL budget 10−4 on 50 clips per block. At layers 24 to 27, 47 clips have a TNAS row and 49 a random row within the budget.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and steers text-action divergence in reasoning vision-language-action models, directly relevant to VLA safety and embodied AI.
papers.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
papers.tldr: Visual perturbations can make reasoning VLAs take dangerous actions while producing exactly the same rationale, so safety monitors must inspect actions directly.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
authors: Tianle Zhou, Yang Zhang, Tianyu Wu, Zhuohan Wang, William Nixon, Juncheng Yang
bullets: Looped transformers keep separate KV caches per loop, creating substantial memory pressure during serving.
An offline profile estimates quantization and sharing sensitivity for each (loop, layer) cell.
A planner selects 4-bit, 2-bit, or final-loop KV reuse under damage and storage budgets.
Runtime decoding fetches low bits only when attention requires 4-bit precision, using a fused vLLM kernel.
On Ouro-1.4B, LoopKV-M stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit KIVI-4 and achieves 1.7–2.2× higher goodput under the stated latency objective, without significant benchmark degradation versus BF16.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression for looped transformers; directly targets memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopKV compresses loop-specific KV caches by assigning per-cell precision or reuse, reducing memory while preserving model quality and improving serving goodput.

papers.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.
authors: Roberto Dailey, Kajetan Schweighofer, Jamieson Warner, Conor F. Hayes, Elliot Meyerson, Babak Hodjat, Risto Miikkulainen, Xin Qiu
bullets: The paper characterizes this counterintuitive behavior across models, tasks, and modalities.
In high-dimensional spaces, perturbations often reduce performance but reveal informative directional signals.
Aggregating these signals enables local parent-model improvements despite uniformly worse sampled offspring.
The phenomenon arises from the interaction between reward-landscape curvature and the ES estimator’s noise.
The findings offer guidance for using perturbation-based optimization in LLM fine-tuning and other high-dimensional problems.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Best-of-30 selection ablation: (a) Training performance of scaled best-of-30 perturbation selection compared with the actual aggregated ES update. (b) Fraction of the perturbations with the best-of-30 method that are better than the parent. When scaled from a size where the best perturbation performs worse to the size of a typical ES update, the model is able to improve. However, the aggregated ES update direction still significantly outperforms this best-of-30 direction, suggesting that aggregation contributes further to performance.

Figure 8: Update reward improvement and update magnitude vs. population size. (a) Distributions of reward improvements from ES updates for different population sizes for CNN on MNIST. (b) Magnitude of ES updates in MNIST. (c) Mean and confidence intervals of improvement from ES updates at different population sizes for the Sudoku LLM fine-tuning task. (d) Magnitude of ES update for various population sizes. Distributions were wide, so for clarity, only means and CIs are shown. The model was Qwen 2.5 7B. In both settings, update reward improvement increases with population size and then plateaus, while the norm of the ES update decreases with population size.

Figure 1: The Evolution Strategies Paradox across three examples: OLMo 2 7B fine-tuned on Sudoku, Qwen 2.5 7B fine-tuned on Countdown, and a 60K parameter CNN on MNIST. Left plots show the fraction of offspring models better than the parent model; right plots show the training curves (i.e. the performance of the parent models over time). In each case, offspring models perform worse than the parent model for nearly all of training, while the parent models consistently improve.

Figure 2: Tracking the ES paradox: (a) A visual representation of the ES paradox over iterations in a training run. At each iteration, offspring are generated which are all worse than the parent model in measured reward. (b) Fraction of perturbations better than the parent in the Sudoku fine-tuning task over iterations in the training run. Larger batch size leads to less noise in the reward landscape, and makes the paradox more prominent.

Figure 9: (a): A visual representation of reward vs. perturbation magnitude, demonstrating why the offspring are worse than the parent. Perturbations happen at a fixed size; if they are too small, observation noise drowns out differences between good and bad directions, and if they are too big, the correlation between perturbation reward and direction quality breaks down. The paradox occurs when the magnitude is at a distance where all perturbations have a reward worse than the current model, but they still differentiate the good directions from the bad. (b) A demonstration of the tradeoff in perturbation size empirically, with performance of Qwen 2.5 7B on the Sudoku task after 300 ES iterations varying σ, holding all else constant. Results illustrate observation noise deteriorating performance at small values of σ, and correlations breaking down at large values, demonstrating the tradeoff visualized by (a).

Figure 5: Correlation between rewards at various perturbation magnitudes σ at iterations 200 and 500 iterations in the Sudoku Fine-Tuning task. The σ range at which the paradox occurs, i.e. the best of the 30 offspring has a lower reward than the parent, is labeled with red arrows. The rewards at small and large σ correlate significantly. Thus, the same good directions can be identified at various perturbation magnitudes, even at which all the perturbations are worse than the parent.

Figure 3: Reward distributions at different perturbation magnitudes. Checkpoints in Countdown and Sudoku training runs were perturbed 300 times at each specified magnitude, and distributions of rewards were plotted. As the magnitudes increase, the means decrease, and the variance increases. Thus, the offspring are likely to perform worse than the parent.

Figure 7: Average accuracy of Qwen 2.5 7B on Sudoku task along a random direction from −2σ to +2σ. Left: Landscape on a set of 800 problems. Right: Landscape on a set of 50 problems. A significant portion of the variance occurs at frequencies much higher than the perturbation size used in ES, and can thus be treated as observation noise.

Figure 4: Effect of perturbation magnitude: a) A comparison in fine-tuning performance on Sudoku with perturbation magnitudes where the paradox occurs (σ = 1e − 3) vs perturbation magnitudes where offspring produce viable improvement (σ ∈ {1e − 4, 2.5e − 4}). b) The fraction of better offspring compared to the parent under different perturbation magnitudes. Even though the smaller perturbation magnitudes produce better candidates, the larger perturbations produce better directions and thus a better overall training run.

Throughout, ρ = σ∥g∥/σR is the gradient correlation of the population rewards, equal to 1 and c in the two linear cases; λg = ĝ⊤Qĝ; and δQ = 2σ4 tr[P⊥Q 2P⊥]/((d − 1)σ2 R) ≤ 4/(d− 1). The O(1/N) and tr[Q3] terms of equation 49 are omitted.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes an optimization paradox in ES-based LLM fine-tuning; relevant to LLM optimization and training.
papers.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
papers.tldr: Evolution Strategies can improve large models even when every perturbed offspring performs worse, because their aggregated signals still identify useful local improvement directions.

papers.abstract: Large 3D repositories make it easy to collect assets, but difficult to determine whether they can be reused reliably across scene assembly, editing, rendering, game production, and training-data construction. An asset can look plausible in RGB while hiding disconnected geometry, problematic UV organization, or materials that fail to resolve correctly after import. We introduce Diagnostic Rendered Evidence (DRE): aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by pass-specific frozen ViT classifiers and combined through late fusion. On 1,234 human labeled TexVerse assets, nested grouped evaluation achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. On a separate, balanced 764 external reference test, DRE achieved 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy. Our method requires only an imported asset and renderer-derived evidence, without repository identity, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata at inference. Our results support cross-corpus portability and show that purpose built diagnostic views expose defects that just the beauty views can miss. Webpage: https://rbz-99.github.io/is-this-3d-asset-usable/
authors: Rushikesh Zawar, Vladimir Kim
bullets: Addresses unreliable reuse of 3D assets whose geometry, UVs, or materials may fail despite plausible RGB renders.
Uses aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by frozen ViT classifiers and combined with late fusion.
Achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall on 1,234 human-labeled TexVerse assets.
Reaches 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy on a separate 764-asset external test.
Operates from imported assets and renderer-derived evidence without repository, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata.

Figure 2: Three failure cases revealed by diagnostic rendered evidence. (A) An incomplete scan-like fragment is visibly unusable in beauty views. (B) A plausible-looking character shows unusually broad UV-seam coverage. (C) A regression failure rated Superior by the external baseline reveals disconnected and intersecting geometry in wireframe views. These examples illustrate diagnostic evidence rather than universal rejection rules.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.
authors: Kevin Weekly, Alexandre M. Bayen

papers.abstract: Object rearrangement planning in cluttered environments is often non-monotone, requiring objects to be temporarily relocated before reaching their final destinations. Although search-based planners can solve such tasks, they incur substantial computational cost and require expensive replanning when the environment changes. We propose the Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner (VARP), which learns non-monotone rearrangement directly from visual state representations generated from expert demonstrations. VARP predicts pick-and-place actions from the current and goal visual state representations, and incorporates an Action Refinement Strategy (ARS) to improve action feasibility and a Progress Enforcement Strategy (PES) to mitigate progress stagnation. By continuously updating actions from the latest visual state representations, VARP adapts online to disturbances without replanning from scratch or performing online combinatorial search. In challenging rearrangement benchmarks, VARP achieves a 98.3\% success rate with only 0.4 s planning time per task, 97.5\% success under execution-time disturbances, and 94.5\% under continuous severe disturbances, while generalizing effectively to unseen object counts. These results demonstrate that VARP provides a scalable and robust solution for non-monotone object rearrangement.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

The best mean score is 0.53/1; native-artifact workflows outperform rendered-image workflows by 17.2 percentage points on average.
Tasks require interpreting geometric and topological evidence with domain knowledge.

papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) aims to segment objects from unseen domains using only a few annotated references. Recent Segment Anything Model (SAM)-based methods have advanced CD-FSS, yet their reference-target visual matching is highly sensitive to target appearance variations. SAM3 introduces text-conditioned segmentation, enabling natural-language descriptions to guide segmentation across target images, but directly using the category name as the condition still yields unstable performance under severe domain shifts. We propose Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3) that leverages SAM3's large-scale vision-language pre-training to learn suitable textual tokens for each target category. RI-SAM3 comprises three core designs: (i) Bi-level Reference Inversion that learns complementary tokens before and after the frozen text encoder: the former remain anchored in SAM3's text space while the latter represent the category more flexibly; (ii) Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning combines these tokens differently as object queries evolve across decoder layers; and (iii) Presence-aware Confidence Supervision that jointly supervises query confidence and target presence for reliable predictions. With SAM3 frozen, RI-SAM3 optimizes around 12K parameters only per category and it efficiently segments each target in a single forward pass with reusable textual conditioning without per-sample reference-target visual matching. Extensive experiments over multiple widely adopted benchmarks show that RI-SAM3 achieves superior performance consistently in CD-FSS tasks, together with strong robustness, efficiency, and generalization.
authors: Jiahao Nie, Yun Xing, Wenbin An, Qixin Zhang, Yap-Peng Tan, Alex C. Kot, Shijian Lu

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistently superior performance, robustness, efficiency, and generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed RI-SAM3 framework. Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning (LTC) combines them with layer-specific fusion coefficients α∗ to produce the bi-level reference tokens T ∗ c for conditioning frozen SAM3. Presence-aware Confidence Supervision (PCS) jointly supervises query-level classification and global presence scores. Once learned, T ∗ c is reused for target segmentation without references or visual matching.

papers.abstract: As robot learning moves beyond the tabletop, many tasks require mobility, adjustable reach, active perception, and bimanual dexterity. Commercial platforms combining these capabilities are costly, while affordable open-source alternatives cover only a subset and require software integration. We present MABEL, an open-source anthropomorphic mobile bimanual robot with 56 degrees of freedom (DOF) and a US$8.1k parts cost. It combines two 7-DOF arms with 17-DOF hands, a pitching torso, a lift, a 3-DOF neck, and a holonomic base. Back-drivable arms and torso support compliant interaction, with fingertip reach from floor level to 2.23 m. The head and torso roughly triple modeled camera coverage relative to a torso-fixed camera. Apple Vision Pro head and hand tracking enables whole-body teleoperation without handheld controllers, with 137 ms mean glass-to-glass stereo video latency over the robot's Wi-Fi hotspot. We demonstrate an end-to-end imitation learning pipeline, from teleoperated data collection to policy deployment, using a shared command interface and whole-body controller.

papers.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to "put the toys away in the toy box" must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning. Project website: https://williamshen-nz.github.io/feijoa/.

papers.abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.

papers.abstract: Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component -- tutorials, the judge, and the world model -- to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them. To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations. We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures. This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge's ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts. Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge's ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion. This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.
authors: Phuc Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Hieu Nguyen, Parshin Shojaee, Chinh Duc La, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Rui Zhang, Khoa D. Doan, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawl
bullets: Mixed-data RLVR disproportionately improves problems the base model already solves well, with limited gains on harder problems.

The findings reconcile conflicting RLVR results across in-distribution and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.abstract: As large language models are fine-tuned for increasingly specialized tasks, their performance depends more on which training examples are selected than on how many. Given a large heterogeneous training pool and a small target set specifying the desired capability, targeted data selection aims to find a compact subset that maximizes downstream performance. Existing methods score each candidate independently against the target and select the top-ranked examples, yet this point-wise strategy ignores inter-example interactions: at tight budgets the selected subset is dominated by near-redundant points that waste capacity on overlapping information. We propose Query-based Submodular functions with Gradient-guided Synthesis (QSGS), which formulates targeted selection as a submodular graph cut over a gradient similarity graph. A modular relevance term pulls selected examples toward the target task, while a pairwise dispersion penalty suppresses intra-subset redundancy. The resulting objective balances target relevance and intra-subset redundancy using the same formulation across different selection budgets. Empirically, the benefit of diversity-aware selection becomes increasingly pronounced as the data budget decreases. To further close coverage gaps that no selection from existing data can bridge, we introduce a gradient-guided synthesis step that identifies under-covered target directions via residual subspace analysis and generates synthetic examples to fill them. Experiments on MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA across Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, show that QSGS at a 0.5% budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B, outperforms the strongest baseline across all benchmarks, and yields increasing gains as the budget shrinks.
authors: Zhenghao Zhao, Yasutomo Kawanishi, Huihuo Zheng, Michael E. Papka, Yan Yan
bullets: Targets task-relevant examples while reducing redundancy through a submodular graph-cut objective over gradient similarities.
Uses a modular relevance term and pairwise dispersion penalty under one formulation across selection budgets.
Adds gradient-guided synthesis to fill target directions not covered by the available data.
Diversity-aware selection becomes more beneficial as the data budget shrinks.
Across MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA, QSGS matches or exceeds full-data performance for Mistral-7B at 0.5% budget and outperforms the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed QSGS framework. Given a candidate pool D and a target validation set V , QSGS constructs a high-quality coreset through three stages. (1) Gradient feature computation. A warmup model is trained on a small random subset of the training data and used to compute per-sample gradient features for all examples in D and V . (2) Query-based graph cut selection. For each candidate x, we compute the similarity w(x,x′) to already-selected samples, and the influence score I(x,v) measuring its relevance to the validation set. The submodular graph cut objective maximizes I(x,v) while penalizing w(x,x′), jointly promoting candidate–target relevance and minimizing intra-subset redundancy to yield a diverse yet task-aligned coreset. (3) Gradientguided synthesis. To fill coverage gaps, we compute the gradient residual to find uncovered directions, then use the warmup model to generate synthetic candidates and select to the coreset.

papers.abstract: In mixed-vendor accelerator fleets, many training jobs can run on several hardware types, and the best choice depends on each job's throughput on each type. Routing a job needs a throughput estimate for every candidate type before the job runs. We present LEAP, a machine learning performance prediction service that predicts each training job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks the candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of training job attempts a day across hundreds of different model types and more than 20 hardware types in a production fleet. LEAP predicts throughput from submission-time training configuration, including each job's prior throughput. LEAP reaches an accuracy of 77% over 30 nightly retrains, higher than the lookup table it replaced and at least as high as every alternative model we tested, including fine-tuned language models. Over six months, the share of eligible training GPU-hours that received a ranking by LEAP grew from 58% to 95%, and we estimate that it saves about 3% of training computational cost. In this paper, we identify the drivers that actually move accuracy and those that do not. We offer these as lessons for teams building performance predictors at fleet scale.
authors: Hossein Askari, Wei Sun, Chenguang Zhu, Bin Zan, Sreen Tallam, Keyu Man
bullets: Addresses hardware-selection decisions in mixed-vendor fleets where job throughput varies by accelerator type.
Uses submission-time training configuration, including a job’s prior throughput, to predict performance on each candidate type.
Ranks hardware by predicted throughput per unit cost and routes tens of thousands of daily job attempts across 20+ hardware types.
Achieves 77% accuracy over 30 nightly retrains and replaces a lookup table while matching or exceeding tested alternatives.
Coverage rose from 58% to 95% of eligible training GPU-hours, with an estimated 3% reduction in computational cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2 LEAP architecture. Serving: (1) jobs are submitted to the job launcher, which (2) calls the inference API with the job and its candidate hardware types. (3) Inference builds the job’s features with the same code as training, taking its prior throughput from the history snapshot, scores every candidate with the bin classifier and that bin’s gradient-boosted model, and ranks candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. (4) The preference list goes to the cluster scheduler, which (5) places the job on the fleet. Training: (6) each completed job attempt records its measured throughput in the job history; (7) a nightly trigger retrains the 13-bin cascade on the last 30 days and evaluates it on the next, unseen day; (8) the run publishes a versioned model and history snapshot to blob storage; and (9) inference loads the latest version through a stable pointer.

Figure 3 LEAP end to end. (1) A fungible job arrives with several candidate hardware types. (2) LEAP builds features from the job’s configuration, its prior throughput, and each type’s specifications; bars give each feature group’s share of importance. (3) A 13-bin cascade of gradient-boosted models, retrained nightly, predicts the job’s throughput on every candidate. (4) The ranking stage orders the candidates for the cluster scheduler. The job’s measured throughput becomes training data for the next night’s models.

Figure 6 The prediction model. For each candidate hardware type, the job’s feature row x goes to the bin classifier, a gradient-boosted classifier that outputs a probability for each of 13 throughput bins. The selector passes x to the expert of the most likely bin, k̂ = argmaxk gk(x), a gradient-boosted regressor trained under the pinball loss, which predicts log throughput. Exponentiating gives the prediction (Equation 4). Experts are ordered from the lowest to the highest throughput range.

papers.abstract: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.
authors: Haiyu Wang, Sai Qian Zhang, Zechun Liu, Steven Li
bullets: Verification cost rises sharply with length in hybrid GDN-MoE targets because GDN state updates and MoE expert execution dominate.
The GPU selects verification length using draft acceptance estimates and measured target latency.
A routing correction uses early MoE expert assignments to determine whether to retain the first uncertain token.

Across three models, HybridSpec achieves 1.75×–1.88× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.30×–1.33× over DFlash in single-request greedy decoding.

papers.abstract: Intracardiac flow is driven by complex, and time-varying cardiac motion and interaction with the heart valves, producing complex flow features that may provide valuable information for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. 4D Flow MRI enables non-invasive, time-resolved measurement of three-dimensional cardiovascular velocity fields. However, substantial noise and limited spatial and temporal resolution limit its ability to accurately resolve flow features. We propose 4D-MRAR (4D Magnetic Resonance Augmented Reconstruction), a deep learning (DL) method to super-resolve and denoise 4D Flow MRI data. Unlike prior DL methods that train and infer on static vascular regions, our method predicts intracardiac flow within hearts undergoing large deformation. Moreover, it uniquely allows for simultaneous super-resolution in 3D space and time. The method combines a residual convolutional neural network, a recurrent neural network, and an implicit neural field to predict high-resolution velocity and pressure fields while efficiently enforcing the governing equations of fluid flow during training. Trained on a synthetic dataset obtained from computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of left ventricle (LV) flow, our method generalizes to synthetic whole-heart 4D flow MRI data, and demonstrated promising performance on real 4D Flow MRI. The produced super-resolved flow fields exhibit significantly improved accuracy and greater consistency with the governing equations of blood flow compared with prior methods.
authors: Yusuf A. Ozturk, Jie Zheng, Fanwei Kong
bullets: Addresses noise and limited spatial-temporal resolution that obscure clinically relevant intracardiac flow features.

Trained on CFD-generated left-ventricle flow, it generalizes to synthetic whole-heart data and shows promising results on real 4D Flow MRI.
Produces more accurate, physically consistent flow fields than prior methods, though training relies on synthetic CFD data.

papers.abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.
authors: Erkang Zhu, Yin Lin, Xiaorong Shi, Xuanrui Lin, Jingren Zhou
bullets: Addresses domain adaptation when expert-created data and reliable training signals are scarce.

Improves held-out all-pass rates on Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark for both evaluated models.
Scope: evaluated on a single benchmark and two model settings described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.

papers.abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. In this paper, we propose Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a unified sequence-modeling framework that leverages a single large language model (LLM) for both trajectory augmentation and multi-task policy learning. LaMA-DT uses natural-language task descriptions to guide task-aligned trajectory augmentation through a set of supervised generation and alignment objectives, and incorporates a scoring-and-filtering mechanism to retain high-quality augmented trajectories. The same LLM is then repurposed as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer and fine-tuned on a mixture of real and augmented data. Experiments on Meta-World and MuJoCo multi-task benchmarks demonstrate that LaMA-DT consistently outperforms competitive baselines, particularly in low-data regimes, showing that language-guided data augmentation substantially improves cross-task generalization.
authors: Xinbo Zhao, Yuhang Liu, Xin Zhang, Lei Le, Zhaohan Xi, Yu Yang, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Addresses per-task data scarcity and weak cross-task generalization in offline multi-task RL.
Uses natural-language task descriptions to guide trajectory generation and alignment.

Repurposes the same LLM as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer.
Outperforms competitive baselines on Meta-World and MuJoCo benchmarks, particularly in low-data settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LaMA-DT consists of three components: (i) Multi-Objective Fine-Tuning. We adapt the LLM to generate meaningful, task-specific trajectories from limited offline data and natural-language task descriptions by training objective-specific LoRA adapters together with a shared LoRA adapter, enabling both trajectory generation and task–trajectory alignment. (ii) Data Preparation. Candidate trajectories are generated per task using O3, scored using aggregated multi-objective likelihoods, and the top-K trajectories are retained and merged with the original offline data. (iii) Multi-Task Policy Learning. We repurpose the LLM and shared LoRA adapter as a prompt-conditioned DT, trained on the combined real and augmented dataset, with task descriptions pi and a provenance token zprov.
