papers.abstract: Effective world modeling requires compressing salient history information that facilitates future prediction. However, most existing approaches inherit tokenization and conditioning mechanisms from video generation, where objectives are centered around perceptual realism rather than predictive utility. This discrepancy limits the world model's effectiveness, especially in environments dominated by visual nuisances or task-irrelevant background details. To this end, we introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a general framework that aligns history compression with the predictive objective of world modeling. Compression Forcing features Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history observations into a sequence ordered by decreasing dynamics saliency. Built on a diffusion backbone, this structure enables Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), allowing selective amplification of dynamics-salient information during inference. Extensive experiments across various environments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making performance, establishing Compression Forcing as a highly flexible and effective approach for world modeling.
authors: Siqiao Huang, Partha Kaushik, Michael Chen, Hengkai Pan, Kaiwen Geng, Omar Chehab, Fernando Moreno-Pino, Max Simchowitz
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between video-generation tokenization and world-modeling objectives, particularly under visual nuisances.
Introduces Dynamics-Aware Tokenization, which orders compressed history tokens by decreasing dynamics saliency.
Uses Hierarchical History Guidance with a diffusion backbone to selectively amplify salient information during inference.
Experiments across varied environments report better prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making.
Scope: designed for environments where task-irrelevant visual details can hinder predictive modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the Compression Forcing Framework. (a) DAT encodes history context into a hierarchical token sequence, with leading tokens capturing dynamics and trailing tokens capturing static details. (b) The Diffusion Backbone predicts the next frame conditioned on arbitrary-length prefixes of DATencoded latents and the agent’s action. (c) HG-H composes score estimates from varying-length prefixes, enabling inference-time amplification of dynamically salient history information.

Figure 2: Tokenization Attention map. We visualize attention maps in the cross-attention layer between DAT tokenized tokens and image patches in the dynamic decoder. As the slot index increases, cross-attention shifts from regions with dynamic motion (the athlete in motion) to static objects in the background.

Figure 5: Qualitative Generation Results on Multiple Domains. Compression Forcing enables accurate and high-fidelity auto-regressive predictions in CS:GO, RT-1 and Kinetics. Zoom in for details. Extended visualizations in Appendix D.

papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting causal data and training robots directly in human-populated environments.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art bronchoscopy guidance systems and computer-aided diagnosis methods have emerged as important tools for early lung cancer detection. Effective use of these tools depends on being able to accurately link a patient's bronchoscopic airway exam video to their pre-operative 3D chest CT scan. Unfortunately, the derivation of such links, which include bronchoscope depth and camera motion, from the exam video remains an open problem. Building on recently proposed 3D-vision foundation models, we propose DUNEDepth, a hybrid architecture that combines a shared DUNE ViT encoder, a twin MASt3R cross-attention decoder structure, and a prediction head that includes elements of the MASt3R and Reloc3r models. To fine-tune the architecture to our application, we utilize an integrated hybrid synthetic-supervised/self-supervised training strategy that draws on both bronchoscopic video and CT-derived virtual bronchoscopic views. Experiments drawing on bronchoscopic video sequences demonstrate that DUNEDepth more accurately derives depth information and camera motion trajectories than previously proposed self-supervised methods.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to support prediction and planning in embodied agents, but the knowledge is usually established before deployment and then carried into later encounters. Continual operation faces a different problem. A familiar environment may change, and the agent must use previous experience without allowing old expectations to override current physical evidence. This study asks what repeated physical experience must contribute for a spatial world model to become progressively more useful rather than simply more persistent. A physics-grounded dynamic maze separates recurring spatial change from the continuous consequences of action. Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory learns relations among environmental transformations, while state-action-outcome experience refines predictions of motion. Structured experience progressively reduces the need for future route correction and transfers to spatial transitions not encountered during learning. The advantage disappears when past changes contain no information about future ones. Continuous navigation further shows that predictive memory changes behavior when a previous decision becomes invalid but leaves behavior unchanged when the decision remains correct. Physical tests expose a complementary limit: correct topology does not guarantee correct action prediction, and accumulated physical experience reduces this mismatch within the modeled dynamics. The results characterize continual world knowledge as experience that improves future prediction and action beyond stored episodes while remaining revisable by the physical outcomes it is intended to predict.

bullets: Continual operation requires using past experience while remaining responsive to current physical evidence.

Navigation behavior changes when prior decisions become invalid but remains stable when they are still correct.
Physical experience reduces mismatches between correct environmental topology and inaccurate action predictions within the modeled dynamics.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is pivotal for computer-assisted intervention, yet demands compositional reasoning across instruments, anatomy, and workflow. Existing surgical vision-language models rely on instruction tuning with large-scale question-answer pairs, entailing laborious data curation and costly retraining. To bridge this gap, we propose SurgEye, a perception-reasoning framework that grounds reasoning in a vision foundation model without instruction tuning. Specifically, we devise Routed Multi-Task Perception (RMP) that routes the vision foundation model through task-specific pathways learned from public perception labels, producing spatial and temporal evidence. We further introduce Agentic Compositional Reasoning (ACR) that employs a frozen large language model to coordinate RMP specialists and temporal memory as callable tools, composing evidence across tasks and time into grounded answers. Moreover, we construct SurgEye-Bench spanning eight surgical procedures, pairing each question with perception labels for verifiable evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgEye outperforms state-of-the-arts in surgical reasoning. The source code will be available.

papers.abstract: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
authors: Xinbo Zhao, Yuhang Liu, Xin Zhang, Lei Le, Zhaohan Xi, Yingxue Zhang

Conditions a Decision Transformer policy on the learned task representations for task-aware meta-policy learning.
Uses a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy for zero-shot and few-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.

Results: It improves simulation success rates by up to 5.28 pp and 1.68 pp on two benchmarks, with an average 19 pp gain across five real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
authors: Peizhi Niu, Ge Shi, Vaibhav Gorde, Sarthak Ghosh, Christos Faloutsos, Min Cheng, Kevin Chen
bullets: Addresses gaps in static agent harnesses, including proprietary policies, undocumented behavior, and state-dependent recovery paths.
Distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages containing reusable actions and recovery strategies.
Improves TheAgentCompany checkpoint pass rates by 4.6–6.1% over the strongest compared baseline across three models, while using 57–61% less storage.
Controlled studies find that human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication can hurt performance, whereas human diagnosis substantially improves failed-trace learning.
One round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0–10.9%, suggesting agents should organize memory while humans diagnose failures.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
authors: Kunming Shao, Xijie Huang, Jierun Chen, Jiaqi Shao, Yanli Wang, Jiangnan Yu, Qiwei Li, Wei Zhang, Kwang-Ting Cheng, Chi Ying Tsui
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks by making 2-bit quantization more reliable.
For each 32-channel key piece, chooses between rotation and no rotation using calibrated attention error.
Rotates queries at read time to match each stored key representation.
Decision frequency follows the cache axis: per head for per-channel caches and per key for per-token caches, using existing sign bits for storage.
At 2.5 bits per value, reduces KIVI’s twelve-model KL divergence from 18.7 to 12.4 × 10⁻³ and improves long-context benchmark scores in affected models.

papers.abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.
authors: Anant Bhide, Akarsh Gupta, Edmond Cunningham, Justin Domke
bullets: Addresses candidate-model misspecification and overly concentrated Bayesian model averaging in LLB.
Preserves LLB’s language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline.
Optimizes model weights for predictive performance using a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective.
Uses a variational lower bound because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable for latent-variable models.
On real-world probabilistic inference tasks, matches Bayesian model averaging’s predictive performance while producing more dispersed weights.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
authors: Sinuo Wang, Jiacheng Lu, Zeyu Zhang, Maojia Song, Rui Sun, Beidi Luan, Yutong Xie, Jing Li, Daxin Jiang, Qi Wu, Zuo Bai
bullets: Addresses the slow or imbalanced recovery of expert capabilities during multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
Treats the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a differentiable model optimized with the distillation objective.
Uses expert parameters as priors while keeping the student trainable, avoiding confinement to the experts’ parameter span.
Evaluated across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales; it surpasses MOPD’s final average recovery in half the training steps.
At 1.7B, it reaches 94.7% average recovery versus 80.9% for MOPD at the end of training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of P2-MOPD. Each projection of the student is composed as its own learnable full weight plus a learnable linear combination of frozen expert directions, Wm = Bm + ∑ k αk,mτk,m (Equation (4)), and the composed weights are used as one model for the forward pass. The student generates rollouts on prompts of all domains; the frozen teacher of each prompt’s domain scores the student’s tokens. The sampled tokens and the teacher logits are passed as detached data flow (gray lines), and the resulting MOPD loss is back-propagated to the student weights (student weight channel) and to the coefficients α (coefficient channel). No gradient reaches the experts or the teachers, which come from the same expert bank.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes parameter-prior-based multi-teacher on-policy distillation for language models at 1.7B and 4B scales.
papers.title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
papers.tldr: P²-MOPD accelerates multi-teacher on-policy distillation by jointly learning parameter-mixing coefficients and trainable student weights, achieving faster and more balanced capability recovery than MOPD.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA) and free-text QA (Med-O1). Results show that neither method is universally best: on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA), SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most; notably, Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. In contrast, medical-domain models show smaller or even negative gains on MCQs. On free-text QA (Med-O1), UaS performs best for nearly all models and provides consistent improvements across both model types, with the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaching the performance of much larger 7B medical-domain models. We also find that excessively long CoT generation is associated with lower performance in some models on either multiple-choice or free-text QA tasks, suggesting that limiting the CoT length during training may benefit selected models. Overall, the results show that CoT loss weighting should be matched to the task format and the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using a single fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.
authors: Le Zhou, Xiao Luo, Chinmay Chandra, Zhan Zhang
bullets: SwS, which weights reasoning and answer losses separately, generally works better for multiple-choice QA, especially with general-purpose models.
UaS, which weights the full sequence uniformly, performs best for nearly all models on free-text QA and improves both general- and medical-domain models.
Qwen3.5-4B gains up to 44.8% over its zero-shot MedQA baseline, while medical-domain models show smaller or negative MCQ gains.
A 3B Llama-3.2 model approaches much larger 7B medical models on free-text QA when fine-tuned with UaS.
Excessively long chain-of-thought outputs can correlate with lower performance, suggesting that limiting reasoning length may help selected models.

papers.title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering

papers.abstract: Computing distances between sets is important in many robotic applications, such as motion planning and control. In many applications, derivatives of the distance are needed as well. It is well known that the Euclidean distance is not always differentiable, which create issues to algorithms that need a derivative. In this paper, we introduce NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function between two general (with mild regularity assumptions but possibly non-convex) sets. This metric is still not differentiable, but it allows us to introduce a generalization, $h$-NESDF, which has a smoothing parameter $h$ such that the metric is infinitely differentiable for all $h>0$ and that reduces to the NESDF when $h$ goes to $0$. The metric is amenable to GPU parallelization, and thus can be computed efficiently. We show extensive simulation results to evaluate its viability in motion planning.
authors: Vinicius Mariano Gon\c{c}alves, Pedro Antonio de Souza Campos Rodrigues
bullets: Addresses the nondifferentiability of Euclidean set distances, which can hinder derivative-based robotics algorithms.
Introduces NESDF, a normal Euclidean signed distance for general, possibly non-convex sets under mild regularity assumptions.
Generalizes NESDF to h-NESDF with smoothing parameter h>0, yielding infinite differentiability and recovering NESDF as h approaches zero.
Designed for efficient GPU-parallel computation.
Extensive simulations evaluate its viability for motion planning.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a differentiable distance function useful for motion planning and control, transferable to learning-based navigation.

papers.tldr: h-NESDF provides an infinitely differentiable, GPU-friendly signed distance between general sets for gradient-based robotic motion planning and control.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception systems to operate safely under diverse environmental conditions. While cameras provide high-resolution visual data, their performance significantly degrades in low-light and adverse weather. High Definition (HD) radar offers superior reliability and angular resolution under such conditions but lacks rich visual feature recognition. LiDAR, though expensive, delivers highly precise distance measurements and dense point clouds. Each sensor exhibits unique trade-offs, necessitating the development of advanced sensor fusion algorithms to harness complementary strengths while minimizing computational complexity and maintaining accuracy. In this study, the proposed fusion architecture performs early fusion by combining camera images with perspective-view point cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR sensors. The proposed model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously. Experiments are performed on the RADIal dataset where we demonstrate that fusing point cloud data with camera images in front-view surpasses the performances of the most recent standalone and fusion models.
authors: Kavin Chandrasekaran, Sorin Grigorescu
bullets: Addresses camera degradation in low-light and adverse weather by combining complementary camera, radar, and LiDAR sensing.
Uses perspective-view point-cloud projection for early fusion with camera images.
Trains a multi-task model for simultaneous vehicle detection and free-space segmentation.
Evaluated on the RADIal dataset.
Reports performance exceeding recent standalone and fusion models, without quantitative results in the abstract.

Fig. 2: Deep Seeing Through Sensors: Early fusion is performed using inputs from (a) the camera, (b) a sparse radar point cloud, and (c) a dense LiDAR point cloud. The encoder comprises a pre-encoder followed by four ResNet-50-style blocks, whose output feature maps are denoted as x0, x1, x2, and x3. A thick purple arrow indicates the connection from the encoder to the decoder, through which the encoded features are upsampled to higher spatial resolutions. The dashed lines indicate skip connections that preserve spatial information. The final outputs are produced by a Detection Head and a Segmentation Head, and the corresponding prediction results are illustrated in Fig. 1 and Fig. 3.

Fig. 3: Qualitative evaluation on the test set: (a) ground truth, (b) camera-only predictions, and (c) camera–radar–LiDAR fusion results. The green regions denote free-space segmentation, while the blue regions indicate detected vehicles.

papers.selection_reason: Fuses camera, radar, and LiDAR point-cloud projections for 3D perception tasks such as detection and drivable-space segmentation.
papers.title: Camera Radar LiDAR Fusion via Point-Cloud Projection for Multi-Task Learning
papers.tldr: An early-fusion architecture projects HD radar and LiDAR point clouds into the camera view to jointly detect vehicles and segment drivable space.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
authors: Aman Upganlawar
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of Psi-0.6 from 52.1% to 61.7%. FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/liuyifan22/FlowBench.
authors: Yifan Liu, Baihan Zhang, Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Daniel L. K. Yamins
bullets: Introduces Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) as a benchmarkable capability for spatial reasoning and robotic planning.
Provides 428K automatically generated training examples across simulated and real scenes, household environments, tabletop manipulation, and varied question types.
Finds that VLMs struggle to infer motion outcomes without observing them, while open-source models perform near chance.
Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B improves accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, indicating sim-to-real transfer.
FlowBench training improves text-to-flow prediction across four tested world-model families, including Psi-0.6.

figures.caption: Figure 3. A scalable, fully automatic, and accurate pipeline for counterfactual data that others can adapt to new simulators and tasks. (a) Four stages: find informative views, plan answer-changing motions, execute them in the simulator, and annotate. Answers are computed by rules on simulator metadata, so they are exact; a VLM only adds reasoning and language variation. (b) The pipeline needs no human labeling, scales to 420K questions across 9.7K houses, and records depth, flow, masks, and reasoning for every example. (c) A training example. The model sees only (I0, tm, tq); coloured nouns refer to the marks of the same colour. The outcome image, flow, depth, metadata, and the reasoning chain cgt→c1→c0 (excerpts) are training annotations that supervise both VLMs and world models.

Figure 5. FlowBench-Real. (a) Four-stage curation pipeline; answers come only from the measured 3D geometry, and a VLM only names objects and checks marks. (b) FlowBench-Real test set: 1,083 questions, one per image pair, over seven categories and five robot datasets. (c) A test question. The model sees only (I0, tm, tq); the after frame, masks, depth, tracks and distances are what the pipeline measured to derive the answer.

Figure 2. FlowBench is diverse and comprehensive: simulated homes and real robot tabletops, nine question categories, and 428K training questions. FlowBench-Sim covers kitchens, living rooms, bedrooms, and bathrooms in about 10K procedurally generated houses (420K training questions; 714 test questions from 120 held-out AI2-THOR scenes). FlowBench-Real covers tabletop manipulation from five robot datasets (8,575 training and 1,083 test questions). Questions probe visibility, relative position, proximity, depth order, feasibility, and contact: eight categories in Sim and seven in Real, six of them shared (shares of the training and test split, respectively).

Figure 1. Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) is a core capability for acting in the world. Given the initial image and a hypothetical motion, a human imagines the outcome, whereas open-source VLMs such as Qwen3.5 reason in text and fail (top). Even proprietary models show an imagination gap (bottom left): on FlowBench-Real-Test, Claude-Fable-5.1 and GPT-6 Astra lose 5.0 and 3.1 points when they must imagine the outcome instead of seeing it; Qwen3-VL-8B loses 13.0. Training on FlowBench-Sim transfers to real scenes (bottom right): finetuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train alone adds 29.5 points on Sim and 16.9 on Real.

Figure 4. World-model-assisted VQA. Ψ-0.6 [6] first imagines the motion as optical flow and a future frame, decoding highP (motion) patches first with text-enhanced guidance (+2/− 1), then reasons over the imagined outcome to answer. One model performs every step (Ψ badges).

papers.title: FlowBench: Counterfactual Imagination Training for Spatial Intelligence

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
authors: Aman Upganlawar
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
authors: Mi Li, Eibe Frank, Bernhard Pfahringer
bullets: Targets the computational costs of exact k-nearest-neighbor construction and dominance-component processing in FastDEC.
Uses SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN GPU kernel based on search symmetry, upper-triangular traversal, and warp-cooperative top-k selection.
Introduces WP-DC, a warp-parallel reduction method that removes dominance-component processing as a runtime bottleneck.
Achieves about 1.7–4.9× higher performance than a FAISS GPU exact-k-NN variant, with gains generally increasing in higher dimensions.
Reports up to about 2.5 × 10^4 speedup over the original single-threaded Python implementation in a very high-dimensional case; this extreme result is not typical.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The grid of point blocks used by the exact self-k-NN kernel. (a) Because the reference set and query set are identical, only the upper-triangular and diagonal tiles (j ≥ i) are computed. Each computed tile is reused, through a second (reverse) selection pass, for its transposed position rather than recomputed, reducing the number of GEMM calls by approximately one half. Diagonal tiles (i = j) require updates only once. (b)Detail of a computed tile. A single GEMM computes the−2QR⊤ term for the entire tile, which is combined with precomputed squared norms to form the distance tile. The resulting distances are then processed by two independent warp-cooperative kernels that update the top-k heaps of both the query block and the reference block from the same computation.

papers.selection_reason: GPU-accelerated exact k-NN and clustering reductions reduce computation time for ML workloads.
papers.title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs

papers.abstract: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.
authors: Robert J. Wang, Charles Ling, Boyu Wang
bullets: Avoids fixed-grid confidence prediction, reducing the need for costly high-resolution grids.
Uses recurrent updates to propagate information and progressively improve correspondence coordinates.
Combines a Deep Aggregated Transformer for global context with a lightweight regression head for localization refinement.
Performs well on indoor and outdoor benchmarks, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running over 10× faster on embedded edge hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CoReMatch. We propose a recurrent continuous coordinate refinement framework for semi-dense feature matching. Given an image pair, CoReMatch first predicts initial correspondences using low-resolution 1/16 feature maps. A recurrent coordinate refinement module then progressively updates the correspondences through iterative coordinate-space optimization using a Deep Aggregated Transformer (DAT) for global geometric reasoning. The resulting correspondences are further refined by a lightweight CNN that performs sub-pixel regression within compact local feature windows. This coarse-to-fine coordinate refinement design enables efficient and accurate matching for real-time robotic perception.

Figure 1: Memory–Speed–Accuracy Trade-off of State-of-the-Art Matchers on MegaDepth. Memory usage and runtime are measured on NVIDIA AGX Orin and RTX 3090 GPUs using batch size 1 and FP16 precision. Higher values on the y-axis indicate better performance, while lower values on the x-axis indicate higher efficiency. Across both equal-resolution and equal-accuracy comparisons, CoReMatch consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. Additional quantitative results are provided in Table 1 and Table 7.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on visible–thermal cross-modal matching. CoReMatch demonstrates stronger robustness and produces more reliable correspondences across severe modality differences. In contrast, ELoFTR and EDM generate substantially more incorrect matches, highlighting the effectiveness of recurrent coordinate refinement and robust feature representations for cross-modal matching.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison under wide-baseline geometric scenes and challenging robotic perception scenarios. Red indicates an epipolar error greater than 5 × 10−4 in normalized image coordinates. CoReMatch produces more consistent correspondences across challenging appearance and scene variations than ELoFTR and EDM.

Figure 4: Inference time of different attention mechanisms on NVIDIA AGX Orin across varying input resolutions. The proposed Deep Aggregated Transformer (DAT) achieves over 4× lower inference time than the AAM used in Efficient LoFTR at 1024× 1024 resolution.

Figure 3: Runtime breakdown of refinement mechanisms. Compared with RoMa-style multi-scale correlation-volume refinement at 1/16, 1/8, and 1/4 resolutions, CoReMatch performs three recurrent refinement iterations entirely at 1/8 resolution, achieving over 5× faster runtime at 512×512 and over 8× faster runtime at 1024× 1024.
Figure 7: Failure cases on indoor and outdoor data. Red denotes correspondences with an epipolar error greater than 5× 10−4 in normalized image coordinates.

Table 1: Relative Pose Estimation Results. All methods are trained on MegaDepth and evaluated on both the MegaDepth and ScanNet datasets. We report the AUC of relative pose error at multiple thresholds and average inference time (ms). Inference time is measured on an AGX Orin with batch size 1 and FP16 precision. CoReMatch-S outperforms ELoFTR by a large margin while being more than 11× faster on MegaDepth.

Table 2: Homography Estimation on HPatches. All methods are evaluated with models trained on MegaDepth to assess cross-dataset generalization. CoReMatch outperforms both sparse and semidense methods, and surpasses the state-ofthe-art dense method RoMa.

Table 7: Efficiency Comparison Across Input Resolutions. We compare ELoFTR, EDM, and CoReMatch in relative pose estimation accuracy (AUC), GPU memory usage, and inference time on the NVIDIA AGX Orin and RTX 3090. CoReMatch achieves a favorable trade-off between accuracy and efficiency across input resolutions.
Table 3: Ablation Studies on MegaDepth. Each component in CoReMatch improves AUC@10 while maintaining efficient inference.

Table 6: Refinement Ablation. Results on the MegaDepth dataset with different refinement iterations and top-confidence ratios. All results use the same model without retraining. Inference time is measured on an AGX Orin with batch size 1 and FP16 precision.

Table 4: Visual Odometry Evaluation. We report unaligned ATE RMSE (↓) on selected sequences. Best results are in bold. CoReMatch achieves the lowest ATE on 3/4 evaluated sequences and remains comparable to both baselines on TUM.

Table 5: Comparison with Alternative Attention Mechanisms. SCT denotes Simple Compact Transformer, while PTA denotes Proxy-Token Attention. Inference time is measured on an RTX 3090 with batch size 1 and FP16 precision.

papers.selection_reason: Recurrent continuous-coordinate feature matching for robotic perception, localization, and SLAM supports embodied perception, though it is not a navigation or manipulation policy.
papers.title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
papers.tldr: CoReMatch enables fast, accurate robotic feature matching by iteratively refining correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space.

papers.abstract: A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory. On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
authors: Chih-Hsuan Yang, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Feng Yan, Rajeev Thakur
bullets: Measures how much a memory changes a frozen reader’s answer to a task, using identical filler with and without the memory.
On factual-recall tasks, answer-bearing memories produced a larger mean paired reward gain than matched controls: +0.33, with a 95% interval of +0.21 to +0.46.
Tested task-blind summaries and structured records yielded smaller gains than raw memories, including at fixed total context; budget results suggest retaining answer-bearing content matters.
The effect persisted with randomized memory position and a second reader, but generic retrieval missed most screen-defined answer-bearing memories.
The effect did not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where raw memories had no measurable impact.

papers.selection_reason: Measures task-conditioned utility of long-term agent memory, directly addressing persistent/external agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: What Is This Memory Useful For? Measuring Task-Conditioned Utility in Long-Term Agent Memory
papers.tldr: Memory usefulness depends on the future task, so compression should be evaluated by task-conditioned utility and resource cost rather than a single importance score.

papers.abstract: Koopman representations describe nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space, offering an attractive framework for their linear simplicity and generality. Yet these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved performance in deep latent data assimilation (LDA). We systematically compare seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems spanning approximately periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics and a broad range of state dimensions. We evaluate forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behavior, and dynamical consistency, and assess Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity, and uniqueness of analysis solutions. Our results reveal a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability. Linear evolution of the latent state can stabilize short-term forecasts but restrict expressiveness in strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems, without consistently improving assimilation accuracy. Parameterized linear operators offer greater flexibility, yet their joint optimization with the encoder--decoder remains nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and exhibit greater robustness in our experiments, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck. These findings show that the practical benefits of Koopman structure depend on both sufficient observational information and the choice of assimilation procedure.
authors: Zhiwei Zhang, Wenxuan Yuan, Xiaoyuan Cheng, Pouria Behnoudfar, Chuanqi Chen, Charlotte Moser, Yuta Tarumi, Jin-Long Wu, Rossella Arcucci, Takemasa Miyoshi, Nan Chen, Marc Bocquet, Sibo Cheng
bullets: Compares seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems, from near-periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics.
Evaluates forecasting, assimilation, physical-state recovery, latent trajectories, dynamical consistency, Gaussian-error assumptions, convexity, and solution uniqueness.
Fixed linear latent evolution can stabilize short-term forecasts but may limit expressiveness in chaotic and high-dimensional systems without reliably improving assimilation.
Parameterized linear operators are more flexible but require nonconvex joint optimization with the encoder–decoder.
Closed-form analysis updates are generally more robust, while matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks learned latent dynamics representations for forecasting and data assimilation, relevant to environment dynamics prediction.
papers.title: When Latent Dynamics Meet Data Assimilation: A Benchmark of Koopman-Type Representations
papers.tldr: A benchmark of Koopman-style latent representations finds that their practical value for deep latent data assimilation depends on system complexity, observation quality, and the assimilation procedure.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.
authors: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
bullets: Targets the growing latency cost of running LoRA adapters as separate kernels alongside FP8 or 4-bit base-model GEMMs.
Launches each adapter’s down-projection first, then fuses the up-projection into the dependent GEMM’s epilogue.
Implemented as a vLLM plugin for serving multiple tenants and adapters.
On NVIDIA Hopper, reduces single-adapter decoding time per token by up to 24% versus vLLM’s fastest configuration and outperforms SGLang and TensorRT-LLM in the reported comparison.
An FP8-based LoRA RL trainer avoids a 16-bit model copy, allowing a 27B model to train on one 48 GB GPU; results are reported primarily for tested GPU-model pairs.

papers.abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.
authors: Rostislav Gusev, Evgenia Romanenkova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Characterizes how different continuous paths consistent with the same sparse observations can yield different terminal states in planar Neural CDEs.
Approximates compatible terminal states with a zonotope based on feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets.
Provides a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate by projecting terminal-state uncertainty onto a scalar prediction.
Shows optimal worst-case uncertainty scales as N⁻¹ with bounded speed and N⁻² when acceleration is also bounded.
Synthetic experiments evaluate the certificate under admissible path completions and varying path regularity.

papers.abstract: One big challenge in physical AI is interacting with systems whose states are defined by implicit equilibrium. Learning in these systems is difficult because their responses can be multistable, path-dependent, and sensitive over long horizons. Adjoint learning provides an efficient way to optimize trajectories without unrolling iterative equilibrium solvers, but its gradient relies on the frozen-tangent approximation, which neglects higher-order sensitivity terms and can become inaccurate when the local equilibrium varies rapidly. In this work, we introduce Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), optimizing trajectories along which sensitivity variations are explicitly controlled. We derive a mathematical bound on the resulting gradient error and develop a practical finite-difference approximation. We validate the framework on deformable objects, which are representative of implicit equilibrium systems, ranging from simple quadratic energy models such as elastic rods to complex systems including thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures. Compared with the adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baselines, SCNC achieves faster convergence and more stable optimization by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches, doubling the stable optimization rate over adjoint learning 83.3% vs. 41.7% and reducing the average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude on thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced.
authors: Hengyi Zhou, Haobo Fang, Xiaonan Huang, Dezhong Tong, M. Khalid Jawed
bullets: Addresses inaccurate gradients caused by the frozen-tangent approximation in rapidly varying, path-dependent equilibrium systems.
Optimizes trajectories to control sensitivity changes and uses a practical finite-difference approximation.
Derives a bound on the resulting gradient error.
Evaluated on deformable objects ranging from elastic rods to thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures.

Compared with adjoint learning and gradient-free iCEM, achieves faster, more stable optimization, including an 83.3% versus 41.7% stable optimization rate and substantially lower loss on thin-walled tubes.

papers.abstract: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
authors: Farid Hasanov, Riccardo Renzulli, Bahram Zonooz, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Decebal Constantin Mocanu
bullets: Addresses overconfident answers unsupported by available visual or textual evidence.
Mines sparse autoencoder features linked to abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set during prefill.
Evaluated with LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B and Qwen3.5-2B across multimodal and language abstention benchmarks.
Produces a better balance between correct answers and appropriate abstention than uncertainty-based post-hoc rejection baselines.
Works best for image–question or question–answer incompatibility and mathematical reasoning, but is weaker for absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA.

papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
authors: Anton Hristov
bullets: Long reasoning traces improve problem-solving but can be expensive due to repetition and low-value text.
The study compacts earlier reasoning before pending tool results are revealed, then compares generation from original versus rewritten histories without retraining.

The results motivate model-specific compaction policies that balance efficiency with retained capability.

papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
authors: Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou, Hongru Zhang, Kai Ye, Shuyuan Hu, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Bo Zhao

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
authors: Louis Bradshaw, Irmak Bukey, Daniel Chenyu Lin, John Thickstun, Chris Donahue
bullets: Introduces PianoBench, a benchmark for musical perception and reasoning across matched acoustic and symbolic inputs.
Built from a multimodal dataset containing over 20,000 hours of piano instruction transcripts and musical commentary.
Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8% accuracy, only modestly above a no-audio control.
Frontier models achieve up to 93.2% with chain-of-thought when musical content is provided as text, revealing an audio-perception gap.
Instruction tuning on interleaved musical instruction improves Qwen 3.5 9B Base’s transcript-based zero-shot accuracy from 42.8% to 56.0%.

papers.tldr: PianoBench shows that language models reason far better about explicitly transcribed musical events than they perceive and reason about music directly from audio.

papers.abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-order curvature information. LHM consists of three components: (1) a low-rank Hessian approximation that efficiently estimates per-layer Hessian traces via Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, eliminating the need for task-specific data; (2) a Layer Second-Order Sensitivity (LSOS) index that combines Hessian trace with task-vector norm to quantify per-layer fusion difficulty; and (3) a Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM) that converts LSOS scores into layer-adaptive merge coefficients while jointly satisfying a fusion-error bound and a global length-reduction target. Experiments across six mathematical benchmarks on 1.5B and 7B models show that LHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as ACM-TIES and ORCA, achieving over 4\% accuracy gain and up to 93.1\% reduction in output length relative to the long-CoT model.
authors: Zeqiu Yu, Xuesheng Zhang, Wenxiao Zhao, Shixiao Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of linear interpolation and first-order statistics in merging long-chain-of-thought and concise models.
Uses low-rank Hutchinson-based Hessian estimates, an LSOS layer-sensitivity score, and DCCM layer-adaptive coefficients.
Requires no task-specific data and jointly enforces a fusion-error bound and target length reduction.
Across six mathematical benchmarks and 1.5B/7B models, it reports over 4% higher accuracy and up to 93.1% shorter outputs than the long-CoT model.
The abstract evaluates mathematical reasoning; broader task or domain scope is unspecified.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM). The framework then comprises three modules: (1) Low-Rank Hessian Approximation, which estimates loss-landscape curvature using Rademacher random vectors to compute per-layer Hessian traces; (2) LSOS Index, which combines these traces with the ℓ2 norms of the task vector via element-wise multiplication to evaluate layer importance; and (3) Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM), which applies min–max normalization and dual orthogonal constraints (balancing accuracy preservation and length reduction) to generate layer-wise merge coefficients λi. The merged model θmerged preserves strong reasoning accuracy while producing substantially shorter outputs.

Figure 1: (Left) Accuracy–length Pareto plot across merging methods on the 1.5B benchmark suite. LHM (star) dominates all baselines by simultaneously achieving higher accuracy and shorter responses. (Right) Relative accuracy degradation when the merge coefficient is reduced by 0.2 for high-LSOS versus low-LSOS layers, confirming that second-order sensitivity identifies layers critical to reasoning performance.

Figure 6: (Left) Average accuracy and average response length as a function of the Hessian rank k on the 1.5B benchmark suite. Performance stabilises at k ≥ 16. (Right) Pareto curves of accuracy vs. response length for different global target coefficients λ̄ ∈ {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6}.

Figure 5: Ablation study visualisation. (Left) Average accuracy across configurations on TA and AIM baselines, each with incremental addition of LHM components. (Right) Corresponding average response lengths, showing that DCCM is the primary driver of length reduction.

Figure 2: (Left) LSOS index distribution across the 28 transformer layers of DeepSeek-R1-DistillQwen-7B. High-LSOS layers cluster near the beginning and end of the network, correlating with known reasoning-critical regions. (Right) Comparison of Hutchinson Hessian trace estimates (rank k = 16) against a finite-difference ground truth, showing < 2% relative error with negligible computational overhead.

Figure 4: (Left) Normalized Hessian trace estimation error as a function of the rank k, showing rapid convergence beyond k = 16. (Right) Wall-clock time for Hessian trace computation at different ranks compared with the full finite-difference baseline (×), confirming O(dk) scaling.

papers.title: Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging for Efficient Long-to-Short Reasoning
papers.tldr: LHM is a training-free, curvature-aware model-merging method that improves long-to-short reasoning while substantially reducing output length.

papers.abstract: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.
authors: Heejoon Koo
bullets: Aggregate metrics can hide differences in predicting persistent, new, and recurrent diagnoses, especially across varying history depths.
The proposed evaluation framework compares heuristics, prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent methods along distributional and temporal dimensions.
Repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM approaches overall but cannot predict new or recurrent diagnoses.
LONGINUS uses retrieved patient-record evidence, trajectory memory, and cross-view agreement to preserve or adjudicate predictions.
Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, it achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive on aggregate metrics.
