papers.abstract: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.
authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco, Alessio Caporali, Miguel Aranda, Gianluca Palli, Gonzalo L\'opez-Nicol\'as, Youcef Mezouar
bullets: Uses singular value decomposition to characterize easily produced, costly, and locally unavailable shape changes.
Examines how shape-feature selection affects regulation behavior and deformation during motion toward a target.
Identifies three failure modes: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and mechanical instabilities.
Extends shape control to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

papers.selection_reason: Learns bimanual manipulation from handheld human videos with no robot data, strongly fitting embodied AI, VLA, and human-video learning.
papers.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data

papers.abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train $\pi_{0.5}$ policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. Finger design, dataset, and data processing code: https://lute-corp.github.io/soft-yubi-site/
authors: Kobi Kelemen, Tomasz Niedzia{\l}kowski, Marcin Paszczak, Victoriano Montesinos
bullets: Collects 99.7 hours of demonstrations across 53 objects using soft, angled fingers that wrap around objects and visibly deform under load.
The handheld interface is built on YUBI, avoids external base stations, and matches the robot’s grippers.
Training uses 49 objects, with 4 held out to evaluate generalization to unseen objects.
A top camera improves success by 13 percentage points, while multi-task pretraining raises unseen-object fine-tuning success from 35% to 57%.
The released resources include the finger design, dataset, and data-processing code.

Left: on the R1 Pro, we compare midtraining and SFT on UMI data. Right: on the R1 Lite, we compare the same policies fine-tuned on teleoperation data (hatched). Error bars show 95% Wilson intervals.

papers.selection_reason: Directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation via data collection for pick-and-place policies.
papers.title: Robot-Matched Soft Fingers for UMI Data Collection: Lessons from 100 Hours of Pick and Place
papers.tldr: A battery-powered UMI with robot-matched soft fingers enables large-scale pick-and-place demonstrations and reveals design and data practices that improve policy success.

papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.
authors: Fengzhi Guo, Nate Morrill, Shiqi Li, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified approach for 3D rigging and temporally stable 4D skeleton generation.
Generates an entire 4D sequence jointly in a single feedforward pass, while also supporting single-mesh 3D rigging.
Provides explicit control over skeleton count, uncertainty-based candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.
Uses a curriculum from large-scale 3D rigging data to mid-scale 4D mesh–skeleton data to reduce dependence on paired 4D training data.
Reports strong 3D rigging quality and high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FLOWRIG unifies rigging for both 3D and 4D meshes. Compared with prior methods such as Puppeteer (Song et al., 2025a) and UniRig (Zhang et al., 2025a), our model delivers accurate 3D rigging, preserves 4D temporal consistency, supports controllable bone count, achieves faster inference, and enables 4D skeleton prediction, including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.

Figure 2: FLOWRIG overview. We encode meshes into conditioning tokens, and initialize noisy skeleton slots, which are processed by a flow matching transformer to predict temporally aligned skeleton representations. The predicted features are decoded by the skeleton, graph, and uncertainty heads to recover 3D/4D rigging outputs, with uncertainty used for sample selection. n denotes the skeleton count, and ϕ denotes the unconditional token.

Figure 4: Static Reconstruction. Numbers from top to bottom are J2J, J2B, and B2B for each instance. Compared with baselines, our model preserves finer geometric details and achieves more accurate mesh alignment.

Figure 3: Data-efficient curriculum training. We first train on static 3D rigging, then adapt to 4D reconstruction, and finally enable prediction through masked conditioning. During the final stage, we use diverse masking patterns, including interpolation, forecasting, backcasting, and random masking, to expose the model to different temporal prediction settings. This schedule transfers large-scale 3D supervision to the data-scarce 4D setting.

Figure 5: Dynamic reconstruction and prediction. Blue indicates reconstruction with mesh guidance, while yellow indicates predictions without mesh guidance. In (b), from top to bottom, it shows interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting, respectively. Refer to the demo video for a clearer comparison.

Figure 6: Analysis of bone count control. Our model can freely control the number of bones to adjust skeletal detail, while existing baselines do not provide this level of controllable output granularity.

Table 1: Static skeleton reconstruction comparison. Our methods achieves strong reconstruction fidelity across diverse out-of-domain static datasets. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples and outperforms all baselines on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose. On ModelsResource, its zero-shot performance approaches that of RigAnything trained directly on the same dataset. See the "Baselines" paragraph for citations of these models.

Table 2: Dynamic quantitative comparisons on TexVerse dynamic dataset. N is time window length. PuppeteerD* means we finetuned Puppeteer-diverse model (Song et al., 2025a) on TexVerse training dataset. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified framework for 3D/4D skeleton generation using flow matching, bridging 3D vision, video generation, and robotic rigging/kinematics.
papers.title: FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for 3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching
papers.tldr: MoTWorld uses flow matching to generate controllable, temporally consistent skeletons for both static 3D and dynamic 4D meshes in one feedforward framework.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.

Left: per-request decode speedup over the unmodified model; right: LongBench macro-F1 change (symmetric-log axis so the 1/32 collapse fits). Light: IndexCache alone; dark: IndexCache+MLI at the same retention; hollow: distilled arms.

Right: Multi-layer Indexer. The indexer of layer ℓ+1 and the attention of layer ℓ read the same hidden state and run concurrently (green step); a selection is attended one step after it is produced.

The indexer of layer ℓ forks onto the side stream once hℓ exists and runs under the attention, output projection and feed-forward block of layer ℓ; its selection is joined at the prepare step of layer ℓ+1, which attends it. The whole pattern is captured once into the decode CUDA graph.

Figure 1: Per-layer decode latency of the DSA attention path (DeepSeek-V3.2, H100, one request; kernels timed in isolation). (a) Standard DSA runs the indexer and attention in sequence, so their latencies add; the prefix scan grows with context and comes to dominate. (b) MLI overlaps them on a second stream, so the per-layer time is the bottleneck, not the sum; the full-width bar is the bottleneck and the striped bar the hidden component, the indexer split into scan and top-k as in (a). Idealized ceiling; the realized gain is smaller and bandwidth-bound (Section 5.2).

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes sparse attention and long-context LLM decode, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context model developments.
papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) hides DeepSeek Sparse Attention’s expensive indexer scans by reusing the previous layer’s token selection, delivering faster long-context decoding without retraining.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.
authors: Yang Qu, Qiang Fu, Zonghao Ying, Jiayi Zhao, Yaoyuan Zhang, Jinyang Guo, Jian Yang, Aishan Liu, Yingxun Wang, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Introduces Ambient Context Illusion: removing non-essential details can impair task execution without changing instruction semantics.
Builds VagueBench in AI2-THOR with 1,303 instruction pairs spanning four categories and nine subtypes of omitted context.
Uses semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformations, and semantic-invariance verification to create the benchmark.
Evaluation across six embodied agents shows relative task-success drops of 19.65% and empty-plan rates rising by 54.10%.
The issue also appears in real-world robotic systems, potentially causing incorrect decisions and safety risks.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks embodied agents on instruction following under minimal context in AI2-THOR, directly matching embodied instruction-following navigation.
papers.title: VagueBench: Benchmarking the Robustness of Embodied Agents on Ambient Context Illusions
papers.tldr: VagueBench reveals that embodied agents often depend on unnecessary contextual cues and fail when semantically equivalent instructions are made contextually minimal.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Validation performance of models trained on three datasets representative of natural language, code, and mathematics. Dots represent models trained with different seeds or nonlinearities (see legend on the left). Coloured outlines represent approximate distributions. The architectures specialized for each target dataset (D1=D2 ) almost always improve over the baselines, whereas the transfer across domains (D1 ̸=D2) varies a lot. The patterns formed by the markers indicate whether the improvements on one dataset correlate with improvements on the other. This likely requires different inductive biases than standard subword tokenization because of longerrange interactions, different typical entropy in the predictions, etc. As a result, the architectures optimized for this dataset (SHAKESPEARE-CHAR, vertical axis) work badly on others (FINEWEB, ENWIK8) and vice versa.

Figure 1: Our experimental setup quantifies the compatibility of inductive biases across subsets of data. We specialize a transformer variant for a source domain D1 (left) by replacing nonlinearities with parameterized splines, pre-trained in a warm-up phase. We then reuse these frozen components to train a model on a target dataset D2 (right). Only very few parameters are transferred.

Figure 2: Typical training curves during the warmup phase (on CSN-PYTHON here), where we optimize both the weights of transformers and their nonlinearities, initialized as constant functions (left). We train multiple models in a staggered schedule. They share the same nonlinearities, providing a regularizing effect that makes them more likely to transfer later to other models.

Figure 14: More examples like Figure 7. The baseline with standard LR decay (--) often improves late during training when the LR reaches very small values. In comparison, our model converges more easily both with (–) and without (–) LR decay.
Figure 11: Learned nonlinearities for various datasets (MLP/attention).
Figure 13: Comparison of nonlinearities learned with models of 4 vs. 12 layers for different MATH question types.

Figure 12: Learned layer-specific nonlinearities for ENWIK8.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., learned splines) improve LLM training efficiency and generalization, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.tldr: Domain-specific transformer inductive biases can improve language-model training efficiency or generalization, but their benefits often do not transfer across domains.

papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
authors: Ajitabh Kumar
bullets: Models answer typed finance questions with probabilities in one forward pass across 0.8B–32B parameters and multiple model families.
Narrow fine-tuning reduces general decision competence by 9–45 percentage points, with the effect weakening as models scale.
On realized-return questions, models show no detectable conditional edge and instead produce flat, well-calibrated probabilities that follow horizon-specific base rates.
Calibration is strongest at mid-scale, while larger models degrade under prior drift.
A mixed-corpus adapter preserves policy performance and near-specialist outcome calibration, supporting domain-specific temperature regimes and escalation by confidence bands.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The specialization trade-off and its remediation at Qwen-2B (three seeds; mean with min–max whiskers, Table 6). Left: policy development accuracy against public-benchmark accuracy; right: outcome development Brier (lower is better) against public-benchmark accuracy. Narrow training buys one finance axis at a large cost in general competence (and leaves the untrained finance axis at chance); mixed training recovers the generalist position on the public benchmark while holding both finance axes near their specialists.

Figure 1: Calibrated 𝑃 (yes) by realized label for the Q-2B mixed adapter, post domain temperature (policy 𝑇=1.54, outcome 𝑇=1.28), common axis. papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.
authors: Mehrnoush Mohammadi, Kamal Berahmand, Mohammad Morsali, Shazia Sadiq, Wojtek Tomaszewski, Hassan Khosravi
bullets: Addresses the retrieval-inference alignment gap in retrieval-augmented KT, where relevant evidence may not be predictively useful.
Uses an Evidence-Graph Cache to build query-specific evidence subgraphs from persistent question relations and temporally valid interactions.
Encodes retrieved learning trajectories with the target learner’s history using outcome-supervised contrastive learning.
An attention mechanism combines retrieval relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility to determine predictive influence.
Outperforms strong KT baselines across five benchmarks and remains robust with sparse histories and cold-start learners.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.
authors: Zhishang Xiang, Yunbo Tang, Zhongqiao Liu, Junkai Chen, Zerui Chen, Qingguo Hu, Yuxuan Zhang, William Grant, Qinggang Zhang, Jinsong Su

papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
authors: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle
bullets: Addresses staypoint fragmentation caused by spatial noise and prolonged signal dropouts.
Uses a dynamic centroid, an n-step lookahead heuristic, and temporal bridging to tolerate drift and missing observations.

Evaluated on the ExtraSensory dataset against Trackintel’s sliding-window baseline.

papers.abstract: Continuous video scales in cost with camera count, resolution and recording duration, yet many monitoring tasks seek events rather than complete images and can operate on a compact single-pixel measurement stream. Recovering a chosen interval as video is then desirable, but at 0.24\% of the pixel count the scene correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimization takes minutes. Correlating the residual of an estimate with the coding patterns nevertheless gives a residual image, the gradient of a centered measurement loss. Lifted through a pretrained video decoder, its agreement with the true error exceeds that of control decoders. Video-latent inversion (VLI) then outperforms frame-wise image-latent reconstruction at 1{,}000 bucket values. Measurement-Gradient-Conditioned Video Flow (MGV-Flow), trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames, reconstructs five frames in 1.55\,s at 22.9\,dB median PSNR, against 398\,s and 18.1\,dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. Directional fidelity ranks 30 coding configurations and selects one needing a third fewer bucket values. On a physical system, MGV-Flow outperforms per-frame reconstruction without retraining. A sliding window over the bucket-value stream yields 3.2 frames per second on one RTX~4090 and, in theory, 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator. Demonstrations are available at https://cavedweller509.github.io/MGV-Flow.
authors: Hongjun An, Shuaizhe An, Tong Tian, Zhe Sun
bullets: Single-pixel monitoring can detect events without recording full video, but reconstructing chosen intervals is difficult because measurements are only 0.24% of the pixel count and residual images resemble noise.

The method correlates measurement residuals with coding patterns, lifts the resulting gradient-like image through a pretrained video decoder, and conditions a video flow model on it and preceding frames.
MGV-Flow reconstructs five frames in 1.55 s at 22.9 dB median PSNR, compared with 398 s and 18.1 dB for video-latent inversion at 1,000 bucket values.
It performs especially well in high-motion scenes, ranks coding configurations to reduce required bucket values by one third, and works on a physical system without retraining.
A sliding-window implementation reaches 3.2 frames per second on one RTX 4090; the approach targets selected intervals rather than continuous full-video recovery.

papers.abstract: Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

papers.abstract: Learned temporal models are moving beyond offline forecasting toward interactive environments for decision making, yet logged-trajectory accuracy need not predict closed-loop behavior under policies optimized in the learned model. This forecasting-control gap matters in tokamak magnetic control, where coupled plasma-circuit dynamics and actuator constraints can amplify errors through feedback. Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, we collect four datasets in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage. At matched budgets of 500, 1k, 3k, and 5k rollouts, we train 16 action-conditioned Transformers; PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are then evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions. Only joint-coverage D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, whereas D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution. Binary completion masks substantial closed-loop differences: D2-D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions, but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7%, and 90.5% of the evaluation horizon, while their worst conditions reach 94.2%, 68.2%, and 43.2%. Policies trained with action noise complete 5/24 matched conditions, compared with 19/24 under nominal training, and have a lower mean horizon-capped episode length. Based on one trained policy per configuration and one evaluation realization per condition, the results support combining prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration, and tracking quality.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Siqi Ding, Xuanhe Wang, Pei Guo, Changquan Yu, Jiale Hu, Jiayi Zhi, Zhengyuan Chen, Jianguo Chen, Tianyuan Liu

papers.abstract: Novels tell rich stories, but their textual form cannot directly present the sights and sounds of the worlds they describe. Film adaptations offer an audiovisual experience but require substantial production effort and viewing time; film recaps are shorter but depend on existing footage. Neither route directly provides a concise audiovisual account of a novel. We therefore study novel-to-recap video generation: producing a self-contained, source-grounded audiovisual retelling directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget. This task requires compressing the story while preserving causal connections, allocating sufficient time to retained events, and aligning narration with newly generated visuals. We propose ReVi, a dual-loop multi-agent framework guided by edit first, generate second. Its Inner Loop plans story content, narration time, and corresponding shots before video generation. Across novels, its Outer Loop performs recursive self-improvement by revising both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision. Experiments on two evaluation sets show that ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, with human ratings and multi-round improvement results providing further support.

Human evaluations and multi-round improvements further support the approach.

papers.abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
authors: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni
bullets: Evaluates LLM causal discovery across model scale, graph complexity, prompting, metadata quality, data quality, and uncertainty.
Finds a consistent optimism bias: LLMs overestimate causal relationships, resulting in low precision.
Shows that conventional metrics can overstate performance when uncertainty is ignored; uncertainty-aware evaluation lowers scores.
Larger models perform better, but their gains degrade sharply with lower-quality metadata.
Provides practical guidance on when LLMs may support causal discovery and when they risk misleading researchers.

papers.abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
authors: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting concepts distributed across many model dimensions.

Demonstrations include detecting hazardous requests, inducing refusals, and changing an angle-related prediction from “sides” to “degrees.”

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a novel sparse feed-forward architecture for LLMs that uses fixed, disjoint output coordinates to improve feature interpretability, directly relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
papers.tldr: MoWE uses sparse experts with fixed output coordinates to make language-model features more interpretable and directly reusable while largely preserving predictive performance.

papers.abstract: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.
authors: Sabarish Radhakrishnan, Nathalie Japkowicz
bullets: Lifelong anomaly detectors must retain recognition of previously learned anomaly types while learning new tasks.
The study disentangles latent cluster separation from distance-based anomaly scoring in a VAE-based detector.
Using cluster separation only during training can improve detection quality and backward transfer without changing scoring.
Distance-based scoring is identified as the main source of common instability in this method family.
Which design is preferable depends on the dataset’s underlying representation.

papers.tldr: Separating latent-cluster regularization from centroid-based anomaly scoring shows that the regularizer—not distance-based scoring—typically drives better detection and backward transfer, while scoring can cause instability.

papers.abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.
authors: Basavaraj R M, Aryan Bharat Kumar
bullets: Two-tier routers need to assess whether retrieved evidence supports an answer and account for load-dependent escalation cost.
TRIAGE conditions escalation on post-generation reliability and GPU price; a semantic evidence judge is evaluated as a post hoc enhancement.
On one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B/32B, escalation cost increased 21.9× from 1 to 10 requests/s, without monotonic dependence on KV-cache headroom.
The pre-registered corrupted-evidence detector failed its AUROC≥0.70 target, reaching 0.571; the semantic judge later reached 0.846, or 0.926 on never-served items.

The GPT-3.5→GPT-4 cascade stayed about 3 percentage points from GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost, while open-model pairs could underperform random routing; the 7B→32B end-to-end gain was only 2.88 points.

papers.selection_reason: Two-tier LLM serving with load-conditioned escalation and a semantic evidence judge reduces inference cost, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
papers.tldr: TRIAGE shows that reliability- and load-aware escalation can reduce API cost, but a failed pre-launch reliability gate and weak open-model results limit its end-to-end benefit.

papers.abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.
authors: Basavaraj R M, Manav Verma
bullets: Addresses early optimization instability when adding non-text modalities to frozen language models.
Uses zero-initialized, learnable gated cross-attention inserted across six decoder layers.
At initialization, the bridge preserves pretrained behavior exactly, with reported output discrepancy of 0.00e+00.
On Falcon-40B held-out evaluation, gate-on performance improves loss from 4.3469 to 2.2201 versus the gate-off baseline.
The approach is evaluated with frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b backbones; results reported primarily for Falcon-40B.

papers.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
papers.tldr: IGCA stabilizes multimodal conditioning of frozen language models by starting as an exact no-op and gradually enabling cross-attention.

papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.
authors: Tiejin Chen
Maunil Vyas
Huaiyuan Yao
Hua Wei
bullets: The study extends steering vectors from inference-time behavior control to parameter updates during SFT, distillation, and RL with verifiable rewards.
It tests hidden-state injection for supervised training and correctness-contrast advantage repair on wrong GRPO rollouts.
Supervised steering improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains increasing with the off-policy gap and reaching up to 12% when distilling from thinking-mode teachers.
In RL, advantage repair restores learning signals for otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups and transfers to held-out math benchmarks.
Effectiveness has boundaries: directions may fail for code generation, layer placement may not transfer across model families, and inference-time steering may fail on SV-trained checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a novel method for using steering vectors as a training signal during LLM post-training (SFT, distillation, RLVR). This directly contributes to the architecture and training of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Steering vectors can improve LLM post-training when injected into supervised learning or used to repair RL advantages, but their effectiveness depends on the direction, placement, and intervention regime.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability. NDD makes safe-and-live deconfliction a controllable, locally tunable emergent property of local agent interactions, without requiring communication, preassigned priorities, models of neighbors' objectives or future actions, or estimates of group size or global network properties. By design, NDD couples the dynamics of internal decision and attention states with changing physical states and locally observed relative motion. Each agent continuously modulates its speed along its prescribed path, responding as soon and as much as conflict resolution requires. Agents self-organize into disjoint, locally engaged groups that resolve conflicts concurrently. When any group's conflict becomes safety-critical, decision-action feedback destabilizes collective indecision, and coordinated conflict-resolution emerges that stabilizes a safe traversal order within the group. Order persists as conflicts clear, but groups may split or merge as agents autonomously adapt to new conflicts and those with resolved conflicts resume their nominal motion. We derive explicit conditions on sensing range, feedback gains, response time scales, and actuation limits that guarantee collision avoidance and traversal-order formation in finite time with no deadlock or livelock for finite, heterogeneous agent populations of arbitrary, changing size. Computational cost scales with the number of local interactions sensed by each agent. Large-scale simulations, comparisons with existing approaches, and hardware experiments demonstrate NDD in complex congested scenarios and validate its scalability.
authors: Himani Sinhmar
Vaibhav Srivastava
Naomi Ehrich Leonard
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance and coordinated passage without communication, priorities, neighbor-intent models, or global population estimates.
Couples internal decision and attention dynamics with physical state and locally observed relative motion, allowing agents to modulate speed along prescribed paths.
Agents self-organize into local conflict groups that resolve interactions concurrently; feedback breaks indecision and establishes a safe traversal order in finite time.
Provides explicit conditions for sensing, feedback, response times, and actuation that guarantee safety, liveness, and no deadlock or livelock for finite heterogeneous populations.
Simulations, comparisons, and hardware experiments demonstrate operation in complex congested scenarios and support scalability; computational cost depends on sensed local interactions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Multitime scale embodied control architecture for safe-and-live deconfliction. All layers operate concurrently at distinct characteristic time scales. The slow planning layer supplies a prescribed path and nominal motion command 𝑈nom

Fig. 6: NDD remains safe and on-path as congestion increases. Methods are compared using homogeneous Dubins-car agents in the same 50 randomized start–goal scenarios per population size, 𝑁 ∈ {4, 8, 12, 24, 32} (minimum crossing angle 𝛼𝑒 = 70◦). Points are means over 𝑛 = 50 scenarios for each method and population size; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. (A) Safe-agent success is the percentage of agents reaching their goals without a safety violation. NDD maintains 100% success, whereas the success rate of LivePoint, the strongest baseline by this measure, remains below 100% and declines as congestion increases. (B) Mean minimum pairwise separation versus mean time per agent to reach its goal. Marker size denotes population size; the dotted line marks the 𝑑safe = 0.7 m safety threshold. NDD retains a safe separation margin across all group sizes, although its completion time increases with population size. Shorter baseline times should not be interpreted as faster safe-and-live deconfliction when separation falls below the safety threshold. (C) Mean deviation from prescribed paths. NDD maintains zero deviation, resolving conflicts through speed modulation rather than spatial detours. The panels distinguish safe completion from goal attainment alone and show that baseline path deviation does not ensure safety in these tests.

Fig. 1: Emergence of safe-and-live deconfliction under an NDD-driven controller. (A) Colored bodies show six agents at time 𝑡; faded poses project motion along prescribed paths at equally spaced future times, assuming current speeds persist. Closer spacing indicates slower motion. Dotted portions show motion after projected conflict clearance. (B) An arrow 𝑖 → 𝑗 means agent 𝑗’s motion influences agent 𝑖’s conflict evidence. Darker edges indicate stronger influence; node size represents aggregate conflict-evidence magnitude |ℎ𝑖 (𝑡) |. (C) Decisions 𝑧𝑖 (𝑡) initially indicate collective yielding, then differentiate. The bracket marks negotiation time𝑇neg; shading identifies negotiation, hold, and release. (D) Realized speeds 𝑣𝑖 (𝑡) track decision-dependent commands. Positive and negative decisions raise and lower commanded speeds, respectively, relative to nominal 𝑣nom = 1 m/s

Fig. 5: Conflict release smoothly reconfigures the selected differentiated response. Left graphs show reciprocal interaction sensitivities; right graphs show traversal orders, with arrows from the agent selected to pass first to its follower. Coordinates 𝜉1 = (𝑧1−𝑧2)/ √ 2 and 𝜉2 = (𝑧1+𝑧2−2𝑧3)/ √ 6

Fig. 4: Graph hierarchy from local sensing to locally engaged groups. (A) Agent 2 evaluates the egocentric sensed-interaction set E2(𝑡). Under the convention 𝑒 = (𝑖, 𝑗), an arrow 𝑖 → 𝑗 indicates that agent 𝑗’s motion enters agent 𝑖’s evidence. Solid arrows are the current conflict interactions E2(𝑡)∩Econf (𝑡). Dashed gray double-headed links denote mutually sensed but nonconflicting pairs– the dashed gray edge from agent 2 belongs to E2(𝑡) \ Econf (𝑡). (B) The weighted directed conflict graph G(𝑡) = (V(𝑡), Econf (𝑡),𝝎(𝑡)) contains the reciprocal pair (𝑖, 𝑗) and ( 𝑗 , 𝑖) generated by every physical-conflict pair {𝑖, 𝑗}. For 𝑒 = (𝑖, 𝑗), arrow thickness represents the directional weight 𝜔𝑒 𝑖 (𝑡), so reciprocal directions may have unequal weights. The 2–7 conflict illustrates pronounced asymmetry: taking 𝑒 = (7, 2) and 𝑒 = (2, 7), the graph depicts 𝜔𝑒 7(𝑡) ≫ 𝜔𝑒 2(𝑡) > 0. Dashed gray double-headed links are mutually sensed nonconflicting pairs shown for context and do not belong to G(𝑡). (C) The strongly connected components {G𝑐 (𝑡)}𝑐∈C(𝑡) of G(𝑡) are the locally engaged groups. The dashed box highlights the component containing agent 2. Sensed nonconflicting interactions do not merge these components.

Fig. 7: NDD enables safe-and-live deconfliction through shared crossing regions. Panels show Dubins-car agents with unlimited sensing range and nominal speed 1 m/s. (A to D) Near-antipodal exchange, with agents starting around a circle and moving toward roughly opposite goals. (E to H) Intersecting groups of approximately parallel paths. Columns compare NDD (A and E), ORCA (B and F), LivePoint (C and G), and decentralized CBF-QP (D and H) using the same start–goal configuration within each row. Colors identify agents; filled and open circles mark starts and goals, respectively. Small dots mark positions at 2 s intervals, so closer spacing indicates slower motion. Crossed circles mark pairs whose separation fell below the 𝑑safe = 0.7 m safety distance; insets enlarge the corresponding regions. NDD-controlled agents remain collision-free in both scenarios while following their prescribed straight paths: spatial path intersections need not cause collisions because agents can traverse the same region at different times by modulating their speeds to create temporal separation. In contrast, ORCA, LivePoint, and decentralized CBF-QP record 9, 6, and 16 colliding pairs in the top row and 20, 15, and 41 in the bottom row, respectively.

Fig. 3: Contested-region construction from instantaneous local kinematics. (A) The dashed rays extend the currently measured velocity directions and are instantaneous heading projections; the physical paths may subsequently smoothly curve. The intersection of the rays defines the geometric crossing point 𝒒𝑒c and crossing angle 𝛼𝑒. On each projected ray, the markers 𝑖−, 𝑖+ and 𝑗−, 𝑗+ delimit the segment over which simultaneous occupancy can reduce inter-agent separation below 𝑑safe. Together, these segments define the contested region. The current along-ray distances and speeds determine the projected entry and exit times and hence the occupancy intervals of the two agents. Conflict evidence depends on possible temporal overlap of these intervals and does not require equal arrival at 𝒒𝑒c . (B) The right-triangle constructions locate the upstream segment boundaries. The perpendicular clearance satisfies 𝑑safe = 𝑟𝑒c sin𝛼𝑒, giving 𝑟𝑒c = 𝑑safe/sin𝛼𝑒. Shallower crossing angles therefore produce longer contested segments and, for a fixed speed, longer projected occupancy intervals.

Fig. 8: Emergent traversal order and continuous adaptation in six-robot experiments. Six TurtleBot3 robots follow prescribed paths without inter-robot communication. Columns show decisions 𝑧𝑖 , measured speeds 𝑣𝑖 , and planar trajectories; colors identify robots. Positive and negative decisions raise and lower commanded speeds relative to nominal. (A to F) Two antipodal repetitions with initial positions differing by 0.8–2.5 cm per robot produce traversal orders 2 ≺ 4 ≺ 6 ≺ 3 ≺ 1 ≺ 5 (A to C) and 6 ≺ 3 ≺ 4 ≺ 1 ≺ 5 ≺ 2 (D to F). Robot 2 (orange) passes first in one trial and last in the other, illustrating how small motion asymmetries can be collectively amplified into distinct traversal orders without preassigned priorities. (G to I) In orthogonal crossings, robots 3 and 6 switch from yielding to speeding up at different stages of the encounter, illustrating continuous adaptation of their responses. (J to L) Mixed lanes show differentiated speed adjustments across multiple intersections. Across trials, decisions relax toward zero as robots complete their crossings. Gray dotted lines mark nominal speed 𝑣nom = 0.2 m/s. Trajectories darken with distance traveled; circles and crosses mark recorded starts and ends.

papers.selection_reason: Decentralized safe navigation controller for congested environments; fits robot navigation.
papers.title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
papers.tldr: NDD is a decentralized, event-based navigation controller that enables heterogeneous agents to safely and deadlock-free resolve conflicts in congested environments using only local sensing and motion adaptation.

papers.abstract: The last decades have seen a revolution in autonomous robotics. Deep learning approaches and their hardware implementations have made it possible to endow robots with extraordinary perceptual capabilities. In addition, they can also benefit from advances in Automated Planning, allowing them to autonomously solve complex tasks. However, on many occasions, the robot still acts without internalising and understanding the reasons behind a perception or an action, beyond an immediate response to a current state of the context. This gap results in limitations that affect its performance, reliability and trustworthiness. Deep learning alone cannot bridge this gap, because the reasons behind behaviour, when it emanates from a model in which the world is a black-box, are not accessible. What is really needed is an underlying architecture based on deeper reasoning. Among other issues, this architecture should enable the robot to generate explanations, allowing people to know why the robot is performing, or has performed, a certain action, or the reasons that may have caused a certain plan failure or perceptual anomaly. Furthermore, when these explanations arise from a cognitive process and are shared, and thus validated, with people, the robot should be able to incorporate these explanations into its knowledge base, and thus use this understanding to improve future behaviour. Our article looks at recent advances in the development of self-aware, self-evolving robots. These robots are designed to provide the necessary explanations to their human counterparts, thereby enhancing their functional capabilities, in the quest to gain their trust.
authors: Rebeca Marfil
Pablo Bustos
Antonio Bandera
bullets: Deep learning and planning enable capable autonomous robots but often do not expose the reasons behind perceptions, actions, failures, or anomalies.
Black-box models limit explainability, reliability, and human trust.
Causal, reasoning-based architectures are presented as a way to generate meaningful explanations.
Robots could incorporate explanations shared and validated with people into their knowledge base to improve future behavior.
The article reviews recent advances in self-aware, self-evolving robots, without reporting specific experimental results.

papers.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.
authors: Xingyi He
Zhiwen Qiu
Adhitya Polavaram
Yunhao Cao
Cory Fan
Julius Samwer
Saleh Kalantari
Kuan Fang
bullets: Learns behavior together with spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry and estimating hand motion from each video.
Aligns geometry and hand motion at a shared scale using a 3D hand-size prior.
Uses gated residual fusion to ground a pre-trained vision-language model in geometry, while predicting future geometry and wrist/finger actions.
Generates finger motion conditioned on predicted trajectories of both wrists.
Pre-training on reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over hand-motion-only pre-training; the method also reports gains on simulated and real-world bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an {appearance-driven paradigm}: multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. However, calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, \textbf{Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction}, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce \textbf{GeoForward}. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Multi-instance partial-label learning (MIPL) addresses inexact supervision in both the instance and label spaces, which can be applied to video classification. However, bag-level labels do not explicitly supervise the correspondence between candidate classes and temporal evidence. We propose {\ours}, which couples label disambiguation with temporal evidence allocation through a joint class--time assignment. Occupancy-regularized spherical matching associates contextualized video features while learning nonuniform temporal mass and discouraging excessive concentration. During training, candidate-restricted inference recomputes the assignment within the candidate label set. A dual-marginal KL projection then constructs a structured teacher that incorporates momentum-refined class beliefs while preserving the proposal's temporal occupancy. A single plan-level KL objective aligns the full-space predictor with this teacher. Our analysis characterizes when candidate re-solving differs from masking and shows that, under the stated construction, the joint objective decomposes into class-marginal and class-conditional temporal supervision. We construct VCMIPL benchmarks from Breakfast, DoTA, and FineAction using model-generated candidate labels and evaluate the method across four feature representations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that PIVOTMIPL outperforms existing MIPL algorithms in both effectiveness and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer reasoning from stronger teachers to frozen students through reusable prompts, but avoiding weight updates does not eliminate supervision. Without ground-truth answers, teacher solutions are unverified, and agreement with the teacher can reward shared mistakes. We introduce Knowledge-to-Prompt (K2P) for label-free knowledge distillation to prompts. K2P synthesizes reusable instructions from teacher solutions, refines them using paired teacher and student responses, and guides search and selection with answer agreement. It retains candidates that adaptive search may undervalue and selects on reserved questions. Deployment uses only the frozen student and selected prompt. Our theory separates generation and selection gaps and gives conditions under which agreement-guided construction yields accuracy guarantees despite imperfect teacher references. Across reasoning tasks and students, K2P outperforms label-free alternatives overall and remains competitive with supervised prompt optimization. Ablations and archive diagnostics assess the contributions of teacher solutions and refinement, while revealing the limits of agreement-guided selection.

papers.abstract: Physical parameter estimation from video aims to recover the parameters of a known family of governing dynamical equations from pixel observations. Existing identifiability theory for this setting has focused on linear time-invariant (LTI) second-order systems, leaving open what can be identified for nonlinear scalar dynamics. We develop an identifiability theory for nonlinear scalar second-order ODEs, organized by how their velocity dependence interacts with changes of the learned state coordinate. Under a shared non-collapsed state map and explicit same-state velocity-coverage conditions, we show that parameter identifiability depends on the ODE family: some parameters are uniquely identifiable, while in other families only invariant parameter combinations are identifiable or external physical calibration is required. For laws that are at most linear in velocity, compatibility forces affine coordinate alignment, yielding explicit parameter relations, invariants, and calibration conditions. This affine conclusion extends to broader finite velocity-feature families when coordinate curvature can be separated from the declared velocity dependence. For families admitting a squared-velocity term, nonlinear coordinate ambiguity can remain; a law-derived normalization instead enables affine comparison between canonical laws. Experiments on synthetic systems and real pendulum and free-fall videos support the predicted parameter relations, coverage effects, and calibration requirements.

papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation is widely adopted to accelerate sampling, and the resulting few-step models are broadly believed to match or even surpass their multi-step teachers in generation. However, standard evaluations such as GenEval2 typically draw only one sample per prompt, so improved scores may fail to reveal losses in distribution coverage. We therefore revisit whether distilled models truly match their teachers beyond single-draw performance using \textbf{pass@$\mathbf{k}$}, which measures the probability that at least one of $k$ independent samples satisfies a quality criterion. At $k{=}1$, pass@$k$ reduces to standard single-draw evaluation. As $k$ grows, the curve reveals whether additional draws find genuinely different successes or merely revisit the same modes, directly exposing how broadly a model covers the space of valid outputs. We first show that classifier-free guidance (CFG), whose quality--coverage tradeoff is well established, is the clearest case: higher guidance improves pass@$1$, but its advantage shrinks and reverses at larger $k$. Applying pass@$k$ to few-step distilled models, we find the same tradeoff splits along training objectives: distribution-matching objectives concentrate the student's output distribution, boosting early-hit rates while eroding large-budget coverage, whereas consistency and trajectory-based objectives better preserve the teacher's coverage even at large $k$. We further show that this tradeoff extends to few-step causal video generation. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked cost of diffusion distillation: across both image and video generation, the choice of training objective fundamentally determines whether a few-step model inherits its teacher's distribution coverage or trades it away for single-draw quality.
